Case study: Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement (Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Isle de Jean Charles (IDJC) Resettlement — Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, coastal Louisiana, United States of America.

**Hazard(s):** The primary hazards driving retreat are coastal land loss through erosion and subsidence, sea-level rise, chronic flooding of the sole access road (Island Road), and hurricane storm surge. These hazards interact in a compounding relationship: subsidence exacerbates flooding, storm surge accelerates erosion, and the loss of protective wetlands amplifies all impacts. They are driven by natural processes and substantially accelerated by anthropogenic factors — particularly levee construction that cut off Mississippi River sediment replenishment, and oil and gas extraction that carved canals through wetlands and caused additional subsidence and saltwater intrusion (Jessee 2022; Birch et al. 2024).

**Type of Retreat:** Community resettlement — a structured, voluntary relocation of the Island's permanent residents and displaced former residents to a newly developed inland site ("The New Isle"), approximately 40 miles north of Isle de Jean Charles, near Schriever in Terrebonne Parish. The program combines individual household assistance with community-scale master planning. It departs from standard HUD buyout models by allowing residents to retain ownership of their Island properties for cultural, recreational, and ceremonial use rather than requiring title transfer and demolition (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021).

**Scale:** As of the Phase I census (October 2016), 26 active residential units housed 37 households and 99 total residents on the Island (OCD 2017). The program materials identify up to 42 eligible households across current and displaced former residents across multiple option types (OCD 2020b). The New Isle spans approximately 515 acres — some documents reference 508 acres, reflecting the surveyed parcel configuration prior to final transaction — and is planned for approximately 120 residential lots plus commercial, community, and recreational uses (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021).

**Key Actors:** The primary implementing agency is the Louisiana Office of Community Development (OCD), Disaster Recovery Unit, which administers a $48.3 million federal grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), awarded through the National Disaster Resilience Competition (NDRC) (OCD 2017; OCD 2021). The Isle de Jean Charles Band of Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw (BCC) Tribal leadership and the Lowlander Center (a nonprofit founded in 2010 and incorporated in 2013) were foundational to the original resettlement vision and contributed to the successful NDRC grant application (Jessee 2022). The United Houma Nation (UHN) also has members on the Island. Key planning partners included CSRS (prime engineering consultant), Waggonner & Ball (architecture), OLIN (landscape architecture), the Center for Planning Excellence (community engagement), and others (OCD 2021). The Louisiana Land Trust (LLT) acquired the New Isle site on behalf of the state and serves as development partner (OCD 2021).

**Timeline:** The BCC Tribe began planning inland resettlement in approximately 2002 after the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers excluded the Island from regional hurricane protection (Jessee 2022; Simms et al. 2021). The Lowlander Center was founded in 2010 and incorporated in 2013 as a nonprofit collaborating with Tribal leaders (Jessee 2022). Louisiana received the HUD NDRC grant on January 25, 2016 (OCD 2017). Phase I (data gathering and engagement) ran June–November 2016. Phase II (site selection, acquisition, and master planning) ran December 2016–February 2019. The LLT purchased the Evergreen site on December 28, 2018; the master plan received unanimous Terrebonne Parish Planning Commission approval on February 21, 2019 (OCD 2021). The formal program launched on March 9, 2019 (OCD 2020b). Infrastructure construction began in May 2020. Houses were under construction in 2021, with move-in expected in 2022; as of the most recent sources, the resettlement remains ongoing in Phase III (OCD 2021; Soundararajan 2022).

**Key Outcomes:** The New Isle site was purchased, master-planned, and is under construction. Between the program's July 2017 launch and March 2019, 20 households moved into off-island rental housing through the Optional Relocation Assistance (ORA) program; the Phase 2 Report states "nearly 20 island families" were in ORA-funded rental units as of that report's coverage period (OCD 2021). By the later sources, 37 of 42 eligible households had applied to participate (Simms et al. 2021). The program introduced an innovative policy allowing residents to retain ownership of Island properties for non-residential use, explicitly described as "a significant departure from traditional HUD-funded relocation programs" (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021; Simms et al. 2021). However, the process was significantly marked by conflict between the state and BCC Tribal leadership. Jessee (2022) argues that the state systematically transformed the Tribal-driven resettlement — originally framed as cultural survival and self-determination — into a scalable "managed retreat" model, erasing Indigenous planning, weakening commitments to Tribal identity and governance, and failing to honor its partnership with the Tribe. Broader Louisiana coastal planning (the Coastal Master Plans and LA SAFE initiative) increasingly recognized managed retreat as a necessary adaptation strategy but — as Birch et al. (2024) document — produced only limited, largely non-scaled relocation action, without developing the social infrastructure or governance structures necessary to implement it systematically.

---

### Narrative Summary

Isle de Jean Charles is a narrow strip of land in the southernmost Louisiana bayou, once encompassing over 22,000 acres and home to a community of predominantly American Indian ancestry — primarily members of the Isle de Jean Charles Band of Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw (BCC) Tribe and the United Houma Nation. For over a century, the Island has been disappearing: subsidence from natural deltaic processes has combined with levee construction (which cut off sediment replenishment from the Mississippi River) and oil and gas extraction (which carved canals through wetlands, enabling saltwater intrusion and causing additional subsidence) to reduce the Island from over 22,000 acres to approximately 320 acres remaining (OCD 2020a; Jessee 2022). The Island's sole road floods regularly, cutting residents off from jobs, schools, and health care. After the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers excluded the Island from regional hurricane protection in 2002 based on a cost-benefit analysis that found protection extension unjustified, BCC Tribal leaders began planning an inland resettlement as "an act of cultural survival" — intending not simply to move houses, but to reunite a displaced Tribe, preserve heritage, and create a teaching and learning community (Jessee 2022).

In January 2016, HUD awarded Louisiana $48.3 million through the NDRC to implement the Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement — the first federally funded, community-scale, climate-driven resettlement in the United States. The state's OCD took the lead, conducting extensive community engagement over multiple phases, purchasing approximately 515 acres of farmland near Schriever, developing a detailed master plan in collaboration with residents, and beginning construction of "The New Isle." The program offered eligible households either a new home at The New Isle (Option A), homebuyer assistance toward an existing home elsewhere in Louisiana (Option D), or an improved lot at the new site (Option B). A key innovation was allowing residents to retain ownership of their Island properties for cultural and recreational use, after residents made clear that demolition and title transfer were non-negotiable conditions of their non-participation (Simms et al. 2021; OCD 2020a).

The process was, however, deeply contested. Jessee (2022) documents — through five years of ethnographic research alongside Tribal leaders — how the state progressively transformed the Tribal-driven resettlement into a more generic managed-retreat model: opening eligibility broadly under Fair Housing Act rationale, replacing a planned Tribal community center with a parish recreation center, prioritizing individual property transfers over communal land ownership, erasing pre-NDRC Tribal planning from public timelines, and reducing commitments to Tribal identity, sovereignty, and reunification. Tribal leaders described this as a "bait and switch," likening it to historical colonial land dispossession (Jessee 2022; Soundararajan 2022). Meanwhile, broader Louisiana coastal planning — analyzed by Birch et al. (2024) across the 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2023 Coastal Master Plans and the LA SAFE framework — increasingly recognized managed retreat as a necessary adaptation strategy, but consistently failed to develop the actionable governance structures, social infrastructure, or sustained funding mechanisms needed to implement relocation at scale. As of early 2022, house construction at The New Isle was nearing completion, but significant uncertainty remained about Tribal futures, community cohesion, and whether the process could serve as a replicable model for other communities.

---

Case study: Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement (Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Both **Proactive** and **Reactive** apply.

**Narrative:** The BCC Tribe's initial resettlement planning began proactively in approximately 2002, following the Army Corps of Engineers' decision to exclude Isle de Jean Charles from the Morganza to the Gulf hurricane protection system — an anticipatory response to foreseeable future risk before major irreversible loss of habitability occurred (Jessee 2022; Simms et al. 2021). Tribal leaders described resettlement as a planned act of "cultural survival" for a community that had already experienced decades of land loss. The Lowlander Center was founded in 2010 and incorporated in 2013 specifically to support this Tribal-driven proactive planning (Jessee 2022).

The receipt of federal funding was tied reactively to Hurricane Isaac (August 28, 2012), which served as the qualifying disaster for the HUD National Disaster Resilience Competition. The Isaac landfall date defines program eligibility cutoffs for displaced former residents, and the NDRC competition itself was structured as a post-disaster resilience investment (OCD 2020b; OCD 2021). The OCD Background & Overview notes explicitly: "This date marks Hurricane Isaac's landfall, which qualified the Resettlement for funding through HUD's National Disaster Resilience Competition" (OCD 2021, p. 5).

The broader Louisiana Coastal Master Plans analyzed by Birch et al. (2024) were largely reactive in framing — responding to the compounded disasters of Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (2005) and subsequent major storms — though they did increasingly advocate for proactive relocation planning over time.

**Coding:** Both **Reactive** and **Proactive** apply. The Tribal-driven planning was proactive (anticipatory risk reduction before catastrophic loss); the federal funding mechanism was reactive to a qualifying disaster event (Hurricane Isaac). The auditor's finding that the narrative should not overemphasize hurricane events as direct triggers for the project itself is accepted: hurricanes were contextual urgency factors, not the initiating trigger of the resettlement concept.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date of HUD grant award:** January 25, 2016 (OCD 2017)
- **Date of program launch:** March 9, 2019 (OCD 2020b)
- **Date of New Isle site purchase:** December 28, 2018 (OCD 2021)
- **Date of Planning Commission approval:** February 21, 2019 (OCD 2021)
- **Households affected:** 26 active residential units housed 37 households and 99 total residents as of the October 2016 Phase I census (OCD 2017). Program materials identify up to 42 eligible households across all option categories (OCD 2020b; Simms et al. 2021). By later sources, 37 of 42 eligible households had applied (Simms et al. 2021).
- **Population affected:** Approximately 99 residents on the Island at time of Phase I engagement (2016) (OCD 2017). The broader eligible community including off-Island displaced former residents is larger but not precisely quantified in the reviewed sources.
- **Total funding:** $48.3 million (precisely $48,379,249) in HUD Community Development Block Grant – National Disaster Resilience (CDBG-NDR) funds for the IDJC Resettlement, part of a larger $92.6 million Louisiana NDRC award that also funded the LA SAFE planning process ($39.75 million) (OCD 2021; OCD 2020b; Birch et al. 2024).

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards.**

**Narrative:** The retreat decision addresses several interacting hazards: chronic coastal land loss through erosion and subsidence, sea-level rise, regular flooding of Island Road (the sole access route), hurricane storm surge, and saltwater intrusion that kills vegetation and accelerates wetland loss. These operate concurrently and in a compounding relationship. Louisiana's 2017 Coastal Master Plan included Isle de Jean Charles on a list of eleven locations that would experience flooding "high enough to make daily life next to impossible, even without future hurricane damage" (Jessee 2022, citing Clipp et al. 2017). This is coded as **Multiple Hazards** because multiple distinct hazard types drive the retreat decision simultaneously and interact in a cascading manner.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** (primary), with significant anthropogenic exacerbation that is best characterized as accelerating natural processes rather than constituting an independent technological hazard.

**Narrative:** The primary hazard processes — coastal subsidence, sea-level rise, wetland erosion, and hurricane storm surge — are natural in origin. However, they are substantially exacerbated by anthropogenic activities: levee construction since the early eighteenth century (cutting off sediment replenishment), oil and gas extraction (over 220,000 wells drilled in Louisiana; thousands of kilometers of canals cut through wetlands, enabling saltwater intrusion and subsidence), and the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill (Jessee 2022; Soundararajan 2022). These factors are described in sources as "development-induced disaster" (Jessee 2022).

The codebook defines **Technological Hazard** as "related to the built environment and human technologies (industrial accident, dam collapse, oil spill, etc.)" and **Natural Hazard** as natural processes such as earthquakes. The anthropogenic factors here are better characterized as exacerbating natural hazard processes rather than constituting an independent technological hazard event. Accordingly, the primary and most accurate coding is **Natural Hazard**, with narrative note of the substantial anthropogenic exacerbation. The auditor's correction on this point is accepted: overstating Technological Hazard as equally applicable was not warranted by the codebook definitions or source evidence.

**Coding:** **Natural Hazard** (primary), with explanatory note of anthropogenic exacerbation throughout the narrative.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Coastal Flooding/Erosion** (primary); **Hurricane** (secondary); **Land Subsidence** (contributing).

**Narrative:** The dominant hazard framing throughout all sources is coastal land loss through erosion and sea-level rise, classified here as **Coastal Flooding/Erosion**. The Island is surrounded by saltwater; its protective wetlands have largely disappeared; and storm surge and tidal flooding regularly inundate Island Road. The OCD documents state: "The sole connecting road to the mainland — Island Road, built in 1953 — is often impassable due to high winds, tides, sea level rise or storm surge" (OCD 2020a). **Hurricane** events are consistently cited as triggers of displacement and amplifiers of ongoing land loss — Katrina (2005), Gustav and Ike (2008), Isaac (2012), and Ida (2021) are all referenced (Jessee 2022; Soundararajan 2022; Birch et al. 2024). **Land Subsidence** is explicitly identified as a contributing process, driven by both natural deltaic dynamics and oil and gas extraction (Jessee 2022). Riverine or pluvial flooding is not the primary driver and is not separately coded.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project?

**Answer:** **Entire community** and **Individual homes.**

**Narrative:** The resettlement is designed as a community-scale relocation — the entire permanent residential population of Isle de Jean Charles is the intended beneficiary, and the program involves the co-design and construction of a new settlement ("The New Isle") as a unified community development of approximately 120 lots (OCD 2021). This is not a neighborhood within a larger municipality but rather an entire small community (fewer than 100 people at time of program launch). At the same time, the program also offers individual households the option to receive homebuyer assistance toward purchasing an existing home elsewhere in Louisiana outside the 100-year floodplain (Option D), operating at the individual household level. The community scale is the primary design intent; individual assistance is an option for those who prefer not to join the new community. Both **Entire community** and **Individual homes** apply.

---

### Who or what was retreated?

**Answer:** **Individuals** and **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (functioning as a community).

**Narrative:** The primary beneficiaries are individual households and families — permanent residents and eligible displaced former residents of Isle de Jean Charles. However, the retreat is explicitly designed to maintain and reconstruct community cohesion: one of the stated goals is to "create an opportunity for past island residents to rejoin the community in its new location" and to co-design the new community with current and former residents (OCD 2021). The design process sought to replicate Island social patterns, lot spacing, density, and cultural identity at The New Isle. Thus, the retreat operates at both the individual household level and the community/group level. **Individuals** and **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (or communities) both apply. No retreat of critical infrastructure, hazard protection structures, or industrial assets is documented in the reviewed sources.

---

Case study: Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement (Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project?

**Answer:** **Community buyout/retreat** (primary), with elements of **Individual buyout/retreat** (Option D) and a note that this is a modified community resettlement model — participation is not contingent upon a standard buyout of Island property.

**Narrative:** The IDJC Resettlement is designed as a collective community relocation — a coordinated, master-planned resettlement of an entire community to a purpose-built new settlement. This aligns with the codebook definition of **Community buyout/retreat**: "collective relocation of a neighborhood or settlement through coordinated planning and community engagement." The program also includes **Individual buyout/retreat** elements through Option D, which provides homebuyer assistance to individual households purchasing existing homes in Louisiana outside the new community.

Importantly, the program explicitly departs from the standard buyout model: "participation in the resettlement is not contingent upon a buyout. In other words, no one must give up their island home or property to receive assistance through the resettlement" (OCD 2021, p. 46). This is a material program innovation — Island property is not purchased by the state, but instead restricted in use through a Homeowner Assistance Agreement. The primary coding remains **Community buyout/retreat** with the explicit qualification that this is a modified resettlement model without mandatory property purchase, and with **Individual buyout/retreat** as a secondary element via Option D.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Multiple legal issues are documented: **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Compliance & enforcement**, **Legal authority over retreat**, and **Other** (Fair Housing Act constraints; federal tribal recognition issues).

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** HUD's CDBG-NDR regulations govern the entire program, including cost reasonableness requirements (2 CFR 200.403, 200.404) and the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The National Environmental Policy Act required environmental review before site acquisition. HUD regulations generally require vacated land to become permanent open space — a requirement the program innovatively modified to allow residents to retain ownership and cultural use of Island properties (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021).

- **Home acquisition / Land acquisition:** The LLT acquired the 515-acre Evergreen site on behalf of the state (purchase price $11.7 million, option entered March 5, 2018, closed December 28, 2018) (OCD 2021). Program Option D facilitates individual home acquisition by participants within Louisiana. Complex land tenure on the Island — where Apache Corporation holds title to extensive holdings and many residents lease rather than own their land — is flagged as a complicating factor (Jessee 2022; OCD 2017).

- **Title(s) transfer:** Option A participants receive title to a new home in The New Isle through a forgivable mortgage (100% of appraised value, forgiven at 20% per year over five years with primary residency compliance) (OCD 2020b; OCD 2021). Homeowner Assistance Agreements govern Island property, restricting residential use and most substantial repairs without requiring full title transfer to the state (OCD 2020a; OCD 2020b).

- **Compliance & enforcement:** Participants must maintain homestead exemption, required insurance, and primary residency for five years under forgivable mortgage terms or face default; violation can trigger foreclosure on the new community home (OCD 2020b).

- **Legal authority over retreat:** The lack of federal recognition of both the BCC Tribe and the United Houma Nation created significant constraints. Federally unrecognized tribes cannot directly access FEMA or Bureau of Indian Affairs resources, making reliance on state-administered federal block grants necessary (Soundararajan 2022). State officials cited the Fair Housing Act as precluding Tribe-exclusive programming; Tribal leaders disputed these legal interpretations and pointed to precedent of Fair Housing Act waivers in other contexts (Jessee 2022; OCD 2020a).

- **Other:** The Fair Housing Act was invoked by OCD to open program eligibility to all Island residents regardless of tribal affiliation, rejecting the Tribe's request for a Tribe-exclusive program (OCD 2020a; Jessee 2022). This is a deeply contested legal interpretation documented in detail by Jessee (2022). Inheritance laws and complex multi-sibling land ownership on the Island were flagged in the Phase I report as complicating eligibility verification (OCD 2017).

**Note on Land Rezoning:** The auditor correctly identified that Terrebonne Parish Planning Commission approval of the master plan (February 21, 2019) is more accurately characterized as a subdivision/site plan approval than a zoning reclassification. Accordingly, **Land rezoning** is not coded; the Planning Commission approval is captured under Relevant regulations/acts and local permitting requirements.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Federal only** for the resettlement program itself.

**Narrative:** The primary and effectively sole funding source for the IDJC Resettlement is a $48,379,249 HUD CDBG-NDR award (OCD 2021). The State of Louisiana (OCD) administered the grant, contributing state administrative capacity but not independently funding the resettlement. The Louisiana Housing Corporation administered the ORA program within the broader state structure. The Lowlander Center (nonprofit) supported early Tribal planning and contributed to the NDRC application, but was not a program funder. The Rockefeller Foundation co-sponsored the NDRC competition design at a national level, not as a project-level funder. BP Oil Spill settlement funds ($3 million via the Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group) funded fishing pier improvements on Island Road — a distinct project from the resettlement itself (Jessee 2022; Birch et al. 2024).

**Coding:** **Federal only** for the resettlement program. The auditor's correction is accepted: coding "Multiple funders" for the resettlement project itself was not warranted — the state is an administrator, not an independent funder, and other entities funded ancillary activities rather than the resettlement program. The broader NDRC ecosystem (LA SAFE + IDJC together) involved $92.6 million in federal funds.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **New housing for BO recipients** and **Livelihoods supports.**

**Narrative:** The master plan for The New Isle explicitly incorporates commercial and retail development to generate revenue and support economic sustainability. A market analysis identified revenue-generating opportunities including assisted living, light manufacturing, regional retail, local retail, plant nurseries, a farmers' market, RV/boat storage, and a solar farm, estimating potential for over $400,000 in annual revenue using a ground lease structure (OCD 2021). OCD documents explicitly state a goal to "ensure that the community is economically sustainable in its new location" (OCD 2021). The program also includes workforce development and job training programs as Phase III activities (OCD 2021).

New homes provided to eligible Option A participants contribute to the Terrebonne Parish property tax base at the receiving location. New homes are assessed at over $250,000 with estimated annual property taxes of approximately $1,700 after homestead exemption (OCD 2021).

**Redevelopment of retreat lands** is not coded for the Island itself: the stated plan is to "return the island's residential parcels to nature" through hazardous waste removal, utility disconnection, and structure removal — leaving the Island "in a state of rest" (OCD 2021). This is the opposite of revenue-generating redevelopment, though Jessee (2022) and Soundararajan (2022) document a governance failure in which a local development firm sought to sell recreational lots on the Island, prompting public objection from Chief Naquin. The auditor's correction to remove "Redevelopment of retreat lands" from Island-side coding is accepted.

**Coding:** **New housing for BO recipients** and **Livelihoods supports**; commercial development at the new site may qualify under a broader reading of tax base maintenance but is primarily coded as livelihoods support.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Free supports and services** (primary); **Other** (Island property retention policy; forgivable mortgage as full grant mechanism).

**Narrative:** The IDJC Resettlement does not provide cash compensation for the Island property left behind. CDBG regulations explicitly list "compensation payments" as an ineligible activity (OCD 2020b). Instead, the program provides:

- **Free supports and services (primary):** Eligible Option A households receive a new home built at The New Isle at no cost, with all closing costs covered and moving expenses covered at flat rates by household size (OCD 2020b). This constitutes non-monetary assistance — house provision, not purchase price compensation.

- **Other — forgivable mortgage as effective grant:** Participants receive a forgivable mortgage valued at 100% of the new property's appraised value (Option A) or the amount of assistance awarded (Option D, up to $200,000), forgiven at 20% per year over five years with primary residency compliance — effectively a full grant of the new home if requirements are met (OCD 2020b; OCD 2021). Under Option D, homebuyer assistance up to $200,000 is provided toward purchasing an existing home in Louisiana.

- **Other — innovative Island property retention:** Rather than requiring residents to sell or abandon Island properties (as in standard buyout programs), participants may retain ownership and cultural/recreational use of Island properties. This is described as "a marked departure from traditional HUD-funded relocation programs" (OCD 2020a; OCD 2021; Simms et al. 2021) and was a direct response to residents' non-negotiable insistence on keeping their ancestral land.

The auditor's correction is accepted: the forgivable mortgage is the core financial structure of the grant mechanism, not an "additional incentive, bonus, or top-up" in the usual sense. It is more accurately coded as **Free supports and services** (the new home itself) and **Other** (the forgivable mortgage structure and Island property retention policy). **Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups** is not applied as a primary code.

---

Case study: Isle de Jean Charles Resettlement (Isle de Jean Charles, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Pre-retreat planning**, **Immediate risks: 1–5 years**, **Anticipated future risks: 10–100 years**, and **Post-retreat follow-up.**

**Narrative:** The program involves extensive pre-retreat planning (Phases I and II, 2016–2019) including data gathering, site selection, master planning, environmental review, and policy development. The risks driving the retreat are both immediate (Island Road regularly floods, blocking access to work, school, and emergency services; the road was described as approaching impassability) and long-term (sea-level rise and land loss projections over decades). Louisiana's Coastal Master Plans and LA SAFE framework explicitly model 50-year and 100-year flood scenarios; the 2017 Coastal Master Plan included the Island among eleven locations where flooding would make daily life impossible (Jessee 2022; Birch et al. 2024). The program anticipates ongoing land loss that will eventually render the Island uninhabitable.

Post-retreat follow-up is built into program structure through ongoing case management (Franklin & Associates; Start Corporation), the ORA transitional housing program, five-year occupancy monitoring and forgivable mortgage compliance, and intended community governance via a nonprofit and homeowners' association (OCD 2021). The Phase 2 Report notes that "The New Isle is intended to allow for additional development to occur in subsequent phases over a longer period of time," indicating multi-generational planning intent (OCD 2021).

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Top-down**, **Bottom-up/Participatory/collaborative** (contested in implementation), **Multi-sectoral**, **Multi-stage retreat**, **Degree of transparency**, **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions**, **Adaptive management**.

**Narrative:**

- **Top-down:** OCD led the planning process and held final decision-making authority. HUD set the regulatory framework. The state administered funding and made final policy determinations. Jessee (2022) documents how the state progressively centralized control despite Tribal leadership's prior ownership of the resettlement vision, and how state planners characterized their goal as creating a "scalable and replicable model" rather than honoring Tribal-specific aims.

- **Bottom-up / Participatory/collaborative:** Multiple community meetings (at least six in Phase II), household interviews, three design charrettes, a nine-member Steering Committee (including five Island residents and representatives from BCC and UHN), and weekly Island visits were conducted (OCD 2021; Simms et al. 2021). Residents shaped site selection, house design, lot spacing, street naming, and the community name. However, Jessee (2022) argues the state used community engagement tactically while progressively marginalizing Tribal authority; Birch et al. (2024) note that LA SAFE "stopped short of suggesting shared authority where community members led." The participatory elements are documented and real, but genuinely contested in their depth and authenticity.

- **Multi-sectoral:** The planning team included engineers, architects, landscape planners, economists, social scientists, legal counsel, community engagement specialists, geotechnical experts, environmental assessors, and American Indian advisors (OCD 2021).

- **Multi-stage retreat:** The program proceeds in four phases (Data Gathering; Site Selection/Master Planning; Development/Construction; Living in New Community). The ORA transitional housing program accommodated residents who moved in advance of house completion.

- **Degree of transparency:** Stated commitment to transparency; land use data made publicly available online; policy documents and program options published (OCD 2017; OCD 2021). However, Tribal leaders and researchers documented instances of insufficient transparency — particularly around the Data Gathering report (which Tribal leaders characterized as a "divide and conquer" strategy), grant amendments, and the timeline of land acquisition (Jessee 2022; Soundararajan 2022).

- **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** Terrebonne Parish (planning approval, road maintenance), Louisiana Housing Corporation (ORA program), LLT (land acquisition), HUD (federal oversight), and multiple state agencies. Cross-agency coordination was noted as a persistent challenge — for example, CPRA spent $3 million improving Island Road while OCD was conducting the resettlement, suggesting different agencies working at cross-purposes (Birch et al. 2024; Jessee 2022).

- **Adaptive management:** Program policies were iteratively revised through six versions of the Program Policies document, and the Island property mortgage requirement was modified following community advocacy — originally proposed as a 40-year mortgage, ultimately replaced with the Homeowner Assistance Agreement (Jessee 2022; OCD 2020b).

- **Cost-benefit analysis (CBA):** CBA is **not** coded as a planning element for the IDJC resettlement project itself. The Phase 2 Report explicitly states: "Given the complex nature of resettlement, this process cannot be evaluated by a simple cost-benefit analysis

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Case Name and Location

**El Caño Martín Peña (CMP) — Eight Communities Aledañas al Caño Martín Peña Special Planning District**
San Juan, Puerto Rico — a U.S. territory with a distinct colonial governance context (classified as Global North by project codebook definition, though Puerto Rico's territorial and colonial status introduces important caveats)

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Hazard(s)

Primary hazard: **riverine/tidal flooding**, driven by the progressive narrowing and blockage of a 3.75-mile tidal channel (El Caño Martín Peña) connecting the San José Lagoon to the San Juan Bay Estuary. The channel was severely obstructed by decades of informal landfill (debris, trash, wetland conversion), leading to chronic flooding that historically affected approximately 70% of the area [Source 1]. Secondary hazard: **hurricane events**, including the 1928 San Felipe and 1932 San Ciprián hurricanes (which originally accelerated migration into the area) and Hurricanes Irma and María (September 2017), after which 1,200 homes lost their roofs and 100 homes were destroyed within the eight communities [Source 1].

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Type of Retreat

A **community-driven, participatory managed retreat** embedded within a broader ecosystem restoration and community redevelopment initiative. The retreat component requires approximately 1,000 families who live along the canal right-of-way to relocate to allow for channel widening and dredging. Households are offered a choice between relocating within the eight communities (within the CLT footprint) or accepting a housing relocation voucher to move elsewhere. It is important to note that relocation is not purely voluntary in the conventional sense: households along the right-of-way *must* move for dredging to proceed; what is choice-based is the *destination and form* of their new housing, not whether relocation occurs at all [Source 1, Source 2]. The retreat is explicitly framed as inseparable from environmental restoration, flood mitigation, and long-term community resilience. It is not a standalone buyout program.

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Timeline

- **1928, 1932**: San Felipe and San Ciprián hurricanes accelerate rural-to-urban migration; people settle along the tidal channel wetlands [Source 1].
- **1930s–1950s**: Informal settlement of wetlands; rapid environmental degradation; mangrove swamps progressively filled in [Source 1].
- **1940s–1960s**: Operation Bootstrap industrialization; urban renewal programs displace thousands, some settling near the Caño [Source 1].
- **2001**: City of San Juan partners with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on canal dredging proposal; residents fear displacement and begin to organize [Source 1].
- **2002**: Residents begin organized coalition meetings; San Juan designates the eight communities as a Special Planning District [Source 1].
- **2004**: Eight communities form the G8 Coalition; Puerto Rico Law 489 enacted, creating ENLACE as a public corporation; CLT established; Caño Martín Peña Comprehensive Infrastructure Master Plan (CIMP) developed [Source 1, Source 2].
- **2016**: UN World Habitat Award received by the CLT/G8/ENLACE model [Source 1].
- **2017**: Hurricanes Irma and María devastate Puerto Rico; 1,200 homes lost roofs and 100 homes destroyed in CMP; ENLACE identified opportunity to accelerate project but encountered CDBG-DR action plan constraints that, by not allowing new infrastructure or construction/rehabilitation of housing within the floodplain, promoted displacement rather than community cohesion [Source 1, Source 2]; approximately 600 families had already relocated by this point [Source 2].
- **2022**: $163 million assigned to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for dredging; $46 million in CDBG-MIT provided by HUD for relocation [Source 1].
- **2023**: Dredging work begins; updated CIMP issued (OLIN, 2023) [Source 1].
- **Current stage**: **Ongoing** — dredging and relocation underway; CLT continues to operate; future land use planning for vacated corridor areas in progress.

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Key Outcomes

- **Achieved**: Collective tenure regularized for approximately 2,000 low-income families through the CLT; flooding incidence reduced through initial infrastructure works (prior to full dredging, flooding historically affected ~70% of the area); approximately 600 families successfully relocated with choice as of 2017; community governance and social cohesion preserved; international recognition (2016 UN World Habitat Award); legal institutionalization of community governance through Law 489 [Sources 1, 2].
- **In progress**: Full-scale dredging and canal restoration; relocation of remaining families from right-of-way; ongoing CLT governance [Source 1].
- **Unresolved/contested**: Tensions between CDBG-DR action plan restrictions (which, by prohibiting reconstruction or rehabilitation within the floodplain, promoted displacement rather than on-site community cohesion) and ENLACE's goals [Source 2]; population decline from approximately 15,693–18,103 to approximately 10,997, linked by community leaders to governmental discrimination and stigmatization, though causal attribution is uncertain [Source 1].

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: Narrative Summary

El Caño Martín Peña is a 3.75-mile tidal channel running through the heart of San Juan, Puerto Rico, surrounded by eight densely populated informal neighborhoods that developed from the 1930s onward as rural migrants — many displaced by the 1928 and 1932 hurricanes and by government urban renewal programs — settled in the wetlands. Over decades, the canal became severely degraded: mangrove swamps approximately 250 feet wide were progressively filled in, narrowing the channel dramatically, and communities were chronically flooded (historically affecting about 70% of the area), lacked basic sewage and water infrastructure, and faced persistent threats of top-down displacement given the high real estate value of their land. With median household incomes of $17,817 and over 61% of residents living below the poverty line, these communities were among Puerto Rico's most economically marginalized [Source 1].

In 2001, when the City of San Juan and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced plans to dredge the canal, residents feared forced removal. Rather than accepting displacement, the eight communities organized. By 2004, they had formed the G8 Coalition and successfully lobbied the Puerto Rican government to pass Law 489, creating Proyecto ENLACE — a public corporation tasked with developing and implementing a comprehensive community-driven plan for the canal and surrounding neighborhoods. Simultaneously, the communities established the Fideicomiso de la Tierra (Community Land Trust), a private non-profit organization that secured collective tenure for approximately 2,000 families and protected residents from speculative displacement [Sources 1, 2]. The CLT and ENLACE together produced a Comprehensive Development and Land Use Plan, developed through a sustained participatory process involving over 700 community engagement activities, that integrated dredging, flood mitigation, housing stabilization, social services, and managed retreat into a single cohesive vision [Source 2].

The managed retreat component requires approximately 1,000 families to relocate to allow for canal widening and dredging. This is choice-based within a constrained setting: households along the right-of-way are required to move, but they select housing within the CLT footprint (preserving community membership and social networks) or accept a relocation voucher [Source 1]. As relocated resident Vicky Castro described: "They give you the option to choose, they don't choose for you, you make your own decisions" [Source 2]. The relocation process is explained clearly and repeatedly at community meetings; ENLACE provides mental health services and comprehensive support throughout [Source 2]. One constraint prompting relocation is that the Government of Puerto Rico does not allow elevation of homes in the floodplain [Source 1]. By 2017, approximately 600 families had already relocated [Source 2]. Funded by $46 million in CDBG-MIT from HUD and $163 million assigned to the Army Corps for dredging, construction began in 2023. The case has received international recognition, including the 2016 UN World Habitat Award, as an example of participatory, equity-driven managed retreat that achieves resilience goals without reproducing the top-down displacement historically imposed on Puerto Rico's informal communities. However, post-Hurricane María complications — including CDBG-DR action plan restrictions that, by prohibiting reconstruction or rehabilitation within the floodplain, promoted displacement rather than community cohesion — have created tensions between federal recovery frameworks and ENLACE's vision [Source 2].

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: GENERAL INFORMATION

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Both **Proactive** and **Reactive** elements are present. The predominant long-term framing is proactive; reactive triggers reinforced and accelerated implementation.

**Narrative:** The managed retreat initiative at CMP originated as a proactive response to long-standing chronic flooding, environmental degradation, and displacement risk rather than as a direct post-disaster response. Residents began organizing in 2002 and formalized ENLACE and the CLT in 2004 — well before any single catastrophic disaster triggered the process [Source 1]. The community-driven process has been more than 20 years in the making, since residents understood they needed to organize and develop a collective plan [Source 1].

However, reactive triggers have reinforced and accelerated the initiative at multiple points. Hurricanes Irma and María (2017) devastated 1,200 homes and destroyed 100 others within the CMP communities, prompting federal funding flows ($46 million CDBG-MIT from HUD; $163 million to the Army Corps for dredging) that enabled the implementation phase beginning in earnest in 2022–2023 [Source 1]. ENLACE initially saw Hurricane María as an opportunity to catalyse its project, though CDBG-DR action plan constraints complicated this [Source 2]. The 1928 and 1932 hurricanes can be understood as the original reactive historical triggers that accelerated settlement into the canal area in the first place [Source 1].

**Coding decision:** Both **Proactive** and **Reactive** are coded. The long-term community organization and planning from 2002 onward is clearly proactive. Reactive elements (post-María federal funding, post-disaster urgency shaping funding timelines) shaped the implementation phase.

- **Households affected**: Approximately 1,000 families required to relocate for the dredging right-of-way; approximately 2,000 families with collective clear title under the CLT (around 16.51% of households); 6,946 total housing units in the eight communities; owners: 2,619; renters: approximately 2,563 [Source 1].
- **Population affected**: Approximately 10,997 current residents; formerly estimated at approximately 15,693–18,103 [Source 1].
- **Total funding**:

  - $163 million assigned to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (2022) for dredging [Source 1]
  - These are the two figures most clearly attributed to CMP specifically in the reviewed sources.
  - Broader CDBG-DR funding (Program R3: $3,025,570,050 island-wide) represents the wider Puerto Rico recovery context; the portion applicable specifically to CMP is not quantified in the reviewed sources [Source 3].
  - No single consolidated total funding figure for the CMP retreat specifically is provided in the reviewed sources.

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards**

**Narrative:** The retreat decision process addresses multiple, interrelated hazards. The primary hazard is chronic **riverine/tidal flooding** caused by the blockage and narrowing of the canal, which historically affected approximately 70% of the area [Source 1]. Compounding this are recurrent **hurricane events** — including the 1928 San Felipe hurricane, 1932 San Ciprián hurricane, and Hurricanes Irma and María (2017) — which represent catastrophic hazard exposure [Source 1, Source 2]. The canal area also suffers from environmental contamination (raw sewage, water pollution) resulting from inadequate infrastructure [Source 1]. The combination of chronic flooding from canal obstruction and episodic hurricane damage creates compound hazard exposure. The broader Puerto Rico context additionally involves landslide hazard zones (estimated 49% of Puerto Ricans live in such zones [Source 2]), though this is not a primary driver of the CMP retreat specifically.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** (with significant anthropogenic degradation compounding the natural hazard)

**Narrative:** Flooding at CMP originates from the natural tidal channel dynamics and storm events (natural hazards), substantially compounded by decades of human-induced environmental degradation — landfill into wetlands, debris accumulation, poor sewage infrastructure — that narrowed the channel and worsened flooding. Hurricanes are natural hazards. Sources acknowledge that climate change is intensifying hurricane impacts [Source 4], and the broader Puerto Rico recovery framework incorporates climate resilience principles [Source 3]. No technological hazard (industrial accident, dam collapse) origin is identified. The primary classification is **Natural Hazard**; the anthropogenic canal degradation represents land management failure that worsened the natural hazard rather than constituting a technological hazard in the codebook sense.

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:**
- ✅ **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding** — primary hazard; tidal channel flooding, canal blockage-induced flooding affecting historically ~70% of area [Source 1]
- ✅ **Hurricane** — Irma and María (2017); 1928 San Felipe; 1932 San Ciprián; explicitly discussed throughout [Sources 1, 2]
- ✅ **Coastal Flooding/Erosion** — the tidal channel connects the San José Lagoon to the San Juan Bay Estuary; tidal and estuarine dynamics are integral to the canal system [Source 1, Source 2]
- ❌ **Landslide/Debris Flow** — mentioned as Puerto Rico-wide context (49% of Puerto Ricans in landslide hazard zones [Source 2]) but not a primary driver of the CMP retreat specifically; not coded as a primary hazard here
- All other hazard types (Wildfire, Volcano, Land Subsidence, Lake Flooding/Erosion, Earthquake, Tsunami): no evidence in reviewed sources

**Narrative:** Riverine/tidal flooding is the central hazard driving both the canal dredging project and the managed retreat. Hurricane events are explicitly discussed as exacerbating hazards and as triggers for federal funding. The coastal/tidal estuary character of the channel makes coastal flooding dynamics relevant. Landslides are mentioned only as broader Puerto Rico context [Source 2].

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project?

**Answer:** **Neighbourhood** / **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (eight informal neighbourhoods constituting the Martín Peña Special Planning District)

**Narrative:** The retreat operates at the scale of eight specific neighbourhoods forming the Martín Peña Special Planning District. It is not an individual-parcel buyout program (though individual families make choice-based decisions) but rather a community-scale, integrated plan affecting the entire district. The 1,000 families required to relocate are concentrated in a defined geographic right-of-way zone within the district. The CLT and ENLACE operate at the scale of all eight communities [Sources 1, 2]. This is neither purely individual-home scale nor city-wide, but rather a defined neighbourhood cluster approaching community scale.

---

### Who or what was retreated?

**Answer:** **Individuals**, **Groups/Neighbourhoods**

**Narrative:** The retreat involves individual families making choice-based decisions about relocation, but within a collective governance framework. The approximately 1,000 families required to relocate are part of eight interconnected informal neighbourhoods, and the CLT structure is designed to preserve social networks and community ties even as individual households move. The relocation process explicitly aims to maintain community cohesion rather than scatter households [Sources 1, 2]. Primary subjects of retreat are residential households. Critical infrastructure (canal infrastructure, sewage systems) is also being realigned as part of the broader project.

Case study: San Juan Managed Retreat (San Juan, Puerto Rico, USA)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project?

**Answer:** **Community buyout/retreat** (primary); **Other acquisition tools** (CLT collective land tenure model); elements of **Leasebacks, easements and buffers** (CLT land management)

**Narrative:** The CMP retreat is fundamentally a community-scale retreat embedded within a comprehensive community development plan — not an individual-parcel buyout program. Families make individual choice-based decisions, but within a collective governance framework (ENLACE, G8, CLT) that ensures decisions serve community-wide goals. The CLT model — which secures collective tenure for approximately 2,000 families and protects residents from speculative displacement [Source 1] — functions as an innovative "other acquisition tool" beyond conventional buyouts: it creates permanent affordable collective ownership rather than simply transferring properties to a public body. Source 1 explicitly states the CLT "decoupled land ownership from property value" [Source 1, Table 1], and Source 2 describes it as "a model for collective land ownership where each family has individual rights over their plot" [Source 2]. Residents relocating within the CLT footprint receive housing within this collectively owned structure. Those relocating outside receive housing vouchers. The physical canal corridor being vacated represents the primary retreat footprint.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Legal authority over retreat**, **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Land rezoning**, **Retreat land development**, **Compliance & enforcement**, **Other** (informal tenure regularization as legal innovation)

**Narrative:**

- **Legal authority over retreat**: Proyecto ENLACE was created by Puerto Rico Law 489 (2004), giving it explicit legal authority to manage the comprehensive plan, relocation, and environmental restoration within the Special Planning District [Source 1, Source 2]. Puerto Rico Act 32 (2009) provided additional legal framework; Puerto Rico Act No. 104 (2013) is also cited as part of ENLACE's mandate [Source 2].

- **Relevant regulations/acts**: Puerto Rico Law 489 (2004); Puerto Rico Act 32 (2009); Puerto Rico Act No. 104 (2013); CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT federal program requirements; HUD regulations; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers project authorization. ENLACE developed its own internal regulatory framework — the *Reglamento para la Adquisición y Disposición de Bienes Inmuebles y el Realojo de Ocupantes* — establishing "safe, decent and sanitary" criteria for replacement housing and step-by-step relocation procedures [Source 2]. Broader Puerto Rico CDBG-DR Action Plan rules constrained reconstruction in flood-prone areas, shaping the wider relocation context: "[a]s most of the District is currently within the floodplain, by not allowing for new infrastructure and the construction and rehabilitation of housing, the Action Plan promotes displacement, rather than community cohesion and on site recovery" [Source 2, quoting ENLACE].

- **Land acquisition**: ENLACE acquires properties along the dredging right-of-way; $46 million CDBG-MIT funds are used for relocation, which includes property acquisition [Source 1].

- **Home acquisition**: The ENLACE relocation program involves acquisition of homes in the right-of-way. The broader Program R3 framework provides government acquisition of flood-zone properties in exchange for relocation assistance [Source 3], though Program R3 is a separate island-wide program.

- **Title(s) transfer**: A critical legal innovation at CMP was the regularization of informal tenure. Before the CLT, most residents lacked clear title [Source 1]. The CLT established collective tenure for approximately 2,000 families [Source 1]. Collective title transfer to the CLT as a legal entity was a defining legal achievement of the project.

- **Land rezoning**: San Juan designated the eight communities as a Special Planning District in 2002, enabling the comprehensive plan [Source 1]. Post-retreat lands (the canal corridor) are managed under specific use designations [Sources 1, 2].

- **Retreat land development**: A construction moratorium is posted at the dredging right-of-way — signage prohibiting construction in acquired areas is visible in Source 1, Figure 1, indicating the planned future width of the channel [Source 1]. Vacated properties are to become the widened canal corridor.

- **Compliance & enforcement**: One constraint prompting relocation is that the Government of Puerto Rico does not allow elevation of homes in the floodplain, limiting mitigation-in-place options [Source 1]. Broader Puerto Rico recovery rules constrained reconstruction in flood-prone areas [Source 2, Source 3].

- **Other (informal tenure regularization)**: The legal challenge of providing collective title to households that originally occupied land informally — without legal title — was a defining constraint and achievement of the CLT model [Sources 1, 2]. This constitutes a distinct legal "other" category beyond standard title transfer.

- **Litigation**: Source 2 references an ACLU complaint regarding forced removals at Villas del Sol (a different Puerto Rico community, not CMP directly) and community protests regarding government discrimination in the broader context [Source 2]. No specific litigation directly against the CMP ENLACE retreat process is documented in the reviewed sources.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Multiple funders** — specifically **Federal** (primary) and **Provincial/State** (Puerto Rico government as intermediary/administrator); **NGOs** (CLT as non-profit institution)

**Narrative:**
- **Federal (primary)**: $46 million in CDBG-MIT (HUD) for relocation; $163 million assigned to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (2022) for dredging [Source 1]. Broader CDBG-DR funding (Program R3, $3,025,570,050 island-wide) through HUD provides the wider recovery context [Source 3].
- **Provincial/State**: Puerto Rico Department of Housing administers CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT funds as the official recipient; ENLACE is a Puerto Rico public corporation. The Puerto Rico government functions primarily as a federal fund sub-recipient and administrator rather than an independent funding source in this context.
- **NGOs**: The CLT as a community land trust institution (described in Source 2 as "a private, non-profit organization") mobilizes non-governmental resources and manages collective assets. The Rockefeller Foundation, Open Society Foundations, and Ford Foundation supported the ReImagina Puerto Rico planning initiative — a non-governmental context mentioned in Source 3 — though this is not directly part of CMP funding.
- **Insurance**: Not documented as a funding source for the CMP retreat. Source 3 notes that only 5,675 Puerto Rican property owners had flood insurance at the time of Hurricane María [Source 3], highlighting the general absence of insurance as a recovery mechanism.
- **Individual**: Not applicable as a primary mechanism; households receive assistance rather than self-funding.
- **Local/Municipal**: No independent municipal funding is documented; the City of San Juan designated the Special Planning District and partnered with the Army Corps in 2001 but is not documented as an independent funder of the retreat [Source 1].

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **No evidence** that tax base maintenance was an explicit planning goal of the CMP retreat process. This question is not addressed in the reviewed sources.

**Narrative:** The reviewed sources do not document tax base maintenance as a planning objective for the CMP retreat. The sources consistently emphasize anti-displacement goals, collective tenure security, flood mitigation, community cohesion, and environmental restoration as the primary objectives [Sources 1, 2]. The CLT model keeps families in place (those not in the dredging right-of-way) as community members, and the broader project aims to improve living conditions and community resilience — but this is not framed in terms of tax base. Source 1 mentions community-led vocational training and micro-enterprises as contributing to economic empowerment and reducing economic vulnerability [Source 1], but these are not framed as tax base measures. The dredged canal corridor will become ecological/recreational space rather than tax-generating redevelopment. No code from the "tax base" category is applied, as the reviewed sources provide no evidence that planners explicitly pursued any of the listed tax base objectives. If any code were applied, it would be **Other** — community economic stability and anti-displacement — but this would be an interpretive stretch beyond what the sources directly support.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups** (housing choice within CLT or voucher); **Free supports and services** (mental health services, relocation counseling, comprehensive support); **Other** (collective CLT tenure as non-monetary benefit)

**Narrative:**
- Within the ENLACE program specifically: residents along the right-of-way are offered a choice of a home within the eight communities (within the CLT) or a housing relocation voucher [Source 1]. Residents select three "safe, decent and sanitary" housing options [Source 2]. This choice-based process constitutes an additional incentive beyond standard cash compensation.
- ENLACE provides comprehensive support throughout the relocation process, including mental health services to mitigate emotional stress, transparent communication, and ongoing resident involvement [Source 2]. These constitute free supports and services.
- For families relocating within the CLT: they receive housing within the collectively owned land trust, maintaining CLT membership, tenure security, and community access — a significant non-monetary benefit [Sources 1, 2].
- Regarding **market value** or **post-disaster value**: The broader Puerto Rico Program R3 framework (Source 3) provides acquisition of affected property at post-disaster assessed value with relocation vouchers up to $185,000 for relocation/reconstruction costs [Source 3]. However, this Program R3 mechanism is an island-wide framework separate from the ENLACE program, and direct application to CMP is not clearly documented in Source 1 or 2. Standard compensation value coding (market value, post-disaster value) applies more clearly to Program R3 in the broader Puerto Rico context than to the CMP-specific ENLACE process. Additionally, many CMP residents lacked formal title before the CLT was established, making standard property value mechanisms difficult to apply [Source 1].
- Source 2 notes that under U.S. federal buyout programs, "homeowners receive cash based on pre-disaster home values" [Source 2], but the ENLACE model goes beyond standard buyouts through comprehensive social support and genuine choice.

**Coding decision:** **Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups** and **Free supports and services** are the best-supported codes for the CMP-specific ENLACE process. Post-disaster value is applicable if discussing Program R3 context specifically, but should not be presented as the primary CMP compensation mechanism.

Case study: Terrebonne Parish Resettlement (Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, USA)
Section: General Information

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Both Reactive and Proactive elements are supported, with the overall LA SAFE program best characterized as Proactive (anticipatory), layered on top of a long history of Reactive, incremental household-level adaptation.

**Narrative:** The LA SAFE (Louisiana's Strategic Adaptations for Future Environments) planning process that produced the Terrebonne Parish Adaptation Strategy (2019) was directly enabled by funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's National Disaster Resilience Competition (NDRC) and the Rockefeller Foundation, which became available in response to Hurricane Isaac (2012) [1]. In this sense, the program's origin is reactive — it was a "Qualifying Disaster" (Hurricane Isaac) that created the funding opportunity [1]. However, once funded, the LA SAFE process was explicitly framed as anticipatory: it sought to plan for "future environments" and used 50-year flood-risk projections (CPRA's 2017 Coastal Master Plan modeling, Medium Environmental Scenario, 2067) to define high-, moderate-, and low-risk zones and to develop strategies before the projected risk materializes [1]. The Terrebonne Adaptation Strategy explicitly states that LA SAFE "complements" reactive structural efforts (the Morganza to the Gulf levee system) with "community-driven, smaller-scale adaptation strategies" oriented toward the future [1].

At the household level, however, Nelson et al. [4] document a long pattern of reactive adaptation: residents in lower Terrebonne Parish communities (Chauvin, Dulac, Isle de Jean Charles, Montegut, Theriot) have historically responded to specific flood events by elevating their homes after the fact (e.g., "Resident 28" raised their home after Hurricane Juan in 1985, and again experienced flooding after Hurricane Lili in 2002, eventually relocating through the Isle de Jean Charles resettlement program) [4]. The Isle de Jean Charles resettlement itself, funded through a $48.3 million CDBG-DR award in 2016, was also tied to a "Qualifying Disaster" / NDRC funding cycle, and followed decades of land loss and repeated storm damage (including Tropical Storm Lili in 2002, documented by Burley et al. [6]) — making it reactive in its funding trigger but framed by the State as a proactive, anticipatory resettlement given the island's documented loss of more than 98% of its land area over six decades [4].

**Category rationale:** Both categories are selected because the evidence shows a mixed picture: program funding triggers are reactive (tied to disaster declarations and post-disaster federal competitions), while the planning content and stated intent of the LA SAFE Adaptation Strategy and the Isle de Jean Charles resettlement are explicitly proactive/anticipatory, using future risk projections (2067 horizon) rather than only addressing damage already incurred [1], [4].

**Uncertainty/Alternative interpretations:** An alternative interpretation could weight the funding origin more heavily and code the case primarily Reactive, since post-Isaac NDRC/CDBG-DR funding was the proximate trigger that made the LA SAFE process possible [1]. However, while post-Isaac funding was a critical trigger, the LA SAFE program encompasses both proactive planning and responses to past disaster impacts: it is built on the explicit forward-looking framing and the 50-year (2067) risk-modeling basis for zoning described above, and states a goal of acting "before major impacts occur" for most of the parish — only approximately 7-12 households are currently being relocated [1], [3], [5], none of which have yet experienced the catastrophic land loss seen at Isle de Jean Charles [4]. The working interpretation therefore favors Proactive as the dominant trigger type for the decision process itself, with Reactive noted as the funding-origin trigger, rather than treating the case as driven solely by reactive, post-disaster motivations.

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:** LA SAFE planning process: 2016-2019 (Adaptation Strategy published April 2019). Buyout/Optional Home Owner Assistance for Permanent Resident Households: approximately 7-12 households, reflecting inconsistencies in source reporting — the LA SAFE Adaptation Strategy and Summary documents state approximately seven households [1], [3], while Birch et al. report approximately 12 for what appears to be the same or a closely related program [5]. Isle de Jean Charles resettlement (related but distinct program): funded 2016, ongoing through the 2020s. Total funding: the only total funding figure documented in the reviewed sources is the $48.3 million CDBG-DR award, which is specifically attributed to the Isle de Jean Charles resettlement [4]; no total funding figure distinct to the Terrebonne Buyout/Optional Home Owner Assistance program was found.

**Narrative:** The LA SAFE program for Terrebonne Parish ran its community engagement process across five rounds of meetings between roughly 2016 and 2018, engaging 371 residents and community leaders, with the final Adaptation Strategy document published in April 2019 [1]. The program was funded through HUD's National Disaster Resilience Competition and the Rockefeller Foundation, in the context of the broader six-parish LA SAFE region (Terrebonne, Plaquemines, Lafourche, St. John the Baptist, Jefferson, and St. Tammany parishes) [1].

Regarding the number of households affected by the relocation/buyout component specifically: the LA SAFE Adaptation Strategy and the LA SAFE Summary document both describe "approximately seven" permanent resident households living outside the Morganza to the Gulf Structural Protection System who are eligible for the Buyout/Optional Home Owner Assistance for Permanent Resident Households program [1], [3]. Birch et al. [5], however, cite a figure of "approximately 12" households for what appears to be the same or a closely related program, and explicitly note this discrepancy as evidence of how peripheral and under-specified the relocation component remained relative to other LA SAFE investments [5]. No single authoritative figure could be reconciled from the sources reviewed.

The Isle de Jean Charles resettlement — administratively separate from the LA SAFE Terrebonne buyout program but geographically and thematically connected — received $48.3 million in CDBG-DR funds from HUD in 2016 specifically to resettle island residents to a new site [4]. The island itself has lost over 98% of its land area over the past six decades [4]. No comprehensive population count for Isle de Jean Charles resettlement participants, nor a parish-wide total funding figure that aggregates all four Terrebonne catalytic projects, was found in the reviewed sources.

**Uncertainty/Missing information:** A precise, single number of households for the Terrebonne buyout program could not be determined due to the inconsistency between sources (7 vs. 12). No total dollar figure specific to the Buyout/Optional Home Owner Assistance program (separate from the $48.3M Isle de Jean Charles figure) was identified. Population (number of individuals, as opposed to households) figures were not found in any reviewed source for either program. This is flagged further in "Fields with Limited or No Evidence" below.
