Case study: Vunidogola Village Relocation (Vunidogola, Koralau Island, Fiji)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

### Case Name and Location
Vunidogoloa Village Relocation (spelled variously as "Vunidogoloa" in McMichael et al. 2019, "Vunidogola" in Tronquet 2015, and "Vunidologoa" in Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023 — all referring to the same village). Located on Vanua Levu, the second largest island of Fiji, in Cakaudrove Province (McMichael et al. 2019). Tronquet (2015) provides additional geographic specificity: the village was in the district of Koroalau, approximately 40 km from Savusavu and 100 km from Labasa, and was formerly situated between Natewa Bay and the Tabia River — these details are drawn exclusively from Tronquet (2015) and are not independently confirmed by the other provided sources. Country: Republic of Fiji, Pacific Island state, Global South.

### Hazard(s)
Coastal flooding (from storm surges and king tides), sea-level rise, coastal erosion, and saltwater intrusion into agricultural land and freshwater. These slow-onset and acute hazards compound one another. Residents of Vunidogoloa described experiences of "higher tides, coastal erosion, flooding, storm surges, and saltwater intrusion" (McMichael et al. 2019, p. 330). The village is also situated in a broader context of exposure to tropical cyclones; Tronquet (2015) notes cyclone Tomas struck Vanua Levu in 2010. Severe drought affecting agricultural yields is also noted by Tronquet (2015).

### Type of Retreat
Planned community relocation — the entire village relocated as a single collective unit to a new site approximately 2 km inland, on higher ground within the community's own customary (mataqali) land. Thirty new homes were built. New livelihood assets were established at the new site, including fish ponds and pineapple plantations (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McMichael et al. 2019; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). The relocation was completed in 2014 (all sources). This is a post-retreat case.

### Scale
Approximately 122–150 people (Tronquet 2015 notes this range; approximately 140 is the most frequently cited estimate across sources) living in 26 houses at the old site. Thirty new homes were built at the new site (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). Geographic scope: a single village, relocating approximately 2 km inland (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McMichael et al. 2019).

### Key Actors
- **Community of Vunidogoloa**: Initiated the process by formally requesting government assistance (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015 note 2007; Tronquet 2015 notes 2006); contributed labour and timber from customary land; participated in design decisions including village layout and house configuration (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015).
- **Government of Fiji**: Central coordinating role; multiple ministries involved including the Ministry of Provincial Development, Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Fisheries, and Ministry of iTaukei Affairs (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015). No single ministry held complete responsibility for the relocation (McMichael et al. 2019).
- **International Labour Organization (ILO)**: Provided tools and equipment; supplied pineapple tops, banana shoots, and a copra dryer (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015; Tronquet 2015).
- **Pacific Conference of Churches (PCC) and Nansen Initiative**: Organised a 3-day awareness-raising workshop in 2012 and undertook community history documentation work (Tronquet 2015). The PCC made multiple subsequent visits and provided community support throughout the relocation process (Tronquet 2015).
- **UN Women**: Funded a solar engineering training programme that enabled electrification of the new village (Tronquet 2015).
- **Commissioner Northern's Office**: On-the-ground coordination (Tronquet 2015).
- **Fiji Red Cross**: Referenced by McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) in interview context regarding disaster risk reduction broadly; not documented as a governance actor in the Vunidogoloa relocation specifically.
- Researchers from the University of Melbourne and the University of Queensland subsequently documented and analysed the case (McMichael et al. 2019; Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023).

### Timeline
- **1950s**: First discussions about possible relocation reportedly occurred; Tronquet (2015) cites the village headman as recalling talks in 1956, though this cannot be independently verified from the other provided sources.
- **2006/2007**: Community formally approaches the Fiji Government requesting relocation assistance. McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) state the approach was made in 2007; Tronquet (2015) states 2006. Both are recorded here.
- **2010**: Cyclone Tomas strikes Vanua Levu, raising awareness of climate risks (Tronquet 2015).
- **2011**: Earthworks initiated at a new site; site levelling problems encountered (McMichael et al. 2019). A second site approximately 2 km inland was identified.
- **2012**: Government officially confirms Vunidogoloa as selected for relocation (Tronquet 2015). PCC and Nansen Initiative hold a 3-day awareness-raising workshop (Tronquet 2015). National Summit for Building Resilience to Climate Change held (Tronquet 2015). Construction planned but delayed.
- **2012–2013**: Protracted construction phase, with delays attributed to ground instability and shortage of tools (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019).
- **Late 2013**: ILO concludes agreement with Ministry of Labour and provides additional tools, accelerating construction; Tronquet (2015) records the ILO agreement was concluded in November 2013 and that 4 houses were built in 15 days following tool delivery — these specific figures are from Tronquet (2015) alone and should be read as single-source.
- **January 2014**: Official inauguration. Prime Minister Bainimarama's opening speech on 16 January 2014 is quoted by Tronquet (2015). The entire community relocated over a three-day period in January 2014 (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).
- **2014 onward**: Second phase of works (drainage, footpaths, evacuation centre) at an estimated additional cost of approximately FJD 200,000 (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019).
- **Current stage**: Post-retreat; the physical relocation is complete, though post-relocation livelihood and infrastructure development continued beyond the initial move. Long-term longitudinal monitoring remains limited (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023).

### Key Outcomes
**Reported positive outcomes:**
- The entire village relocated together, preserving social cohesion; neighbours remained in the same spatial configuration (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015).
- New homes represented an improvement from previous housing: individual family dwellings, running water, solar power, indoor bathrooms (Tronquet 2015).
- Improved proximity to roads, schools, health services, and markets; community members reported that "improved access to services has significantly improved their daily lives" (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023, p. 6).
- Relocation occurred on community-owned customary land, avoiding land acquisition disputes (all sources).
- New livelihood assets established: fish ponds, pineapple plantations (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McMichael et al. 2019).
- The relocation informed the development of Fiji's national relocation policy environment, with national guidelines subsequently finalized in 2018 (McMichael et al. 2019; Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023).

**Documented challenges and costs:**
- Total costs greatly exceeded projections: the final figure cited at the Conference of the Parties in December 2014 was FJD 988,228.89, compared to an initial government budget of approximately FJD 310,000 — roughly three times the original estimate (Tronquet 2015).
- Infrastructure remained incomplete after the initial move: promised kitchens were not finished, and residents salvaged materials from the old village to build their own (McMichael et al. 2019).
- Older residents experienced significant difficulties maintaining access to the coast and associated livelihoods (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McMichael et al. 2019).
- Women were largely excluded from formal consultation processes, given patriarchal and hierarchical social structures (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023).
- Post-relocation negative impacts documented: increased access to and consumption of packaged food and alcohol, disruptions to traditional values, and reduced mental wellbeing (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023, citing McMichael & Powell 2021).
- Scalability questions remain: the model relied heavily on the community owning suitable alternative land with timber resources — conditions that may not apply to other at-risk villages across Fiji (Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).

### Narrative Summary

Vunidogoloa is a small iTaukei (indigenous Fijian) village that spent decades enduring worsening coastal flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion before completing a planned community relocation in 2014. As high tides regularly inundated homes — residents used bamboo rafts to access the hospital at high tide (Tronquet 2015) — and as the sea consumed the shoreline and destroyed crops, the community exhausted in-situ adaptations including house-raising on stilts and seawall construction. Recognising that no further protective measures were viable, the community formally approached the Fiji Government to request assistance with full relocation, an approach documented in both 2006 (Tronquet 2015) and 2007 (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015) depending on the source. What followed was a multi-year process that combined government coordination across several ministries, community leadership, and international support.

A critical enabling condition for the relocation was the existence of suitable higher ground approximately 2 km inland that fell within the village's own mataqali (clan) land, meaning no external land acquisition was required. The community named the new site Kenani — the Fijian word for Canaan, or "Promised Land" — reflecting profound spiritual and cultural dimensions of the move (Tronquet 2015). Thirty new homes were built with solar power and running water. The government funded the majority of costs, the community contributed timber and labour, and international organisations including the ILO and UN Women provided equipment and skills (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). The Pacific Conference of Churches played a documented role in organising awareness-raising activities and community support (Tronquet 2015).

The relocation is frequently presented in the literature as an important early completed example of planned climate-related community relocation, particularly for its participatory design process, its collective nature, and its improvement in living standards. However, the literature also documents significant costs: total expenditure was roughly three times the original budget, infrastructure completion was delayed, older residents lost meaningful access to the coast and associated livelihoods, women were largely excluded from planning consultations, and unanticipated negative health and social impacts have been documented post-relocation (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023). Critically, the case relied on the community's ownership of suitable alternative land — a condition that will not apply to many of Fiji's hundreds of other at-risk villages. Vunidogoloa thus stands as a significant and often-cited case, but one whose replicability is constrained by the specific conditions that enabled it (Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).

Case study: Vunidogola Village Relocation (Vunidogola, Koralau Island, Fiji)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** **Proactive** (primary code), with reactive elements also present.

**Narrative:** The dominant framing across all sources is proactive. The community of Vunidogoloa, experiencing slow-onset climate impacts over decades — sea-level rise, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion — deliberated internally and formally requested government assistance before a catastrophic loss-of-life event occurred. Tronquet (2015) documents that the community's formal request was made in 2006, as flooding impacts were intensifying but before total loss of the village. McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) frame the relocation as community-initiated and forward-looking: "relocation was their option of last resort as a means of sustaining livelihoods in the long-term." The community had previously attempted reactive, incremental adaptations — house-raising on stilts and seawall construction — all of which proved insufficient (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015).

Reactive elements are also present. Cyclone Tomas in 2010 is noted by Tronquet (2015) as having raised awareness and momentum within both the community and government, functioning as a reactive trigger that reinforced the proactive relocation decision already underway. However, the relocation decision pre-dated this event.

**Coding rationale:** "Proactive" is selected as the primary code because the formal decision to relocate pre-dated any single catastrophic event, was based on slow-onset risk accumulation, and was community-initiated in advance of an existential threshold. Reactive elements (prior failed in-situ adaptations, cyclone impacts heightening awareness) are present but secondary to the proactive framing.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date of relocation completion:** 2014. The entire community relocated over a three-day period in January 2014 (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). Tronquet (2015) specifically records 16 January 2014 as the date of the inauguration ceremony, quoting Prime Minister Bainimarama's opening speech — this level of precision derives from Tronquet (2015) alone.
- **Process initiated:** Community formally approached government in 2006 (Tronquet 2015) or 2007 (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015); government confirmed the village for relocation in 2012 (Tronquet 2015).
- **Number of households:** 26 houses at the old site; 30 new homes constructed (McMichael et al. 2019; Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).
- **Population affected:** Approximately 122–150 people; approximately 140 is the most frequently cited estimate (Tronquet 2015). McMichael et al. (2019) describe "approximately 140 iTaukei people living in 26 houses."
- **Total funding:** Figures vary across sources and stages of reporting. Tronquet (2015) provides the most detailed accounting: the figure cited at the Conference of the Parties in December 2014 was FJD 988,228.89 (SPEREP 2014, cited in Tronquet 2015); an IPS news agency report cited FJD 978,000 (Wilson 2014, cited in Tronquet 2015); the government's own January 2014 communication cited FJD 879,000. McMichael et al. (2019, endnote 7) cite the total cost as approximately FJD 978,228, equivalent to approximately USD 492,136. The original government budget was approximately FJD 310,000 (Tronquet 2015); earthworks alone cost approximately FJD 500,000 (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). A second phase of works added an estimated FJD 200,000 (Tronquet 2015). The community contribution in timber was estimated at FJD 250,000, representing approximately 22% of total project cost (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019). The government's share exceeded 75% of total costs (Tronquet 2015). ILO and UN Women contributions were in-kind rather than cash transfers.

**Uncertainty note:** Financial figures vary across sources and reporting stages. The FJD 988,228.89 figure represents the most recently cited total for Phase 1 costs (Tronquet 2015) but is drawn from a single-source government presentation.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards**

**Narrative:** All sources document a combination of co-occurring and cascading hazards driving the relocation. McMichael et al. (2019, p. 330) describe resident experiences of "higher tides, coastal erosion, flooding, storm surges, and saltwater intrusion." Tronquet (2015) adds severe drought affecting agricultural yields and exposure to tropical cyclones (cyclone Tomas, 2010) as part of the broader hazard context. McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) identify "frequent flooding, inundation, and failed seawalls" as immediate drivers in the context of sea-level rise.

These hazards interact: sea-level rise amplifies storm surge and king tide flooding; coastal erosion reduces village footprint; saltwater intrusion destroys soil productivity. The combination constitutes multiple hazard types with cascading dynamics. Piggott-McKellar & Vella (2023) frame the drivers as "increased flooding events, coastal erosion, and saltwater intrusion."

**Coding rationale:** "Multiple Hazards" is clearly supported by all sources. No source treats this as a single-hazard case.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** (with climate change as the primary driver of hazard intensification)

**Narrative:** The hazards are natural in origin — coastal flooding, sea-level rise, erosion, storm surge, and drought. Climate change is identified as the primary cause of hazard intensification across all sources. Villagers attributed the worsening conditions to anthropogenic climate change caused by "big countries" (McMichael et al. 2019, p. 331). Tronquet (2015) documents that by 2012 "inhabitants were clearly aware that the slow-onset events and extreme natural disasters that struck them were caused by climate change." Piggott-McKellar & Vella (2023) note that sea levels near Fiji have been rising approximately 5.5 mm per year since 1992, roughly twice the global average. There is no technological or industrial hazard dimension to this case.

**Coding rationale:** "Natural Hazard" is selected. The codebook notes that "Climate change" as a classification may be adopted in future analyses; for this coding cycle, the relevant category is Natural Hazard, with the climate change dimension noted as the driver of intensification. No technological hazard is present.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:**

- **Coastal Flooding/Erosion:** ✓ Yes — primary driver. Sea-level rise, storm surge, king tide flooding, and shoreline erosion are all explicitly documented across all sources as the main drivers of the relocation decision.
- **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding:** Partial and secondary. Tronquet (2015) notes the village was located between Natewa Bay and the Tabia River, and that floods occurred "when high tides coincided with heavy rains, increasing the level of the river." McMichael et al. (2019, Table 1) include a resident quote: "When it is heavy rain, it came inside the village. It came from the sea and the river as well." This compound coastal-riverine flooding was a contributing factor, but the sources frame coastal flooding/erosion as the primary driver. Riverine/pluvial flooding is coded as a secondary compound hazard only.
- **Lake Flooding/Erosion:** No evidence.
- **Wildfire:** No evidence.
- **Volcano:** No evidence.
- **Land Subsidence:** No evidence as a driver.
- **Landslide/Debris Flow:** **Not coded as a retreat driver.** Landslide risk appeared as a post-relocation planning concern at the new Kenani site (ground instability after earthworks, requiring stabilisation work — Tronquet 2015). A landslide destroyed the primary school in nearby Denimanu, referenced in Piggott-McKellar & Vella (2023) in a comparator village context. Neither instance is a driver of the original Vunidogoloa retreat decision. This hazard is therefore not coded as a retreat driver for this case.
- **Earthquake:** No evidence as a driver.
- **Tsunami:** No evidence as a driver.
- **Hurricane/Tropical Cyclone:** Contextual only. Cyclone Tomas (2010) is noted by Tronquet (2015) as having raised awareness and accelerated momentum, but is not a primary driver of the relocation decision. Coded as contextual/secondary.
- **Other — Saltwater Intrusion/Agricultural Degradation:** ✓ Yes — explicitly identified as a major driver affecting soil productivity and food security (all sources). Drought is also noted by Tronquet (2015).

**Primary hazard codes selected:** Coastal Flooding/Erosion (primary); Riverine/Pluvial Flooding (secondary/compound, not primary driver); Hurricane (contextual only; not coded as a primary driver); Other (saltwater intrusion — explicitly coded as a contributing driver; drought noted by Tronquet 2015).

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Entire Community**

**Narrative:** All sources consistently describe the relocation of the entire village of Vunidogoloa as a single unit. McMichael et al. (2019, p. 329) state: "The entire village relocated together in January 2014." McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) describe the relocation of an entire community. Tronquet (2015) describes the community moving "altogether" over three days. This distinguishes Vunidogoloa from partial relocation cases in Fiji such as Denimanu, Vunisavisavi, and Narikoso, where only subsets of households relocated (McMichael et al. 2019; Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023).

**Coding rationale:** "Entire community" is the only applicable category. The scale was the complete relocation of the village as a social and spatial unit.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Communities** (primary); **Critical Infrastructure** (secondary — newly constructed at receiving site)

**Narrative:** The primary subject of retreat was the entire community — people, households, and their social structures. Additionally, infrastructure was newly established at the new site as part of the relocation package: 30 new homes, water supply (gradient drainage and tanks), solar energy systems, fish ponds, agricultural infrastructure (pineapple plantations, banana crops, copra dryer), and an evacuation centre built in the second phase (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019). Ancestral remains were relocated from the old cemetery to the new site (Tronquet 2015). Old village structures were largely left in place and were not formally demolished or removed as part of the managed retreat process.

**Coding rationale:** "Communities" is the primary selection. "Critical infrastructure" is applicable in the sense that new community infrastructure was established as part of the relocation package. Individual buyout-style property acquisition is not applicable.

---

### Other notes (General Information)

Multiple alternative spellings appear across sources: Vunidogoloa (McMichael et al. 2019), Vunidogola (Tronquet 2015), and Vunidologoa (Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023). All refer to the same village. The new site is named Kenani. The case is presented across sources as one of the earliest completed whole-village climate-related relocations in Fiji and among the first globally, giving it significant exemplary significance. The case informed (though did not alone "catalyse") Fiji's national relocation policy environment, with National Planned Relocation Guidelines finalized in 2018 (McMichael et al. 2019; Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).

Case study: Vunidogola Village Relocation (Vunidogola, Koralau Island, Fiji)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Community buyout/retreat**

**Important qualification:** This was not a "buyout" in the conventional market transaction sense. No private property was purchased from individual owners. Rather, the government funded the construction of new homes on community-owned customary land, while the community contributed labour and timber. The process was collective: all 30 new houses were built and the community moved as a unit. The codebook's "Community buyout/retreat" category — defined as "collective relocation of a neighborhood or settlement through coordinated planning and community engagement" — is the closest applicable code; however, "collective community relocation with government-funded construction" more precisely describes the mechanism.

**Narrative:** McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) characterise the relocation as community-led with government support. Tronquet (2015) describes it as "a well-thought-out, multilateral and participative process." The community retained ownership of the new homes (confirmed by ILO, per Tronquet 2015). The government covered construction costs; the community contributed in-kind through timber and labour.

**Coding rationale:** "Community buyout/retreat" is selected as the closest available category, with the explicit note that no market purchase transaction occurred. "Individual buyout/retreat," "leasebacks/easements," and "managed realignment of infrastructure" do not apply.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? Are there any legal frameworks or regulations that guide the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts; Land acquisition; Home acquisition; Legal authority over retreat; Title(s) transfer; Compliance & enforcement; Other**

**Narrative:**

**Customary land tenure (major constraint and enabler):** The most significant legal/institutional dimension was Fiji's customary land tenure system. Tronquet (2015) notes, citing Anderson & Lee (2010), that customary tenure of approximately 80% of land in the Pacific renders land transactions "almost impossible." For Vunidogoloa, this was both a constraint in general terms and an enabling factor in this specific case: the community owned suitable higher ground within their own mataqali (clan) boundaries, so no external land acquisition was needed. The new site — a 5-acre parcel belonging to Mataqali Nadawa — was donated without compensation (Tronquet 2015). All sources emphasise this as a critical success factor.

**No comprehensive legal framework at the time:** Both Tronquet (2015) and McNamara & Jacot Des Combes (2015) note that no appropriate legal framework for climate-related relocation existed in Fiji at the time of the Vunidogoloa relocation. The 2012 National Climate Change Policy did not mention relocation (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015). The relocation thus proceeded without a formal national legal framework, relying on ad hoc inter-ministerial coordination.

**Procedural requirements:** Tronquet (2015) quotes the divisional planning officer describing the formal procedural chain: villages must inform government through district and provincial council meetings, identify new land with mataqali consent, notify provincial offices, and then approach the Ministry of Provincial Development. This lengthy procedural pathway contributed to the extended timeline.

**Ministry of iTaukei Affairs:** McMichael et al. (2019) describe, in the context of Narikoso, that boundary extension negotiations require acceptance by the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs. For Vunidogoloa, land was within a single mataqali and was reportedly donated (Tronquet 2015), reducing this institutional complexity.

**Logging licence:** A government-issued logging licence was required for the community to harvest timber from their own land for construction materials (Tronquet 2015).

**Property rights and home ownership:** The question of property rights under customary tenure was noted; ILO confirmed that residents own (not merely occupy) the new homes (Tronquet 2015).

**Post-relocation policy development:** Vunidogoloa was an influential early case in the development of Fiji's National Planned Relocation Guidelines, finalized in 2018 with GIZ support (McMichael et al. 2019; Piggott-McKellar & Vella 2023; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).

**Coding rationale:** "Relevant regulations/acts" (customary land tenure; iTaukei land system); "Land acquisition" (customary land boundary negotiation and donation); "Home acquisition" (government-funded construction of new homes); "Legal authority over retreat" (fragmented — no single ministry held complete responsibility, per McMichael et al. 2019); "Title(s) transfer" (community ownership of new homes confirmed); "Other" (logging licence; absence of formal legal framework at time of relocation).

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Multiple funders**: Federal/National Government (primary); International organisations (ILO, UN Women — in-kind); Community (in-kind: timber and labour); NGOs/religious organisations (PCC — support, not primarily financial)

**Narrative:**

1. **Fiji Government (National/Federal):** Covered more than 75% of total costs, including earthworks (~FJD 500,000 per McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015), housing construction materials, government labour coordination, and infrastructure. Multiple ministries contributed (Tronquet 2015; McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015).

2. **Community of Vunidogoloa (in-kind):** Provided timber from customary land (estimated value FJD 250,000, approximately 22% of total project cost) and labour (Tronquet 2015; McMichael et al. 2019). This constitutes the codebook's "Individual" category (community self-contribution in kind).

3. **International Labour Organization (ILO):** Provided tools and safety equipment under a Cash for Work Plus Programme (agreement concluded in November 2013 per Tronquet 2015); supplied pineapple tops, banana shoots, and copra dryer as in-kind livelihood support (McNamara & Jacot Des Combes 2015; Tronquet 2015). This is an "International aid" / "NGOs" category contribution — in-kind rather than direct cash.

4. **UN Women:** Funded a solar engineering training programme that enabled electrification of the new village (Tronquet 2015). In-kind/capacity building.

5. **Pacific Conference of Churches (PCC):** Organised and funded the 2012 awareness-raising workshop in conjunction with the Nansen Initiative (Tronquet 2015). The PCC's contributions were primarily organisational and pastoral support rather than financial contributions to construction costs; it is coded as NGO support rather than as a primary funder.

6. **Access to international Climate Change adaptation funds was limited:** Tronquet (2015) notes that access to international funds such as the Adaptation Fund was constrained by complex application procedures — this was a systemic gap rather than a resolved funding mechanism for this case.

**Coding rationale:** "Multiple funders" applies. Sub-categories: Federal/National (primary, Fiji Government); Individual/community (in-kind timber and labour); International aid / NGOs (ILO in-kind, UN Women

Case study: San Martin Planned Relocation (San Martin Region, Peru)
Section: GENERAL INFORMATION

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** **Reactive** (primary). Some proactive elements are present in the legislative framing and community risk appraisal, but the decision trigger for both communities was flood damage.

**Narrative:** V1/V3's original relocation request in 1999 followed major flood events in 1963 and 1999 — a reactive pattern triggered after damage had occurred. Similarly, V2/V4's formal request in 2015 followed major floods in 1977 and 2015 (Bergmann 2021, p. 367). Both decisions were thus primarily reactive in terms of the immediate trigger: "major floods in undated V2 in 1977 and 2015" and V1 "suffered from single, large floods in 1963 and in 1999" (Bergmann 2021, p. 367).

However, community motivation was not purely retrospective. Bergmann (2021) notes that "risk appraisal, fear and uncertainty, deprivations, and children's future prospects drove their decisions" (p. 367), indicating forward-looking motivations alongside disaster-triggered concerns. Peru's broader DRM framework (French et al. 2020) has shifted toward prospective measures including relocation, but national DRM practice has historically remained reactive (French et al. 2020, p. 30). Law No. 29869 (2012) frames relocation as a prospective risk-reduction tool, but the immediate decision trigger in both cases was flood damage.

**Coding:** **Reactive** is the primary code. The legislative framework introduces a proactive dimension, but the codebook directs coding based on the decision trigger, which was reactive in both cases.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**
- **Dates:** V1/V3 relocation request: 1999; physical relocation completed: 2014; status as of research: still lacking final legal approvals (2019). V2/V4 relocation request: 2015; declared uninhabitable: 2017; no completed relocation as of 2019.
- **Number of households:** Not explicitly provided in household counts in the reviewed sources.
- **Number of population affected:** Approximately 850 people across both communities — approximately 150 (V1/V3) and approximately 700 (V2/V4) (Bergmann 2021, p. 366).
- **Total funding:** No specific budget figures are provided in the reviewed sources for either relocation. The regional government promised funds for land acquisition for V2/V4 in 2015 but had not delivered as of 2019, "allegedly due to changing functionaries and priorities" (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). V1/V3 received no state housing reconstruction support and relied primarily on its own resources and a private land swap (Bergmann 2021, pp. 368–369).

**Uncertainty:** Exact household counts and any formal budget allocations for these specific relocations are not documented in the reviewed sources.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards.**

**Narrative:** While riverine flooding is the primary and most damaging hazard cited in both cases — with close to 100% of interviewees mentioning floods (Bergmann 2021, Fig. 4) — a range of additional hazards were documented. Bergmann (2021, Fig. 4) shows that interviewees also mentioned weather-related diseases affecting humans, pests and diseases affecting animals or crops, temperature changes, rainfall changes, strong winds, declining crop productivity or pastures, and droughts. The legal basis for relocation was primarily the flood risk, but the communities faced multiple overlapping climate-related hazards.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard.**

**Narrative:** The hazards are entirely natural — riverine flooding, climate variability, and associated phenomena. Bergmann (2021, p. 365) notes that "extreme floods have already increased" in the Peruvian Amazon "and are projected to rise further due to climate change." French et al. (2020) provide broader context on the ENSO system and El Niño-related flooding as natural hydro-meteorological phenomena, with a climate change dimension. No technological hazards are discussed in the reviewed sources. Per the codebook, "Natural hazard" is the applicable code; the climate change intensification dimension is noted here in text but does not constitute a separate origin code under the codebook structure.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding** (primary). **Other** (weather-related disease, crop pests, rainfall changes, droughts, strong winds, declining productivity — secondary, mentioned by interviewees).

**Narrative:** Riverine flooding from adjacent rivers is the explicitly identified primary hazard driving both relocation decisions. Major flood events (1963 and 1999 for V1/V3; 1977 and 2015 for V2/V4) were the triggering events for relocation requests (Bergmann 2021, p. 367). The state's uninhabitability declarations were primarily based on flood risk. Peru's broader DRM framework documented by French et al. (2020) is also primarily focused on hydro-meteorological hazards. The additional hazards mentioned by interviewees (Fig. 4 in Bergmann 2021) were part of the broader context but were not the primary basis for formal relocation declarations.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes, A few streets, Neighbourhood, Entire community, Sub-watershed, Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Entire community** (for both villages).

**Narrative:** Both relocations were framed as whole-community relocations. V1/V3 (approximately 150 people) relocated collectively. V2/V4 (approximately 700 people) sought collective relocation to a site approximately one kilometer away near a planned road (Bergmann 2021, p. 370). Bergmann (2021) consistently frames these as community-level processes, and Peru's relocation regulation (Decreto Supremo No. 115-2013-PCM) is designed for collective population relocation from high-risk zones. Neither case involved selective individual household buyouts.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals, Groups/Neighbourhoods, Communities, Critical infrastructure, Hazard protection structures, Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Communities.**

**Narrative:** Both cases involved the collective relocation of entire rural communities. Bergmann (2021, 2024) consistently refers to community-level decision-making and relocation processes. There is no evidence in the reviewed sources of individual household buyouts, infrastructure relocation, or industrial asset relocation. Law No. 29869 is specifically designed for collective population relocation (Bergmann 2021, p. 366).

---

### Other notes (General Information)

The two communities are anonymized in the sources: as V1 (mestizo, approximately 150 people) and V2 (indígena, approximately 700 people) in Bergmann (2021), and as V3 and V4 respectively in Bergmann (2024). Both are located in the San Martín department of the Peruvian Amazon. Bergmann (2021, p. 366) notes that community members self-identify as mestizos and indígenas respectively, and that intersectional factors — including gender, ethnicity, poverty, and low education — heighten vulnerabilities. More than 60% of people in both districts have only primary education or less, and around 15% cannot read or write; approximately 80% of households cook with wood (Bergmann 2021, p. 366).

Case study: San Martin Planned Relocation (San Martin Region, Peru)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat, Community buyout/retreat, Leasebacks, easements and buffers, Other acquisition tools, Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Community buyout/retreat.**

**Narrative:** Both cases involve collective community relocation, not individual property buyouts. Law No. 29869 (2012) and its regulatory decree (Decreto Supremo No. 115-2013-PCM) are explicitly designed for "reasentamiento poblacional" (population resettlement) of communities from zones of "very high, unmitigable risk" (Bergmann 2021, pp. 366–367). Bergmann (2021) consistently frames these as community-level processes with collective decision-making. There is no evidence of individual property acquisition programs or market-based buyout mechanisms in these cases. In V1/V3, land was ultimately acquired through a territory swap with a private agribusiness — a non-formal arrangement not contemplated by the standard legal framework (Bergmann 2021, p. 369).

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? Are there any legal frameworks or regulations that guide the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts; Legal authority over retreat; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer; Land rezoning; Compliance & enforcement; Other (participation rights, ministerial approval requirements).**

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** Law No. 29869 (2012) on population resettlement from areas of "very high, unmitigable risk"; Law No. 30645 (2017) modifying it; and Decreto Supremo No. 115-2013-PCM as the regulatory decree (Bergmann 2021, pp. 365–366). French et al. (2020, p. 22) also reference Law No. 29869, noting that "since its passage, however, the law has seen little implementation." The regulation covers most phases of the relocation cycle: planning, participation, transfer, livelihood restoration, monitoring, and evaluation (Bergmann 2021, Fig. 1).

- **Legal authority over retreat:** Responsibilities are divided across multiple levels. Local and regional governments are responsible for preparing relocation plans; CENEPRED and INDECI have technical oversight; the Ministry of Housing manages land-use approvals (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). V1/V3's case illustrates that the central government had not issued the required final ministerial resolution years after physical relocation had occurred (Bergmann 2021, p. 368).

- **Land acquisition:** A major legal and practical obstacle. The law permits expropriation with compensation at "real costs," but regional authorities declined to apply this tool even when a private landowner allegedly inflated prices for V2/V4's prospective site. Bergmann (2021, p. 369) notes that the government "fail[ed] to exploit all legal options, such as using charges from natural resource exploitation and mining." The state did not provide land for V1/V3, which ultimately had to negotiate a private territory swap.

- **Title(s) transfer:** Property titles at V1/V3's new site could not be issued without a final ministerial resolution approving the relocation and a land-use reclassification from rural to urban — neither of which had occurred as of 2019 (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). This blocked access to social housing programs and other state benefits.

- **Land rezoning:** Required but not completed for V1/V3. Bergmann (2021, p. 368) specifically notes that the absence of a land-use change "from rural to urban" was a prerequisite for property titles and access to social programs.

- **Compliance & enforcement:** The law establishes participation rights and monitoring obligations, but Bergmann (2021, p. 368) documents that "the implementation of their legally guaranteed participation rights has been insufficient." Relocatees were not informed about legally required dispute resolution mechanisms. The Ministry of Women and Vulnerable Populations (MIMP) had a legal mandate to protect relocatees but lacked adequate funding (Bergmann 2021, p. 371).

- **Other:** The law's participation clause is conditional — "when circumstances allow" and "with the necessary availability" (Law No. 29869, Arts. 5, 6, 17, as translated by Bergmann 2021, footnote 7, p. 371) — creating legal ambiguity about enforceability. The exact threshold for "unmitigable" risk is noted as ambiguous by Bergmann (2021, p. 367) and Venkateswaran et al. (2017) as cited in Bergmann (2021).

French et al. (2020, p. 22) provide complementary context on Law No. 29869, noting that "the law has seen little implementation" nationally and describing one case (Chosica) where residents resisted relocation orders.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Individual** (community self-funding in practice for V1/V3); **Provincial/State** (promised but not delivered for V2/V4). No other funding sources are documented in the reviewed sources.

**Narrative:** The legal framework envisages state funding at multiple levels. For V2/V4, the regional government promised funds for land acquisition in 2015 but had not delivered as of 2019, "allegedly due to changing functionaries and priorities" (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). National-level authorities were expected to provide ministerial approvals and reconstruction support but had not done so for V1/V3 as of 2019 (Bergmann 2021, p. 368).

In practice, V1/V3 funded their own relocation almost entirely through their own labor and resources. The enabling factors were a private territory swap with a local agribusiness and employment from a private canalization company: "Without these two private entities, relocation and reconstruction would have failed" (Bergmann 2021, p. 369). Bergmann (2021, p. 368) quotes a V1/V3 interviewee: "All we have, what little we have, is thanks to ourselves" (V1-3).

The reviewed sources do not document international aid, insurance, NGO, or lender funding for these specific relocations. French et al. (2020, p. 23) reference the national DRM budget program PP 068 (PREVAED), contingency funds, and charges from mining-sector profits (canon minero) as legally available mechanisms for relocation of at-risk populations, but these mechanisms are not documented in the reviewed sources as having been effectively accessed for either case.

**Note on terminology:** Peru is a unitary state; references to "national" or "central government" and "regional government" (rather than "federal") are used throughout this memo to reflect the correct governance structure.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **No evidence found in reviewed sources.**

**Narrative:** Tax base considerations are not discussed in any of the reviewed sources in relation to these specific relocations. The communities are subsistence farming villages in remote rural areas of the Peruvian Amazon. No evidence of tax revenue planning, redevelopment of retreat lands for revenue generation, or related considerations is documented in Bergmann (2021), Bergmann (2024), or French et al. (2020) in relation to these two cases.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Free supports and services** (legally promised but largely not delivered in practice).

**Narrative:** Peru's relocation regulation (Decreto Supremo No. 115-2013-PCM) legally entitles relocatees to a range of supports including housing reconstruction assistance, access to social programs, and livelihood restoration (Bergmann 2021, Fig. 1). However, in practice these entitlements were not fulfilled. For V1/V3, "promised support for reconstructing houses and improving infrastructure is pending" as of the time of research (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). For V2/V4, the regional government promised funds for land acquisition but did not deliver (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). Many V2/V4 interviewees "worried that even if they moved eventually, they would not receive promised access to social programs needed for reconstruction" (Bergmann 2021, p. 368).

There is no evidence of cash compensation at market, tax, or post-disaster valuation for either community. The law does envision expropriation of land at "real costs" (fair market value) as a tool for the state to acquire relocation sites, but this was not applied (Bergmann 2021, p. 369). V1/V3 effectively received a private territory swap — a non-monetary, in-kind arrangement outside the formal compensation framework. "Additional incentives" in the codebook sense are not documented as having been provided.

Case study: San Martin Planned Relocation (San Martin Region, Peru)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Pre-retreat planning; Immediate risks (1–5 years); Anticipated future risks (10–100 years); Post-retreat follow-up** (legally required but weakly implemented in both cases).

**Narrative:** The legislative framework contemplates pre-retreat planning activities (risk assessment, community participation, site evaluation, planning approvals) before relocation. Both communities faced immediate flood risks, particularly V2/V4 after being declared uninhabitable in 2017. Climate change projections for the Amazon — documented in Bergmann (2021, p. 365) — situate these relocations within a longer-term horizon of increasing flood extremes. Post-retreat follow-up was legally required under the regulation (monitoring, evaluation, livelihood restoration, data collection — see Bergmann 2021, Fig. 1) but was not implemented for either community as of 2019. The absence of post-retreat follow-up for V1/V3 is illustrated by the lack of property titles, housing support, and final legal approvals five years after physical relocation.

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Top-down; Bottom-up** (community-initiated but not sustained through formal processes); **Multi-sectoral** (in legal design); **Participatory/collaborative** (legally required but poorly implemented); **Degree of transparency** (limited).

**Narrative:** The formal planning structure under Law No. 29869 is multi-sectoral, assigning roles to local and regional governments, CENEPRED, INDECI, the Ministry of Housing, and MIMP (Bergmann 2021, p. 367; French et al. 2020, p. 22). However, implementation was primarily top-down and centralized, with local authorities lacking technical capacity, resources, and political will (Bergmann 2021, p. 367). Community-initiated (bottom-up) relocation requests drove both cases, but communities were largely excluded from meaningful decision-making once formal processes were engaged. Bergmann (2021, p. 368) notes that village authorities "said the implementation of their legally guaranteed participation rights has been insufficient" and that communities "lacked access to decision-makers and traveling regularly to the capital to make their case is prohibitively expensive."

Transparency was low: government promises were broken without explanation, and relocatees "cited numerous grievances, complaints, and conflicts, but the state did not seem to fulfil its obligation to inform them about legally required resolution mechanisms" (Bergmann 2021, p. 371). There is no evidence in the reviewed sources of adaptive management, cost-benefit analysis, or multi-criteria decision analysis being applied to these specific relocations.

---

### What decision support tools were used in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Hazard maps & models** (implied by formal risk zone declarations); **Process guidance** (legally prescribed by the regulation).

**Narrative:** The legal basis for relocation requires a formal risk assessment declaring zones as "very high, unmitigable risk," implying the use of hazard assessment tools. CENEPRED and INDECI produce hazard maps at national and regional levels (French et al. 2020, p. 21). Both V1/V3 and V2/V4 were formally declared zones of very high unmitigable risk, suggesting some form of hazard assessment was conducted (Bergmann 2021, p. 367). Peru's relocation regulation constitutes a form of process guidance (Bergmann 2021, Fig. 1). However, Bergmann (2021, p. 367) notes that "the law's exact threshold of 'unmitigable' hazards remains ambiguous," suggesting that available decision tools were imprecise and inconsistently applied.

There is no documented use in the reviewed sources of CBA, MCDA, demographic projections, social vulnerability assessments, housing assessments, or formal new site evaluation processes for these specific cases.

---

### What planning measures were taken for receiving areas in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Identifying priority areas** (limited); **Individuals vs. neighbourhoods/communities** (community-level planning intended); **Construction of new housing** (legally required but not delivered by the state).

**Narrative:** For V1/V3, a new site was identified adjacent to the existing location through the private land swap, closer to a road facilitating better market access (Bergmann 2021, p. 369–370). For V2/V4, an envisaged site approximately one kilometer away, near a planned road, was identified but not secured because the state failed to acquire land and the private owner "allegedly inflated prices above market standards" (Bergmann 2021, p. 369).

Bergmann (2021, p. 370) notes that relocation planners "paid limited attention to people's lifestyles" at the new site — "the newly designated, smaller lots complicated traditional activities like raising free-range animals" — indicating insufficient co-design of receiving areas. No state construction of new housing is documented for either case; V1/V3 rebuilt homes independently. Social carrying capacity assessments are not documented in the reviewed sources.

---

### What uses were planned for retreat lands?

**Answer:** **Reducing/eliminating servicing** (documented for V2/V4 following the 2017 uninhabitability declaration).

**Narrative:** After V2/V4's original site was declared uninhabitable in 2017, "authorities stopped promised investments in education, health, sanitation, and water" (Bergmann 2021, p. 368) — effectively eliminating servicing before relocation had occurred. Bergmann (2021, p. 368) notes that "such service discontinuation often causes marginalization in relocations." Photographs in Bergmann (2021, Fig. 3) show "decaying houses in abandoned site of V1," suggesting that V1/V3's original site was left to decay.

There is no evidence in the reviewed sources of formal rezoning, ecological restoration, demolition, site design, commemoration, conservation land trusts, or formal ownership transfer for either vacated site. **Demolition/infrastructure removal/asset retirement** is not coded because explicit evidence of deliberate clearing or removal is not established — what is documented is service discontinuation and apparent abandonment/decay, not formal managed decommissioning.

Case study: San Martin Planned Relocation (San Martin Region, Peru)
Section: COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT

---

### What degree of choice was provided to affected people in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Voluntary with strong persuasion** (for V1/V3, which self-initiated and drove the process despite severe structural constraints). For V2/V4, the situation more closely approximates the Aspirations-Capabilities Framework's category of **forced immobility (entrapment)** — high aspiration to move, very low capability due to structural constraints — though the formal legal framing is voluntary.

**Narrative:** Both communities self-initiated their relocation requests, suggesting a degree of voluntariness. However, Bergmann (2021, p. 367) emphasizes that "risk appraisal, fear and uncertainty, deprivations, and children's future prospects drove their decisions" — conditions that substantially constrain the meaning of "voluntary." V1/V3 fought for 15 years before achieving relocation. V2/V4 was effectively unable to move independently due to extreme poverty: interviewees felt like "going in circles, you are trapped" (V2-3, cited in Bergmann 2021, p. 371). Bergmann (2024) explicitly applies the Aspirations-Capabilities Framework to characterize V2/V4 as in "forced immobility (entrapment)" — high aspiration to move, low capability due to structural constraints (Bergmann 2024, Table 2.2).

Law No. 29869's participation rights are conditional — "when circumstances allow" and "with the necessary availability" — weakening their force (Bergmann 2021, footnote 7). Neither community faced completely involuntary mandated relocation; the law frames participation as voluntary. However, the structural reality, especially for V2/V4, significantly limits the meaning of voluntariness.

**Alternative interpretation:** One could code V2/V4's situation as "Involuntary with some degree of opt out" given the state's uninhabitability declaration in 2017, combined with continued trapped immobility due to poverty and government inaction. The codebook's "Voluntary with strong persuasion" better captures the formal framing, while the source material supports interpreting V2/V4's actual situation as closer to entrapment.

---

### What land user groups were involved or considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Homeowners** (community members as land users, though formal titles were absent at the new site); **Community/NGO** (community organizations driving the process); **First Nations/Indigenous** (V2/V4, indígena community); **Government.**

**Narrative:** Both communities are smallholder farming communities whose members are effectively homeowners and land users, though formal property titles were lacking at the new site for V1/V3 as of 2019 (Bergmann 2021, p. 368). V2/V4 represents an Indigenous land user group with distinct cultural identity and collective land governance norms (Bergmann 2021, p. 366). Community organizations played a key role: V1/V3 staged demonstrations and organized collective labour; V2/V4 maintained mutual assistance systems (Bergmann 2021, pp. 369–370). Local and regional government entities were the responsible implementation bodies. No evidence of commercial renters or leased land arrangements is documented.

Case study: High River Buyout Program (High River, Alberta, Canada)
Section: Case Study Overview

**Framing Note:** CS18 does not represent a single, site-specific managed retreat project. Rather, it is a synthesis drawn from three policy-oriented reports examining multiple distinct Canadian managed retreat examples. The primary sources are: a 2020 NRCan report covering six Canadian case studies (Surrey, High River, Great Lakes, Pointe Gatineau, Tuktoyaktuk, and Truro); a 2020 CIGI policy brief focused mainly on property buyout program design considerations, using High River, Gatineau, and Grand Forks as illustrative examples; and a 2023 Partners for Action report providing detailed comparative evaluation of buyout programs in High River, Gatineau, and Grand Forks. This memo synthesizes findings across these three reports rather than describing a single managed retreat project.

**Case Name and Location:** Multiple Canadian locations, spanning British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec, Ontario, the Northwest Territories, and Nova Scotia. All are in Canada (Global North). The primary cases covered are:

- **High River, Alberta** — reactive riverine flood buyout (2013 flood trigger)
- **Pointe Gatineau, Quebec** — reactive riverine flood buyout (2017 and 2019 flood triggers)
- **Grand Forks, British Columbia** — reactive riverine flood buyout (2018 flood trigger)
- **Surrey, British Columbia** — proactive coastal flood adaptation planning (2016–2019 planning phase; no retreat implemented)
- **Tuktoyaktuk, Northwest Territories** — community-scale coastal erosion and permafrost-driven relocation (ongoing)
- **Truro/Onslow, Nova Scotia** — managed realignment of dyke infrastructure with tidal wetland restoration (post-2012 policy window)
- **Great Lakes, Ontario** — reactive and proactive road and infrastructure realignment along Lake Erie's northern coastline

The NRCan report covers all six cases; the CIGI policy brief and the Partners for Action report focus primarily on High River, Gatineau, and Grand Forks.

**Hazard(s):** The primary hazard driving retreat in the three main buyout cases (High River, Gatineau, Grand Forks) is riverine flooding. Coastal flooding, storm surge, and sea-level rise are the primary hazards in Surrey. Coastal erosion and permafrost degradation co-occur in Tuktoyaktuk. Truro faces riverine flooding, tidal flooding, ice jam flooding, and the combined effect of regional tectonic subsidence and sea-level rise. The Great Lakes case involves coastal erosion, bluff erosion, and lake-level rise. Climate change is identified across all three reports as an amplifying driver of the underlying natural hazards [Sources 1, 2, 3].

**Type of Retreat:** Predominantly voluntary property buyouts of individual residences (High River, Gatineau, Grand Forks), with involuntary elements present in some programs. Also includes: managed realignment of dyke infrastructure and conversion of agricultural land to salt marsh (Truro); road and infrastructure realignment (Great Lakes); and phased community-scale relocation from a low-lying peninsula (Tuktoyaktuk). Surrey remains at the planning stage, with no retreat implemented in the Coastal Flood Adaptation Strategy (CFAS) cycle reviewed.

**Scale:**
- *High River:* 94 homes purchased by the Alberta government; mandatory evacuation of all 13,000 residents during the June 2013 flood; over 6,300 buildings damaged; approximately 60% of the town affected [Sources 1, 3].
- *Pointe Gatineau:* Approximately 1,800 properties affected by flooding in the wider Gatineau municipality during the 2017 floods; more than 250 single detached houses demolished as of 2019; over 185 home and condominium buyout acceptances as of November 2019; more than 4,000 people evacuated during the 2017 flood; the Government of Quebec paid approximately $50 million for buybacks, with compensation caps raised to $325,000 as of 2022 [Sources 1, 3].
- *Grand Forks:* 1,471 households ordered to evacuate during the 2018 flood; approximately 400 homes experienced moderate to major damage; 73 properties targeted for buyout; 63 of 73 property owners accepted offers by June 2021; City Council expropriated 3 properties as of 2022 [Sources 1, 3].
- *Surrey:* Population of approximately 520,000; approximately 20% of the city within the coastal floodplain; CFAS involved $76 million in federal DMAF funding plus $61.3 million from the City and $49.1 million in third-party funding, for an expected total investment of $187 million for the study and 13 associated adaptation projects; no properties retreated [Source 1].
- *Tuktoyaktuk:* Population of approximately 900 people, comprised primarily of Inuvialuit; $892,000 in federal funding (Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, Climate Change Preparedness in the North Program) to support relocation of 4 homes at highest risk; $2.84 million for a subsequent hybrid structural coastal design phase [Source 1].
- *Truro:* The $400,000 flood risk study (funded jointly by the Nova Scotia Environment Climate Change groups' Flood Assessment Fund, Town of Truro, and County of Colchester) led to the Truro-Onslow Dyke project; dyke realignment and restoration design work was carried out for a 135-ha wetland site [Source 1].

**Key Actors:** Federal government (Natural Resources Canada, Public Safety Canada, Disaster Mitigation and Adaptation Fund/DMAF, Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada); provincial governments (Alberta, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Northwest Territories); municipalities (Town of High River, City of Gatineau, City of Grand Forks, City of Surrey, Hamlet of Tuktoyaktuk, Town of Truro, County of Colchester); First Nations (Semiahmoo First Nation in Surrey; Millbrook First Nation in Truro; Inuvialuit governance in Tuktoyaktuk, consistent with the 1984 Inuvialuit Final Agreement and the 2008 UNDRIP); consulting and engineering firms; NGOs and community organizations (Canadian Red Cross, Mennonite Disaster Service, Samaritan's Purse, Boundary Flood Recovery Team in Grand Forks); and academic researchers (Partners for Action/University of Waterloo, Saint Mary's University, and others) [Sources 1, 3].

**Timeline:** The cases span from early reactive programs (High River 2013; Pointe Gatineau 2017 and 2019; Grand Forks 2018) to proactive planning (Surrey CFAS 2016–2019) and a long-running incremental community relocation (Tuktoyaktuk, ongoing since the 1970s with active funding from 2019–2020 onward). The Truro flood risk study was commissioned in 2017 following the 2012 storm that opened a policy window. The three reports were published in 2020 and 2023.

**Key Outcomes:**
- *High River:* 94 homes purchased and most demolished; 54 demolished, 26 auctioned for relocation, 14 remain standing but uninhabited; CP Railway bridge removed; characterized as top-down and non-collaborative; compensation at tax-assessed value widely criticized as inadequate; significant community anger, confusion, and mental health consequences; retreated lands received only basic naturalization [Sources 1, 3].
- *Pointe Gatineau:* Over 250 homes demolished as of 2019; ongoing program with successive flood events triggering expansions; community visioning and land beautification process initiated (arboretum, pedestrian walkways, commemorative spaces; $1.4 million municipal beautification budget; $80,000 committee grant); bureaucratic delays and insufficient on-the-ground support documented; compensation caps raised over time [Sources 1, 3].
- *Grand Forks:* 63 of 73 targeted properties acquired by June 2021; notable for one-on-one intake meetings and use of a cost-benefit analysis (ROI 3.4:1); equity concerns documented for the lowest-income neighbourhood (North Ruckle); city controversially converted some acquired homes into temporary rental properties; 3 properties expropriated [Sources 1, 3].
- *Surrey:* Retreat not pursued in the CFAS cycle reviewed; preserved as a potential future option; extensive public engagement documented [Source 1].
- *Tuktoyaktuk:* 4 homes relocated in 2020; persistent challenges with funding, relocation destination planning, and community consent; hybrid structural approach now underway [Source 1].
- *Truro:* Dyke realignment and tidal wetland restoration project emerged from flood risk study; presented as an example of voluntary, community-engaged managed realignment; landowners were free to reject purchase offers [Source 1].

---

**Narrative Summary:**

Canada faces increasing flood risk driven by climate change, and managed retreat — the purposeful relocation of people and property away from high-risk areas — is gaining recognition as a necessary adaptation tool. The three reviewed reports suggest that Canadian retreat efforts are often reactive, fragmented, and unsupported by a dedicated federal funding program. Most retreat programs have been triggered by disasters, implemented under time pressure, and criticized for insufficient community engagement, unclear compensation, and bureaucratic delays.

The three most extensively documented case studies — High River (2013 flood), Pointe Gatineau (2017 and 2019 floods), and Grand Forks (2018 flood) — illustrate a spectrum of approaches. High River represents a rapid but top-down, poorly communicated program that achieved fast property acquisition at significant social cost, generating anger and confusion among flood-affected residents. Pointe Gatineau demonstrates a province-led, multi-wave buyout program that improved over time but was hampered by bureaucratic complexity, capped compensation, and inadequate on-the-ground support. Grand Forks, while also reactive, employed a more systematic approach involving one-on-one homeowner meetings, cost-benefit analysis, and alignment with a broader flood mitigation strategy, although equity concerns persisted for the lowest-income neighbourhood and some residents were frustrated by compensation levels and process uncertainty.

Across all cases, the reports converge on several consistent findings: managed retreat is most effective when pursued proactively rather than reactively; compensation must be adequate for homeowners to replicate their quality of life elsewhere; community engagement must be early, transparent, and ongoing; intergovernmental roles must be clarified; and the needs of vulnerable populations must be explicitly addressed. Surrey demonstrates that proactive, collaborative planning can build public support for retreat even when the option is not immediately implemented. The sources indicate that retreat in remote northern settings — exemplified by Tuktoyaktuk — faces distinct funding, technical, and relocation-site constraints, suggesting that no single model fits all contexts across Canada's diverse geographies and communities.

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** **Reactive** is the primary code across the majority of cases. **Proactive** elements are evidenced in Surrey and, to a limited degree, in the Truro and Great Lakes cases.

**Narrative:** The dominant pattern across all reviewed cases is reactive retreat following disaster events. The NRCan report states: "retreat is most often implemented as a reactive measure, typically following a natural disaster such as a flooding event" [Source 1]. High River's buyout was announced approximately two months after the 2013 flood; Pointe Gatineau's program was launched within weeks of the 2017 flood and expanded after 2019; Grand Forks' program followed the May 2018 flood. The Partners for Action report confirms: "All three case study programs were established reactively to a major flood event" [Source 3].

Proactive elements are documented in several cases. Surrey's Coastal Flood Adaptation Strategy (CFAS), running 2016–2019, was a forward-looking, five-phase planning exercise that included retreat as one of several adaptation options — initiated before any major coastal disaster. The Truro flood risk study, commissioned in 2017 following the 2012 storm, explicitly incorporated climate change projections to 2100, giving it a forward-looking dimension even if the initial impetus was reactive to the 2012 storm event; the NRCan report characterizes this as a study that opened a "policy window for change" [Source 1]. The NRCan report notes that the Great Lakes (Ontario) case represents reactive post-erosion retreat being used "constructively as a trigger and signal about the need for proactive climate change adaptation" [Source 1]; however, this characterization reflects the NRCan report's interpretation of that case rather than a formal proactive classification of the retreat program itself. Tuktoyaktuk has engaged in incremental, research-informed relocation for decades, though the pace has been constrained by funding and logistical challenges rather than driven by pre-emptive planning.

**Category selection:** Reactive is the primary code. Proactive is a secondary code, applicable clearly to Surrey, and with more limited evidence for Truro (proactive study, reactive trigger) and the Great Lakes (proactive assessment following reactive road realignment). The codebook permits multiple selections where both apply.

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards** for several cases; **Single Hazard** (riverine flooding) as the primary documented driver for others.

In Surrey, sea-level rise, coastal erosion, storm surge, and enhanced riverine/pluvial flooding are all considered. Truro faces riverine flooding, tidal flooding, ice jam flooding, and the combined effect of regional tectonic subsidence and climate change-related sea-level rise [Source 1]. The Great Lakes case involves lake-level rise, coastal erosion, and bluff erosion operating together. In High River, Pointe Gatineau, and Grand Forks, the primary documented hazard driving the retreat decision is riverine flooding, though climate change projections of increased precipitation are discussed as future compounding factors.

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** for all cases. Climate change is identified throughout all three reports as a key amplifying driver of these natural hazards, not as a separate hazard origin category.

**Narrative:** The retreat triggers discussed across all case studies are natural hazards: riverine flooding, coastal erosion, sea-level rise, permafrost degradation, storm surge, tidal flooding, lake-level rise, and ice jams. No technological hazards (industrial accidents, dam collapses, etc.) are described as drivers of retreat decisions in any of the reviewed sources. Climate change is consistently identified as amplifying the frequency and severity of these natural hazards, and several cases (Surrey, Tuktoyaktuk, Truro) explicitly incorporate climate projections into planning [Sources 1, 2, 3].

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat / Community buyout/retreat / Leasebacks, easements and buffers / Other acquisition tools / Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (primary across High River, Pointe Gatineau, Grand Forks); **Community buyout/retreat** (Tuktoyaktuk, and partially for the Wallaceville and North Ruckle neighbourhood-wide acquisitions); **Managed realignment of infrastructure** (Truro dyke project; Great Lakes road realignments); **Other acquisition tools** (Grand Forks' temporary title-retention option).

**Narrative:** The dominant form across the three main case studies is individual property buyout — government acquisition of private residential properties from individual owners [Sources 1, 3]. In Wallaceville (High River) and North Ruckle (Grand Forks), the entire neighbourhood was targeted, giving these a community buyout character [Sources 1, 3]. Tuktoyaktuk is explicitly a community-scale relocation [Source 1]. Truro and the Great Lakes cases primarily involve managed realignment of infrastructure (dykes and roads) rather than household retreat, though landowner consultation was part of the Truro process [Source 1].

In Grand Forks, property owners were offered the option to retain title and stay in their homes temporarily even after their offer was settled and funds dispersed; the Partners for Action report identifies this as "an important factor in encouraging property owners to accept a buyout" [Source 3]. This constitutes an "other acquisition tool." The NRCan report mentions land swaps, buy-and-leaseback, and easements as tools used by various communities internationally and noted as creative options, but these are not documented as central mechanisms in the primary Canadian case studies reviewed [Source 1].

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Legal authority over retreat**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Land rezoning**, **Compliance & enforcement**, and **Litigation** (limited — expropriation proceedings) are all evidenced.

**Narrative:**

- *Relevant regulations/acts:* Following the 2017 Pointe Gatineau flood, provincial legislation banned home reconstruction in the 1:20-year floodplain [Sources 1, 3]. New Alberta provincial regulations on floodway development and restrictions on Disaster Recovery Fund (DRF) eligibility were announced alongside the High River buyout program [Source 1]. The federal DMAF funding for Grand Forks required that any acquired property be returned to its natural state [Source 3].

- *Legal authority over retreat:* Jurisdictional complexity is a recurring theme. The CIGI brief notes that local governments have delegated land-use authority but often lack fiscal capacity, while provincial governments have superior capacity but may override local preferences [Source 2]. The Partners for Action report finds that Canada's approach involves "repeated negotiation and contestation between provinces, municipalities and residents" [Source 2, as cited in Source 3].

- *Home acquisition:* All three main case studies involved formal legal acquisition of private residential properties [Sources 1, 3].

- *Land acquisition:* Grand Forks approved a Land Acquisition Program; Pointe Gatineau involved municipal acquisition of land; High River involved provincial acquisition with subsequent demolition authority [Sources 1, 3].

- *Title(s) transfer:* In Pointe Gatineau, property owners transferred ownership to the City of Gatineau for the symbolic sum of $1 after accepting buyout [Source 3]. In Grand Forks, titles transferred to the city.

- *Land rezoning:* Quebec prohibited rebuilding or future redevelopment in the 1:20 floodplain — a de facto rezoning instrument [Sources 1, 3]. Grand Forks' DMAF funding required no further residential development on acquired lands [Source 3]. The NRCan report identifies post-retreat rezoning as an important follow-up step [Source 1].

- *Compliance & enforcement:* Restrictions on future disaster assistance eligibility for homeowners who declined buyouts in High River and Pointe Gatineau function as compliance mechanisms [Sources 1, 3]. Grand Forks reserved the right to expropriate [Source 3].

- *Litigation:* Grand Forks expropriated 3 properties as of 2022, implying legal proceedings [Source 3]. In High River, when some residents suggested waiting for expropriation, the Mayor indicated this would be done at post-flood market value — functioning as a deterrent rather than an actual legal process [Source 1].

- *Retreat land development:* The NRCan report states that the Alberta FRP did not intend to allow rebuilding on vacated lots [Source 3]. DMAF funding conditions similarly prohibit further residential development on acquired Grand Forks properties [Source 3].

**Answer:** **Multiple funders** across all main cases, with combinations of **Federal**, **Provincial/State**, and **Local/Municipal** funding.

**Narrative:**

- *High River:* Provincial (Alberta) government funded the Floodway Relocation Program ($137M provincial allocation; $92.9M spent on High River) [Sources 1, 3]. - *Truro:* Joint provincial (Nova Scotia Environment Climate Change groups' Flood Assessment Fund), Town of Truro, and County of Colchester ($400,000 flood risk study) [Source 1].
