Case study: Allenville (Allenville, Arizona, United States)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

### Case Name and Location
Allenville, Arizona, United States (relocated to Hopeville, Arizona). Allenville was a small, unincorporated rural community situated near the Gila River in the southwestern United States, in the Buckeye Valley area of Maricopa County.

### Hazard(s)
Recurrent, severe riverine flooding caused by upstream water management releases from reservoirs on the Salt River, Verde River, and Agua Fria River — the three rivers converging into the Gila River approximately 15 miles east of Allenville. Perry & Lindell (1997) explain that major water releases were required during periods of heavy rain and snow-melt on northern Arizona watersheds to avoid the possibility of dam collapse, making repeated seasonal flooding of Allenville essentially inevitable once the water management infrastructure was in place.

### Type of Retreat
This was a community-scale, permanent relocation in which an entire small settlement was collectively moved intact to a newly constructed site (Hopeville) on nearby state land, selected jointly by the community organization and government agencies. The process involved the negotiated sale of Allenville properties and acquisition of the new Hopeville site. No demolition of Allenville structures is explicitly documented in the reviewed sources.

### Scale
At the time of relocation, Allenville was composed of 15 permanent homes and 20 mobile homes — 35 housing units in total [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. Twenty-six of these households were interviewed at the new Hopeville site; an additional six households that relocated elsewhere in the Buckeye Valley area were also traced and interviewed [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. The community rarely exceeded fifty households [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. The community was predominantly Black American, older (more than 20% over the age of 60 and another 30% between 41 and 59), and economically disadvantaged, with a median family income of just above $7,000 per year and approximately one-third of families below the federally established poverty level [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50, citing Arizona Division of Emergency Management, 1979, and Army Corps of Engineers, 1980].

### Key Actors
- **Allenville Citizens for Progress (ACP):** A non-profit community organization formed in 1965 with an elected Board of Directors that served as the primary community representative and negotiating agent throughout the relocation process [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **Arizona State Division of Emergency Management (Arizona DEM):** Served as the local sponsor of the relocation [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **U.S. Army Corps of Engineers:** Conducted a cost study of various structural and non-structural mitigation measures and participated in site selection [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA):** Listed among the principal agencies in the multi-organizational relocation context [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 54]; FEMA had also incorporated relocation into its national hazard mitigation strategy [FEMA, 1995, cited in Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 49].
- **Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) — Phoenix office:** Listed among agencies interviewed for the case study and among the principal agencies involved [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50, 54].
- **Maricopa County Department of Community Development:** Listed among agencies interviewed and among the principal agencies [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50, 54]. Perry & Lindell's description refers to "a County Office of Community Development."
- **Private businesses:** Also mentioned among actors in the multi-organizational context, though without detail [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 54].

### Timeline
- **1940s:** Allenville established near the Gila River by unskilled agricultural workers [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **1965:** First flooding along the Gila River to affect Allenville (affecting only a small part of the community); ACP established [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 50–51].
- **March 1978:** A large upstream water release floods the entire community; water marks as high as six feet above ground level; all residents evacuated; extensive property damage; most buildings rendered uninhabitable [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51].
- **Late 1970s–early 1980s:** Additional major floods; decision to pursue relocation emerges; Army Corps of Engineers conducts a cost study of structural and non-structural alternatives; ACP petitions to establish its formal legal standing to represent the community; site selection and property negotiations begin [Perry & Lindell, 1997, pp. 51–52].
- **Interim period:** A period of more than three years elapsed between residents leaving Allenville and occupying Hopeville; most residents lived in a mobile home park (interim housing) administered by Arizona DEM; a few families were scattered in communities throughout the area [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 52].
- **Completion:** Residents moved into the newly constructed community of Hopeville; "both the relocatees and the agencies involved in the relocation characterized the move in positive, successful terms" [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 53].
- **Post-relocation (retrospective):** Perry & Lindell (1997) conducted their research approximately six months after relocated citizens had moved to Hopeville; the case is described as post-retreat in the reviewed literature.
- **1997:** Perry & Lindell's retrospective case study published, documenting outcomes.

### Key Outcomes
The Allenville-to-Hopeville relocation is frequently cited in the managed retreat literature as a positive example of intact community relocation [Greer & Binder, 2017; Greer et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2025; Cross et al., 2025]. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) report that "virtually all citizens questioned expressed satisfaction with the move," and that both relocatees and agencies characterized the move in positive, successful terms. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) also note that "Hopeville has flourished, slightly increasing population size over the years, although remaining a close-knit, racially and economically homogeneous community." Job opportunities increased following the construction of a nuclear power plant in the region; completion of an interstate highway to California improved access and increased commerce; and a cultural museum was constructed and operated by the community association [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 53]. The primary documented challenges included the lengthy interim waiting period (over three years), anxiety during the interim housing phase, concerns about distance to services, and modest financial uncertainty among lower-income residents. A small number of households (six, from Perry & Lindell's interview sample) relocated outside the planned community site rather than to Hopeville.

**Important caveat:** These post-relocation outcomes are reported by Perry & Lindell (1997) in a retrospective case study conducted approximately six months after residents moved to Hopeville, with longer-term positive observations (nuclear power plant, interstate highway, museum) apparently based on the authors' knowledge at the time of writing rather than systematic longitudinal monitoring. The sources do not report independent verification or formal evaluation of these outcomes.

### Narrative Summary

Allenville was a small, predominantly Black American community established in the early 1940s near the Gila River in Arizona's Buckeye Valley. For decades it remained a close-knit, racially and economically homogeneous rural settlement, rarely exceeding fifty households. Residents were predominantly older and working-class, with many living on fixed retirement incomes, and the community operated under an active non-profit organization — the Allenville Citizens for Progress (ACP) — in the absence of formal municipal incorporation. Beginning in 1965, the construction of upstream water management reservoirs made seasonal flooding of the Gila River increasingly severe. After the catastrophic March 1978 flood, which inundated the entire community and left water marks up to six feet above ground level, both the ACP and Arizona emergency management officials concluded that the town was in an untenable position. ACP investigated whether the upstream water releases could be stopped or whether structural flood protection (levees, channelization) was feasible, ultimately concluding neither option was viable. The decision to pursue permanent relocation emerged jointly from the community and state emergency management during roughly the same period.

The relocation process was organized around ACP's formal recognition as the community's legal bargaining agent — established through a community petition — and implemented through a multi-agency consortium including Arizona DEM (as local sponsor), the Army Corps of Engineers, FEMA, HUD's Phoenix office, and the Maricopa County Department of Community Development. A new community site was selected from nearby state lands through a joint process between ACP and the agencies. Most residents lived in a mobile home park administered by Arizona DEM during the interim period of more than three years between leaving Allenville and occupying Hopeville. Throughout this period, ACP maintained regular communications with residents to minimize rumor and maintain morale, and sought visible support from state and county political figures to reassure relocatees.

The case is frequently cited in the managed retreat literature as a positive example of community-centered relocation, notable for the pre-existing strength of ACP, the community's own framing of the process as an effort to preserve Allenville as a community rather than a displacement imposed from outside, and the maintenance of social networks during the transition. Perry & Lindell (1997) report broad resident satisfaction and describe Hopeville as having flourished in subsequent years. The relocation is now used as a reference point for principles of effective, citizen-centered community relocation across the hazard mitigation and managed retreat literature.

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Primarily **Reactive**, with elements of community-level forward planning embedded within the reactive context.

**Narrative:** The Allenville relocation was fundamentally triggered by experienced and repeated flood damage, culminating in the catastrophic March 1978 flood. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 51) document that "several other major floods during the late 1970s and early 1980s made it clear, to emergency managers and to community residents, that the town was in an untenable position." The relocation decision gained serious momentum only after this accumulated damage made the hazard situation undeniable — a classic reactive pattern.

At the same time, modest forward-planning dimensions are present within this reactive context. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 51) note that "dated records appear to indicate that each group was considering relocation as an option during approximately the same period" — suggesting that ACP and Arizona DEM were beginning to explore options concurrently rather than waiting passively for the worst event. ACP also investigated stopping upstream releases and explored structural alternatives before concluding these were unworkable. This represents deliberate information-gathering and option-analysis within the reactive context, but it does not constitute a proactive programme initiated in advance of demonstrated harm.

Greer & Binder (2017) cite the Allenville case in their historical review of home buyout policy as an early example of community-scale relocation. Cross et al. (2025) and Weber et al. (2025) both note that reactive managed retreat is the dominant pattern in the United States — consistent with how this case fits the literature.

**Coding:** **Reactive** (primary). The community's own deliberations had a forward-planning quality, but the overall programme was reactive in nature, responding to accumulated flood loss rather than anticipating future risk before harm occurred.

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**
- **Date:** Relocation process: late 1970s–early 1980s (following the March 1978 flood as the decisive trigger); a period of more than three years elapsed between residents leaving Allenville and occupying Hopeville; Perry & Lindell's case study published 1997.
- **Number of housing units:** 35 (15 permanent homes and 20 mobile homes) [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. Of these, 26 households were interviewed at Hopeville and 6 additional households who relocated elsewhere in the Buckeye Valley area were also traced and interviewed [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **Number of population affected:** Not explicitly stated in any reviewed source. The community rarely exceeded fifty households [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50], with a population skewed older (more than 20% over age 60; 30% between ages 41–59) [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50].
- **Total funding:** Not specified in any reviewed source. No funding figures, grant names, or cost-sharing arrangements are documented in Perry & Lindell (1997) or any other reviewed source. Perry & Lindell (1997) focused on management principles rather than financial details.

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Single Hazard** — recurrent riverine flooding.

**Narrative:** All reviewed sources describe a single hazard — recurrent flooding caused by upstream water management releases into the Gila River — as the basis for the relocation decision. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 51) are explicit: "Recurrent, severe flooding was the ultimate undoing of Allenville." No additional hazards (wildfire, earthquake, or other) are mentioned in connection with the retreat decision. The flooding was recurrent and seasonal rather than a single discrete event, but it represents a single hazard type.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** Best classified as **Technological Hazard** with a natural context.

**Narrative:** While the underlying medium is riverine flood water (a natural phenomenon), Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 51) explain clearly that the recurrent, severe flooding of Allenville was a direct consequence of water management releases from upstream reservoirs on the Salt River, Verde River, and Agua Fria River — releases made necessary to protect those dams from collapse during heavy rain and snow-melt periods. ACP verified this causal mechanism [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51], and the flooding would not have reached Allenville with the severity it did in the absence of the upstream water management infrastructure.

The codebook defines "Technological hazard" as events "related to the built environment and human technologies (industrial accident, dam collapse, oil spill, etc.)" and "Natural hazard" as events like earthquakes that naturally occur. The Allenville case sits at the intersection: the water itself is natural, but the severity and inevitability of the flooding was structurally produced by human water management operations. Classifying it as technological hazard is the more defensible coding given the mechanism Perry & Lindell (1997) describe. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) also note that this framing — as a situation "where human technological capacity has failed in its ability to protect" — helped the community avoid blame dynamics and conceptualize relocation as a self-protective act rather than an external imposition.

**Note on uncertainty:** This classification is an interpretation of the causal mechanism described by Perry & Lindell (1997). A reasonable alternative classification as "Natural hazard" (riverine flooding in its physical manifestation) could be defended. The technological classification is preferred here because the flood risk was structurally determined by upstream infrastructure operations rather than natural precipitation patterns alone.

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), (Lake Flooding/Erosion), (Wildfire), (Volcano), (Land Subsidence), (Landslide/Debris Flow), (Earthquake), (Tsunami), (Hurricane), (Other)

**Answer:** **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding.**

**Narrative:** The hazard was flooding connected to the Gila River system, caused by upstream releases from reservoirs on the Salt, Verde, and Agua Fria Rivers. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 51) describe water marks as high as six feet above ground level in the 1978 flood. This is unambiguously riverine flooding. No coastal, lake, wildfire, seismic, or other hazard types are referenced in the retreat decision.

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Entire community.**

**Narrative:** The Allenville relocation involved the collective movement of an entire small, unincorporated community — approximately 35 housing units — to a newly constructed site (Hopeville) on nearby state land. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) explicitly frame the case as "the specific case where an entire community is moved intact," distinguishing it from partial or household-level relocations. The relocation authority formally recognized ACP as representing the entire community. The process was understood by both residents and agencies as a collective, community-scale relocation rather than a set of individual household transactions.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Communities.**

**Narrative:** Allenville residents were relocated collectively as an intact community. Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 53) note: "Hopeville has flourished, slightly increasing population size over the years, although remaining a close-knit, racially and economically homogeneous community." The relocation was explicitly conceptualized by residents and ACP as an effort to "preserve Allenville" as a community rather than to disperse individuals [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 51]. No infrastructure, industrial assets, or hazard protection structures are described as being retreated in the reviewed sources.

### Other notes (General Information)

The Allenville case is primarily documented through Perry & Lindell's (1997) retrospective case study, published approximately 15–20 years after the relocation occurred. Data collection began approximately six months after relocated citizens moved to Hopeville [Perry & Lindell, 1997, p. 50]. The case is cited in multiple subsequent sources (Greer & Binder, 2017; Greer et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2025; Cross et al., 2025) as a historical reference point for community-scale relocation and buyout principles, rather than as an active or recent case. Those supplemental sources provide general managed retreat framing and do not supply Allenville-specific factual details beyond what Perry & Lindell (1997) contain.

Several supplemental sources listed in the case file — Schwaller et al. (2025), Niemann-Morris et al. (2025), Hotard & Ross (2023), Ahmed Bin Zaman et al. (2026), and Baker et al. (2018) — were reviewed and do not appear to contain substantial case-specific material on Allenville/Hopeville. They are primarily general managed retreat literature reviews or studies focused on other locations. No information from these sources has been attributed to Allenville-specific facts in this memo.

Perry & Lindell (1997) describe the relocation of an intact small community from Allenville to a purpose-built new site (Hopeville), organized collectively through ACP, negotiated as a community-level transaction with state and federal agencies, and implemented with the explicit goal of preserving the community as a social unit. Individual property negotiations occurred within this collective framework. Weber et al. ### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** No direct evidence found for explicit tax base planning during the MR decision process. Limited indirect relevance through **New housing for BO recipients** (new community constructed) and the prospect of renters becoming property owners.

Perry & Lindell (1997, p. 52) note that some relocatees who had been renters "were able to purchase mobile homes at a reasonable price and obtain a relocation cash benefit which enabled them to purchase property" — this converted some non-property-owning residents to property owners at the new site, though the tax implications are not discussed.

Contemporary discussions of tax base management in managed retreat (as discussed in Greer et al., 2021, and Weber et al., 2025) do not address the Allenville case specifically in this regard.

**Coding note:** No evidence of explicit tax base planning. Code as **No direct evidence** for intentional tax base management.

Case study: Portland (Portland, Oregon, United States)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** East Lents Floodplain Restoration Project, Portland, Oregon, United States.

**Hazard(s):** Flooding, including riverine and stormwater-driven (fluvial, pluvial, and infrastructural) flood risk from Johnson Creek, a creek that runs through southeast Portland and is described as a recurring site of flooding.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary property buyout program. The City of Portland's Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) administers a "Willing Seller Program" associated with the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan, through which flood-prone residential properties in the East Lents neighborhood are acquired from willing homeowners, structures are demolished, and the land is converted to floodplain open space and ecological restoration areas.

**Scale:** The reviewed sources do not provide a precise count of acquired parcels or displaced households specifically for the East Lents project, nor do they document total funding amounts for this specific project. Lloyd et al. (2026) describe the Portland Johnson Creek Restoration Plan's "Willing Seller Program" as having "the highest number of buyout homes among our study cities" (Portland, Phoenix, Atlanta, and Baltimore), characterizing it as a successful program implemented at "limited scales." No household counts or dollar figures for the East Lents project specifically are available in the reviewed corpus.

**Key Actors:** The City of Portland Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) is the primary administering agency. Lloyd et al. (2026) list multiple agencies involved in Portland flood risk management, including the Portland Bureau of Planning and Sustainability (PBPS), Portland Bureau of Transportation (PBOT), Portland Water Bureau (PWB), Portland Park Bureau (PPB), Multnomah County Drainage District (MCDD), the Oregon Department of Emergency Management (ODEM), and FEMA Region 10, among others (see Appendix A of Lloyd et al., 2026). Federal funding through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) is identified in the broader Portland program context; Lloyd et al. (2026) also reference "federal and state money" in the context of Baltimore buyout sites, and the general HMGP structure described by Siders (2018) applies to programs of this type.

**Timeline:** The primary source cited in the project's source list is a 2012 City of Portland BES document. However, the full text of this document was not available in the reviewed corpus, so no project-specific start date or milestone chronology can be verified from the reviewed materials. Lloyd et al. (2026) describe Portland's buyout program as ongoing, with practitioners referencing flood events including a recorded peak flow in Johnson Creek in 2015 and the 1996 Oregon flood. The Vanucchi et al. (2025) study notes that exemplary U.S. buyout programs like Austin's began in the 1980s and operate as "standing programs," not solely post-disaster. Whether the broader Portland Johnson Creek program shares this standing-program character is suggested by Lloyd et al.'s (2026) description of BES being "proactive in restoration efforts," but no verified continuous timeline is available from the reviewed sources.

**Key Outcomes:** Outcomes described in the reviewed sources are general and programmatic rather than project-specific for East Lents. Lloyd et al. (2026) cite Portland's Willing Seller Program as an example of success in "negotiating voluntary buyouts" and "restoring floodplains." The intent of the program is to reduce flood exposure, demolish at-risk structures, and convert floodplain land to open space and ecological restoration. Broader literature (Vanucchi et al., 2025; Siders, 2018) notes that buyout programs of this type commonly result in structure demolition and open-space requirements under HMGP, but also that ecological restoration of post-buyout lands is often incomplete, with many parcels remaining as maintained lawns rather than restored floodplain habitats.

---

### Narrative Summary

The East Lents Floodplain Restoration Project is a voluntary property buyout and floodplain restoration effort in the East Lents neighborhood of Portland, Oregon, situated along Johnson Creek in the southeast of the city. Johnson Creek is described by Portland flood risk practitioners as "a site of recurring flooding," and Portland broadly faces "fluvial, pluvial, and infrastructural flood risk" expected to increase in the future (Lloyd et al., 2026). The project is part of Portland's Johnson Creek Restoration Plan and is administered by the City of Portland Bureau of Environmental Services (BES) through a "Willing Seller Program," under which individual homeowners voluntarily sell flood-prone properties to the city. Structures are then demolished and the land is maintained as open space, consistent with FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) requirements.

Portland practitioners interviewed by Lloyd et al. (2026) described Portland's program as having "the highest number of buyout homes among our study cities" — the four cities studied being Portland, Phoenix, Atlanta, and Baltimore — and cited the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan as a positive example of flood risk mitigation through voluntary buyouts. Practitioners noted that BES has been "proactive in restoration efforts to improve their drainage systems" and referenced the importance of integrating buyouts into a broader planning vision for floodplain restoration. The program has also been noted for connecting flood mitigation with other community benefits such as open space, recreation, and ecological function.

The reviewed literature also identifies important challenges. Voluntary buyout programs, as described by Siders (2018) and Vanucchi et al. (2025), typically produce scattered (checkerboard) patterns of acquisition over time, complicate comprehensive floodplain restoration, and leave many parcels in a state of incomplete ecological recovery — often maintained as mowed lawns rather than dynamic floodplain ecosystems. Equity concerns documented in the broader U.S. buyout literature — including unequal access to buyout offers depending on income and insurance status, and inadequate compensation for low-income homeowners — may be applicable to Portland's program context, though they are not directly documented for East Lents in the reviewed sources. The sources also caution against drawing firm conclusions about Portland-specific outcomes from the available evidence, as most detailed project data was not accessible in the reviewed corpus.

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Direct Answer: Reactive, with evidence suggesting some proactive elements at the broader program level.**

**Narrative:** Johnson Creek is described by Portland practitioners as "a site of recurring flooding," and Portland has experienced notable flood events including a major event in 1996 and a historic peak flow on Johnson Creek in 2015 (Lloyd et al., 2026). Siders (2018) notes that most U.S. buyout programs are initiated reactively after disasters, when HMGP and CDBG-DR funding becomes available. This reactive pattern is consistent with how Portland's buyout activity is situated in the context of historic flood events.

However, Lloyd et al. (2026) also describe Portland BES as "proactive in restoration efforts to improve their drainage systems," and the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan is presented as a deliberate, longer-term planning framework rather than solely a post-disaster response. Vanucchi et al. (2025) distinguish exemplary U.S. buyout programs as "standing programs" that operate continuously, including between disaster events, rather than being created only in the aftermath of a disaster. Lloyd et al.'s (2026) reference to Portland having "success in negotiating voluntary buyouts" and "restoring floodplains" as part of a broader resilience approach suggests a degree of proactive planning orientation.

**Coding rationale:** "Reactive" is the primary coding, given the program's historical roots in repetitive flood damage and reliance on disaster-linked federal funding structures described by Siders (2018). "Proactive" is a secondary and indirect inference based on practitioner accounts in Lloyd et al. (2026) describing a standing, anticipatory dimension to Portland's flood management approach. The auditor's preferred reading — "Reactive" as the strongest code, with "Proactive" retained only if labeled as an indirect inference from broader program literature — has been followed here.

**Uncertainty note:** The evidence for the proactive element is indirect, based on practitioner characterizations in a multi-city interview study rather than on documentation of a formal pre-disaster planning decision for East Lents specifically.

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Direct Answer: Individual buyout/retreat (primary); with a community planning context that gives the program a broader scope.**

**Narrative:** The East Lents project is primarily an individual voluntary property buyout program in which homeowners chose to sell their properties to the city. Siders (2018) describes FEMA's HMGP buyouts as voluntary individual transactions, and Lloyd et al. (2026) describe the Portland program as a "Willing Seller Program." The program is embedded within the Johnson Creek Restoration Plan, a broader neighbourhood-scale and watershed-scale planning effort, which gives it a collective planning character beyond purely individual transactions.

**Coding rationale:** "Individual buyout/retreat" is the primary coding. "Community buyout/retreat" is not strongly supported because the reviewed sources do not document a coordinated collective relocation of a settlement; rather, the program aggregates individual parcel acquisitions. The broader planning context (Johnson Creek Restoration Plan) is noted as contextual framing.

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Direct Answer:** Multiple legal categories are relevant. Evidence ranges from directly applicable general HMGP rules to Portland-specific references.

**Narrative by category:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) regulations govern eligibility, cost-benefit analysis requirements, and open-space deed restrictions post-acquisition (Siders, 2018). These apply to any HMGP-funded buyout, including programs of the type described in Portland.
- **Home acquisition:** Voluntary purchase of homes at pre-disaster fair market value as determined by a licensed appraiser is the standard HMGP mechanism (Siders, 2018). All HMGP acquisitions are voluntary; local officials may not use eminent domain or condemnation powers under HMGP (Siders, 2018).
- **Land acquisition:** HMGP-funded acquisitions within the 100-year floodplain require demolition and open-space maintenance in perpetuity (Siders, 2018).
- **Title(s) transfer:** Properties acquired through HMGP are transferred from private to public ownership, with deed restrictions preventing future development (Siders, 2018; Vanucchi et al., 2025).
- **Land rezoning:** Vanucchi et al. (2025) document that rezoning parcels to conservation land status is a best practice to prevent "collective amnesia" and future development pressure; they used local zoning data to assess conservation status of buyout parcels in their case studies. Whether Portland's parcels have been rezoned in this manner is not documented in the reviewed sources.
- **Retreat land development:** FEMA HMGP prohibits redevelopment of acquired floodplain properties; they must be maintained as open space. Since 2013, FEMA allows post-buyout climate resilience activities such as floodplain restoration to be factored into benefit-cost analysis (Vanucchi et al., 2025).
- **Compliance & enforcement:** FEMA deed restrictions enforced by federal requirements ensure permanent open-space status (Siders, 2018).
- **Legal authority over retreat:** Local governments administer HMGP buyouts with state oversight and federal funding; Portland BES administers the program (Lloyd et al., 2026; Siders, 2018).
- **Litigation:** Siders (2018) notes that in some U.S. buyout cases residents have filed lawsuits (e.g., Grand Forks, ND). No litigation evidence is found for East Lents in the reviewed sources.

**Uncertainty note:** Portland-specific legal instruments (Oregon state laws, Portland municipal ordinances) governing this project are not described in the reviewed sources. The above reflects general HMGP legal framework, which applies to programs of this type as described by Siders (2018), not Portland-specific verified documentation.

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Direct Answer: Federal (HMGP) funding is the primary identified source. State and local contributions are referenced in the broader Portland program context but not documented specifically for East Lents.**

**Narrative:** Siders (2018) describes the standard HMGP cost-sharing structure under which the federal government provides 75% of program costs and states or localities provide the remaining 25%, often from CDBG or other sources. Lloyd et al. (2026) reference the use of "federal and state money" in the context of Baltimore buyout sites following flooding, and more broadly describe Portland's program as funded through mechanisms consistent with this structure. The Vanucchi et al. (2025) study notes that exemplary standing buyout programs in the U.S. draw on a distinct mix of federal, state, and local funding that allows them to operate continuously.

**Coding rationale:** "Multiple funders" with Federal (HMGP) as primary is the most defensible coding at the level of the broader Portland program. The auditor's guidance has been followed: this coding is retained but explicitly labeled as applying to the broader program context, with a note that project-specific funding documentation for East Lents is not available in the reviewed corpus.

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Direct Answer: No direct evidence found for East Lents. Indirect evidence from the broader literature suggests this is not a primary consideration.**

**Narrative:** Siders (2018) discusses tax base concerns as a general factor in U.S. buyout programs, noting that buyouts reduce local property tax revenue and that some cities (e.g., New York City) have opposed buyouts partly for this reason. The reviewed sources do not document explicit tax base maintenance strategies for the East Lents project or Portland's Johnson Creek program.

**Coding rationale:** No code is assigned. The codebook category "Redevelopment of retreat lands" was considered but is not directly supported for East Lents; open-space conversion under HMGP prohibits revenue-generating redevelopment. The broader literature references conversion to parks and greenspace as a potential community benefit framing (Lloyd et al., 2026; Siders, 2018), but this is not the same as a tax base maintenance strategy.

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Direct Answer: Market value (pre-disaster fair market value) — this is the standard HMGP mechanism applicable to this program type.**

**Narrative:** Under HMGP, all buyouts require compensation at pre-disaster fair market value as determined by a licensed appraiser (Siders, 2018). This is the standard mechanism applicable to Portland's program, though it is described as a general rule rather than a Portland-specific verified finding. Siders (2018) notes that programs may offer additional incentive payments (e.g., New York's post-Sandy program offered bonuses for relocating within the city), but no such additional incentives are documented for East Lents.

Seong et al. (2025), studying Harris County HMGP buyouts, found that compensation disparities exist — with low-income homeowners more likely to perceive offers as inadequate and wealthier homeowners more likely to view offers as fair. This general pattern is plausibly relevant to Portland's context but is not directly documented for East Lents.

**Coding rationale:** "Market value" (pre-disaster FMV) is the primary coding, based on Siders' (2018) description of HMGP requirements. "Free supports and services (demolition)" was considered but the auditor correctly identified that demolition under HMGP is a project requirement (and a condition of receiving federal funds), not necessarily a benefit offered to individual sellers as compensation. It is therefore not coded as compensation here.

**Uncertainty note:** Whether Portland's specific program offered any relocation bonuses or additional incentives beyond standard HMGP FMV is not documented in the reviewed sources.

### What degree of choice was provided to affected people in the MR decision process?

**Direct Answer: Voluntary with incentives or future restrictions.**

**Narrative:** All FEMA HMGP-funded buyouts in the United States are designated as voluntary — homeowners may choose whether or not to accept a purchase offer, and local officials cannot use eminent domain or condemnation powers under HMGP (Siders, 2018). Portland's program follows this model; Lloyd et al. (2026) describe it as a "Willing Seller Program."

However, Siders (2018) and Bower et al. (2025) note that voluntariness in practice can be more complex: residents may experience coercive elements such as peer pressure, difficulty reselling flood-damaged homes, and legal restrictions against rebuilding substantially damaged structures, which can blur the line between fully voluntary and lightly coerced participation. Future floodplain restrictions and open-space deed restrictions on acquired land also mean that participation, while technically optional, involves future land-use constraints.

**Coding rationale:** "Voluntary with incentives or future restrictions" best captures the situation: participation is technically optional, but future floodplain restrictions create structural incentives that encourage participation. There is no evidence of strong persuasion or involuntary elements in the East Lents case.

Case study: Queens (Queens, New York, United States)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Resilient Edgemere Community Planning Initiative (RECPI), Edgemere neighborhood, Rockaway Peninsula, Queens, New York City, New York, United States.

**Hazard(s):** Coastal flooding is the primary hazard. Superstorm Sandy (October 2012) caused catastrophic storm surge and flood damage in Edgemere, with flood depths of over six feet recorded along the shoreline (Olivotto et al., 2025). The neighborhood also experiences chronic "blue sky" flooding — nuisance ponding during normal weather conditions — caused by historical landfilling of surrounding marshlands, built-over creeks, and high groundwater (Olivotto et al., 2025). Sea level rise and increasing frequency and intensity of coastal storms further elevate long-term risk (Olivotto et al., 2025). All study sites in the broader New York area, including Edgemere, also experienced regular nuisance or "sunny day" flooding due to low-lying topography, high water tables, and existing infrastructure (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).

**Type of Retreat:** A broader resilience and land-use planning initiative that included a limited voluntary buyout and acquisition component. The RECPI introduced zoning changes designating a Hazard Mitigation Zone (HMZ) that eliminates or limits new residential development in the most flood-exposed areas of the neighborhood. Seven property buyouts and acquisitions were completed as of September 2022, associated with NYC's post-Sandy recovery efforts (Olivotto et al., 2025). Olivotto et al. (2025) describe the bay-side area's current approach as consistent with a "soft, delayed retreat philosophy," whereby zoning changes mean that in the event of future catastrophic flooding, retreat may become the only viable option for remaining residents.

**Scale:** The neighborhood of Edgemere has a population of 8,885 (ACS 2015–2019, cited in Olivotto et al., 2025). Only 7 property buyouts and acquisitions were completed as of September 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The broader RECPI is neighborhood-wide, though its zoning and lot-management effects are spatially uneven.

**Key Actors:** New York City's Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) administered the buyout and acquisition program and owns most of the resulting vacant lots. The Mayor's Office of Resilience (MOR) co-led the RECPI. Community-based organizations active in the neighborhood include the Edgemere Community Civic Action (ECCA) and the Garden by the Bay community garden (Olivotto et al., 2025). A community-based organization (CBO) collaborated with researchers on community land visioning workshops (Olivotto et al., 2025). The New York State Governor's Office of Storm Recovery (GOSR) administered a separate state buyout program; the reviewed sources indicate GOSR buyouts were not completed in Edgemere, with the sources primarily discussing NYC-led efforts in this neighborhood (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) has a coastal storm risk management project planned for mid-Rockaway, still in design phase as of the review period (Olivotto et al., 2025).

**Timeline:** Superstorm Sandy struck October 29, 2012 (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024; Olivotto et al., 2025). The RECPI launched in 2015 as a multi-agency effort to address flood risk, post-Sandy recovery, and broader neighborhood conditions (Olivotto et al., 2025). Zoning changes, including the HMZ designation, followed. Seven property buyouts and acquisitions were completed between approximately 2015 and 2022. As of September 2022 (the latest field evidence in the reviewed sources), all 7 buyout and acquisition lots remained vacant; 6 were owned by HPD, and 1 had been transferred to the NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (Olivotto et al., 2025). Community land visioning workshops were held between November 2021 and March 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025). The case remained ongoing in the latest reviewed evidence.

**Key Outcomes:** As of the review period, key outcomes include: (1) seven buyout and acquisition lots completed — all remained vacant as of September 2022, with residents reporting concerns about neglect, rodent infestation, and safety (Olivotto et al., 2025); (2) a Community Land Trust (CLT) was proposed as a possible governance mechanism for 119 city-owned vacant lots for affordable housing and community stewardship, with implementation remaining uncertain (Olivotto et al., 2025); (3) new mixed-use and market-rate residential development was proposed and/or advancing in other parts of the neighborhood, raising gentrification and climate-risk concerns among residents and the local community board (Olivotto et al., 2025); (4) persistent community distrust of city agencies, rooted in decades of unfulfilled urban renewal promises; and (5) the USACE has a $252,544,000 coastal storm risk management project planned for mid-Rockaway still in design phase (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing USACE, 2019, 2023).

---

### Narrative Summary

Edgemere is a predominantly Black and Hispanic, low-lying coastal neighborhood on the Rockaway Peninsula in Queens, New York City. According to the ACS 2015–2019 estimates cited in Olivotto et al. (2025), the neighborhood has a population of 8,885; 59.4% of residents identify as African American and 35% as Hispanic. The neighborhood has long been exposed to coastal flooding and, in October 2012, Superstorm Sandy caused severe damage — flood depths exceeding six feet were recorded along the shoreline, destroying homes and infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat, electricity, or with water damage (Olivotto et al., 2025). In the years following Sandy, the city launched the Resilient Edgemere Community Planning Initiative in 2015, a multi-agency effort intended to simultaneously reduce flood risk, support disaster recovery, and address decades of neighborhood disinvestment (Olivotto et al., 2025).

The RECPI represents a hybrid approach. On one hand, it introduced a Hazard Mitigation Zone that limits or prohibits new residential development in the most flood-prone areas near the bay, and the city completed 7 voluntary property buyouts and acquisitions associated with post-Sandy recovery. On the other hand, the city simultaneously advanced large-scale mixed-use and market-rate residential development on other parts of the neighborhood — framed by city officials as a strategy to bring services and affordable housing to a long-disinvested community, but criticized by residents and researchers as risking climate gentrification and failing to address core community needs (Olivotto et al., 2025). The development plan, when fully built, would bring 1,201 residential units (approximately 38% as affordable housing) and almost 150,000 square feet of retail space (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing City of New York, 2020). Community Board 14 presented a unanimous resolution calling for a moratorium on all upzoning requests until an environmental impact study addressed concerns that new developments were not aligned with existing services and neighborhood character (Olivotto et al., 2025).

As of September 2022, the seven completed buyout and acquisition lots remained vacant, with residents reporting concerns about neglect, rodent infestation, and safety (Olivotto et al., 2025). These realities are inseparable from a long history of racial housing discrimination, failed urban renewal, the closure of the local hospital, inadequate transportation and food access, and broken promises by city agencies dating back to the 1997 Urban Renewal Area designation (Olivotto et al., 2025). Residents — many of whom moved to Edgemere because it was one of the few places they could afford to buy a home in New York City — express strong place attachment alongside justified skepticism of government-led retreat and restoration programs. The literature suggests that managed retreat in a historically disinvested, majority-minority neighborhood cannot be fully understood without attending to the entangled histories of contextual injustice that shape residents' vulnerability, their distrust of institutions, and their capacity to engage meaningfully with adaptation planning (Olivotto et al., 2025).

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Both **Reactive** and **Proactive** apply. Reactive is dominant; proactive elements are embedded in the subsequent planning and zoning framework.

**Narrative:** The immediate trigger for the Resilient Edgemere Community Planning Initiative was Superstorm Sandy (October 2012), a direct disaster event that caused severe flooding and property damage in Edgemere and across the Rockaway Peninsula (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The buyout and acquisition program was initiated through post-Sandy housing recovery mechanisms. In this sense, the retreat process is clearly **reactive** — it was triggered by disaster damage and enabled by post-disaster recovery programs and federal funding. Greer & Brokopp Binder (2017) document that most U.S. buyout programs are initiated using federal assistance made available after a federally declared disaster, a pattern to which Edgemere broadly conforms. Hotard (2026) similarly observes that most buyout programs are initiated reactively in post-disaster settings, providing general context for this pattern.

However, the broader RECPI, launched in 2015, incorporated significant **proactive** planning elements. The initiative introduced the Hazard Mitigation Zone that limits new residential development in the most flood-exposed areas, anticipating future flood risk rather than simply responding to past damage (Olivotto et al., 2025). Olivotto et al. (2025) describe the city's Coastal Land Use Framework as articulating a "soft, delayed retreat philosophy" for Edgemere's bay area, suggesting that anticipatory retreat planning is embedded in the current regulatory framework. Sea level rise and increasing frequency and intensity of coastal storms are cited as drivers requiring forward-looking managed retreat planning (Olivotto et al., 2025).

**Coding rationale:** Both Reactive and Proactive categories apply. Reactive is dominant (Sandy as trigger, post-disaster funding and recovery framing); proactive elements are embedded in the subsequent planning, zoning, and land use framework. The codebook permits multiple selections where both apply.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Direct Answer:**

- **Date:** Superstorm Sandy struck October 29, 2012 (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The RECPI launched 2015 (Olivotto et al., 2025). Buyouts and acquisitions completed approximately 2015–2022 (ongoing as of the review period).
- **Number of households (buyouts completed):** 7 buyout and acquisition lots as of September 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025). Mockrin & Johnson (2024) also reference approximately seven buyouts in Edgemere in their table of buyout participation. The sources.txt reference to a Build It Back Progress Update (October 2017) may contain additional figures, but that document was not reproduced in the reviewed materials and specific household counts for Edgemere buyouts alone are not disaggregated in the reviewed papers.
- **Number of population affected:** Edgemere has a population of 8,885 (ACS 2015–2019, cited in Olivotto et al., 2025). The RECPI planning initiative is neighborhood-wide, but completed retreat affects only the 7 buyout/acquisition households directly.
- **Total funding:** Not specified for the Edgemere buyouts alone in the reviewed sources. For broader context: $4.2 billion in HUD CDBG-DR was allocated to New York City post-Sandy (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024); $145 million was reported for Rockaway Sandy projects (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing Rose, 2017); and the USACE plans to invest $252,544,000 in coastal storm risk management in mid-Rockaway (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing USACE, 2019). Specific funding for the 7 Edgemere buyouts and acquisitions is not reported in the reviewed sources.

**Uncertainty:** The primary source (Spidalieri et al., 2020) is listed in sources.txt but its full text was not reproduced in the reviewed materials. All figures above derive from supplemental academic sources. The exact administrative linkage of all 7 buyout/acquisition lots to a specific program (e.g., Build It Back) is supported but should be stated cautiously, as Olivotto et al. (2025) refer to the Build It Back program in relation to the RECPI and property acquisitions, without specifying all 7 lots were processed through a single mechanism.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards**

**Narrative:** The reviewed sources identify several interacting hazards affecting Edgemere. Coastal flooding — including storm surge (as experienced during Superstorm Sandy), sea level rise, and recurring nuisance/blue-sky flooding — is the primary driver (Olivotto et al., 2025). Olivotto et al. (2025) specifically note that Edgemere experiences "blue sky flooding" related to historical landfilling of surrounding marshlands, built-over creeks, and high groundwater, which causes chronic ponding independent of storm events. Mockrin & Johnson (2024) confirm that all study sites including Edgemere regularly experienced nuisance or "sunny day flooding" due to low-lying topography, high water tables, and in some cases existing infrastructure. The hazard profile thus combines acute storm surge events (Sandy, hurricane risk) with chronic coastal and drainage-related flooding. Multiple hazards are present and interact.

**Coding rationale:** Multiple Hazards is the appropriate code because at least two distinct hazard types — acute storm surge/hurricane events and chronic nuisance/blue-sky flooding — are documented as affecting the retreat decision context.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** (with climate change as an amplifying driver)

**Narrative:** The primary hazards — coastal storm surge, sea level rise, and coastal/drainage-related flooding — are natural in origin. Olivotto et al. (2025) explicitly reference "sea level rise and increasing frequency and intensity of coastal storms" as drivers of managed retreat need in Edgemere. The historical anthropogenic modifications to Edgemere's landscape — landfilling of marshlands, built-over creeks, and delayed drainage infrastructure — increase flood vulnerability, but the hazards themselves are classified as natural rather than purely technological (Olivotto et al., 2025). No evidence of technological or industrial hazard as a primary driver was found in the reviewed sources.

**Coding rationale:** Natural Hazard is the primary code. If the codebook permits selection of Climate Change as a separate hazard origin, this is also supported, as sea level rise and intensifying storms are explicitly linked to climate change in the sources (Olivotto et al., 2025).

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:**

- **Coastal Flooding/Erosion:** ✓ Yes — primary hazard; storm surge from Sandy, sea level rise, and chronic coastal flooding are all documented (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).
- **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding:** Partial. Nuisance/blue-sky flooding from built-over creeks and high groundwater is documented (Olivotto et al., 2025). This is better characterized as chronic urban drainage/pluvial flooding than riverine flooding per the codebook definition. Code with caution; "true" riverine flooding is not clearly evidenced.
- **Lake Flooding/Erosion:** No evidence.
- **Wildfire:** No direct evidence for Edgemere. Mockrin & Johnson (2024) note wildfires in wetland areas (Phragmites) in the nearby Oakwood Beach site, but this is not attributed to Edgemere.
- **Volcano:** No.
- **Land Subsidence:** Not directly evidenced, though land-filling of former marshlands implies some ongoing settlement dynamics (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Landslide/Debris Flow:** No.
- **Earthquake:** No.
- **Tsunami:** No.
- **Hurricane:** ✓ Yes — Superstorm Sandy is the triggering event for the retreat program. The broader hurricane hazard is relevant to this coastal location (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).
- **Other:** Chronic "blue sky" / nuisance flooding from drainage system limitations and groundwater, documented as distinct from storm surge events (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes, A few streets, Neighbourhood, Entire community, Sub-watershed, Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Individual homes** (for completed buyouts/acquisitions); **Neighbourhood** (for the planning framework)

**Narrative:** The actual completed retreat actions involved 7 individual parcels (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). However, the RECPI operates at the neighbourhood scale: it encompasses the entire Edgemere neighborhood through zoning changes, the HMZ designation, and the broader planning initiative for 119 city-owned vacant lots (Olivotto et al., 2025). The HMZ restricts development across a defined zone within the neighborhood. Therefore, both **Individual homes** (for the actual buyouts/acquisitions) and **Neighbourhood** (for the planning framework) apply.

**Coding rationale:** The codebook allows multiple selections. The tension between the small scale of completed retreat (7 properties) and the neighborhood-wide planning framework is a defining feature of this case.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals, Groups/Neighbourhoods, Communities, Critical infrastructure, Hazard protection structures, Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Individuals** (for the completed buyouts/acquisitions); the planning framework anticipates potential future retreat of **Groups/Neighbourhoods**

**Narrative:** Only 7 individual property owners participated in buyouts or acquisitions as of September 2022 (Olivotto et al., 2025). No organized group or community-scale relocation occurred. The RECPI planning framework, through the HMZ and zoning restrictions, creates conditions for a possible future larger-scale retreat, but this has not materialized as of the review period. Olivotto et al. (2025) describe a "soft, delayed retreat philosophy" for the bay-side area, with zoning changes meaning residents who experience future catastrophic flooding may have retreat as their only option. Groups/Neighbourhoods is therefore coded as anticipated but not yet achieved.

---

### Other notes

The Edgemere case is unusual in that the completed "managed retreat" component (7 buyouts/acquisitions) is very small relative to the scope of the broader planning initiative. Much of the literature treating Edgemere as a managed retreat case study does so because of the RECPI's explicit incorporation of land use restrictions and future retreat planning, not because of the scale of completed buyouts. The simultaneous strategy of limiting residential development in the HMZ while permitting large-scale mixed-use development elsewhere in the neighborhood is a defining and contested feature of this case (Olivotto et al., 2025).

Case study: Queens (Queens, New York, United States)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat, Community buyout/retreat, Leasebacks/easements/buffers, Other acquisition tools, Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (completed to date); **Other acquisition tools** (city-owned lot management and proposed CLT)

**Narrative:** The completed retreat actions are individual property buyouts and acquisitions (7 properties), administered by HPD (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The RECPI also designated 119 city-owned vacant lots (including the 7 buyout/acquisition lots) to be managed by a proposed Community Land Trust for a combination of affordable housing and open space purposes — this represents an alternative acquisition/stewardship tool (Olivotto et al., 2025).

The RECPI also established the HMZ, which functions as a regulatory restriction by prohibiting or limiting new residential development in the most flood-exposed areas. This is more accurately coded as **Land rezoning** under the legal issues category (see below) rather than a leaseback/easement/buffer in the strict codebook sense. No leaseback arrangements or managed realignment of infrastructure are described in the reviewed sources for this case.

**Coding rationale:** Individual buyout/retreat is supported by the 7 completed acquisitions. Other acquisition tools reflects the city lot management and CLT proposal. Leasebacks/easements/buffers is not selected because the HMZ is a zoning mechanism rather than a financial leaseback or easement on private land.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? Are there any legal frameworks or regulations that guide the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Evidence for: **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Land rezoning**, **Retreat land development**, **Compliance & enforcement**. Limited/no evidence for **Litigation** directly related to Edgemere buyouts.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** Post-Sandy recovery was funded through federal CDBG-DR appropriations. Greer & Brokopp Binder (2017) describe the HMGP and CDBG-DR federal frameworks that govern U.S. buyout programs, including requirements that buyouts be voluntary, that pre-event fair market value be offered, and that acquired land be maintained as open space in perpetuity. Olivotto et al. (2025) reference the Build It Back program channeling funds for property buyouts and acquisitions through the RECPI Edgemere Resilient Plan Area.
- **Home acquisition / Land acquisition:** HPD administered the buyout and acquisition of individual residential properties (Olivotto et al., 2025; Mockrin & Johnson, 2024).
- **Title(s) transfer:** Post-buyout/acquisition, land ownership transferred to HPD (6 of 7 lots) or NYC Parks (1 lot, transferred June 2022) (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Land rezoning:** The RECPI introduced multiple zoning changes, including the HMZ that eliminates or limits residential uses in the most flood-exposed areas (Olivotto et al., 2025). Community Board 14 presented a moratorium resolution opposing further upzoning (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Retreat land development:** The RECPI's approach of permitting large-scale mixed-use development on non-HMZ land, plus the proposed CLT for 119 city-owned lots, represents contested retreat land development planning (Olivotto et al., 2025). Zoning changes in the HMZ mean no new residential development or home elevations will be permitted there.
- **Compliance & enforcement:** The HMZ zoning restrictions function as a compliance mechanism: future residential development in that zone is prohibited (Olivotto et al., 2025). Whether enforcement mechanisms are robust is not directly addressed in the reviewed sources.
- **Litigation:** Walker et al. (2024) discuss litigation between NYC and watershed communities (Catskills case) and reference NYC's "seemingly endless ability to engage in litigation," but this refers to the Catskills/DEP context, not Edgemere. No evidence of specific litigation arising from the Edgemere buyouts was found in the reviewed sources.
- **Legal authority over retreat:** The RECPI and HMZ were established through NYC's land use planning authority. The sources support HPD's authority to acquire properties and manage vacant city-owned land, but no detailed analysis of contested legal authority is provided for Edgemere specifically.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project? (Multiple funders, Federal, Local/Municipal, etc.)

**Answer:** **Multiple funders** — primarily **Federal** (CDBG-DR through HUD) and **Local/Municipal** (New York City, through HPD and related agencies)

**Narrative:** The Build It Back program referenced in connection with Edgemere buyouts and acquisitions was funded primarily through the $4.2 billion in HUD CDBG-DR funds allocated to New York City following Sandy (Mockrin & Johnson, 2024). The broader RECPI involved multiple city agencies (HPD, MOR, NYC Parks). Federal infrastructure investment through USACE ($252,544,000 for coastal storm risk management in mid-Rockaway) is referenced as adjacent but ongoing (Olivotto et al., 2025, citing USACE, 2019). Community organizations such as 596 Acres provided support for community land access advocacy (Olivotto et al., 2025). Greer & Brokopp Binder (2017) describe the general federal HMGP and CDBG-DR framework that applies to buyout programs in New York.

No evidence of private sector, insurance, or international aid funding was found in the reviewed sources for the Edgemere buyouts specifically.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Redevelopment of retreat lands** (proposed/advancing)

**Narrative:** The RECPI's approach of permitting large-scale mixed-use development on non-HMZ land can be interpreted partly as a strategy to maintain or improve the neighborhood's tax base and economic activity. Olivotto et al. (2025) describe the RECPI as set to bring "1,201 residential units (approximately 38% as affordable housing) and almost 150,000 square feet of retail space" when fully built, alongside new parking spaces.

Mockrin & Johnson (2024) note that the loss of real estate taxes from buyouts was a financial concern for local governments in the New York area, though for Edgemere — part of NYC — this concern was less acute than for smaller Long Island municipalities.

The proposed CLT for 119 city-owned lots was intended to provide affordable homeownership options that could keep residents in the community (Olivotto et al., 2025), which could relate to "assisting BO recipients to find housing in community," but whether buyout participants were specifically targeted for CLT housing is not clearly documented in the reviewed sources. This claim cannot be firmly coded without direct evidence.

**Coding rationale:** Redevelopment of retreat lands is supported by the mixed-use development plans for non-HMZ areas. Other tax-base codes (New housing for BO recipients, Assisting BO recipients to find housing in community, New industry, Livelihoods supports) are not clearly supported by specific Edgemere-focused evidence in the reviewed sources.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Market value** (federal CDBG-DR requirement); limited evidence of emergency repair services that could be classified as **Free supports and services**, though residents questioned their quality.

**Narrative:** Greer & Brokopp Binder (2017) document that CDBG-DR-funded buyouts must offer pre-event fair market value, and this requirement applies to the Edgemere buyouts through the post-Sandy recovery framework. Olivotto et al. (2025) note that homeowners who participated in the Build It Back and Rapid Repair (RR) programs generally found, at best, that these programs did not meet their needs and, at worst, that they were seen as "scams" with shoddy contractor work. The RR program provided emergency repairs to private properties to allow residents to return, which could be classified as free supports and services, but residents described the work as poorly executed. A 2017 NYC Department of Investigation report confirmed contractors overstated quantities of items installed, documenting poor oversight (Olivotto et al., 2025).

Some homeowners with flood insurance did not receive enough payment to rebuild without taking on debt (Olivotto et al., 2025). No evidence of additional financial incentives, bonuses, or top-ups above market value was found for the Edgemere buyouts.

**Coding rationale:** Market value is supported by federal program requirements (Greer & Brokopp Binder, 2017). Free supports and services is coded with caution — the Rapid Repair program functionally provided this, but the quality was widely criticized. Additional incentives/bonuses are not evidenced. Post-disaster value or tax value are not evidenced.

Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Pre-retreat planning**, **Immediate risks (1–5 years)**, **Anticipated future risks (10–100 years)**, **Post-retreat follow-up** (limited and inadequate)

**Narrative:** The RECPI involved substantial pre-retreat planning: risk mapping, zoning changes, environmental impact assessments, and community visioning (Olivotto et al., 2025). The immediate post-Sandy period addressed existing flood risks and emergency recovery. The HMZ and future coastal engineering plans (USACE, $252,544,000) address anticipated future risks over longer time horizons, including sea level rise projections through 2050 referenced in the NYC Panel on Climate Change and the NYC Coastal Land Use Framework (Mayor's Office, 2022, cited in Olivotto et al., 2025). Post-retreat follow-up for the 7 buyout lots has been limited: lots remained vacant, without clear restoration plans as of September 2022, suggesting post-retreat planning has been inadequate (Olivotto et al., 2025).

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Top-down**, **Multi-sectoral**, **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions**, **Participatory/collaborative** (partial and contested), **Degree of transparency** (contested)

**Narrative:**

- **Top-down:** The RECPI was a city-led, multi-agency initiative. Zoning changes and HMZ designation were imposed through city planning processes (Olivotto et al., 2025). Mockrin & Johnson (2024) document "limited partnerships and minimal local government recruitment for buyouts" across New York Sandy sites, and the Edgemere case reflects similar dynamics with a predominantly city-driven approach.
- **Multi-sectoral:** Multiple NYC agencies participated (HPD, MOR, Parks, implied others), engaging housing, environmental, and community development dimensions simultaneously (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** The RECPI involved coordination between city agencies, and the USACE coastal engineering project involves federal-city coordination (Olivotto et al., 2025). The reviewed sources indicate GOSR (state-level) buyout programs did not operate in Edgemere, with the sources primarily discussing NYC-led efforts.
- **Participatory/collaborative:** The RECPI included community engagement processes, including the 2015 community planning initiative and land visioning workshops held between November 2021 and March 2022, conducted in collaboration with a CBO (Olivotto et al., 2025). However, Community Board 14 passed a moratorium resolution opposing further large-scale development, indicating active community voice even if outcomes did not fully align with community preferences (Olivotto et al., 2025). Some residents and observers described participation as feeling like a process with "predetermined outcomes" — a phrase used in the Catskills parallel case by Walker et al. (2024), which resonates with but is not directly attributed to Edgemere residents in the reviewed excerpts.
- **Degree of transparency:** Contested. Residents described a lack of transparency around key decisions; a cited example is the surreptitious decision to convert a local hotel to a shelter communicated via email to the community board district manager rather than through public meetings (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Multi-stage retreat:** The planning framework implies a staged approach — limited buyouts now, with zoning changes that could enable expanded retreat after future catastrophic flooding. However, this is not explicitly called a multi-stage program in the reviewed sources and is better described as implicit in the "soft, delayed retreat" framing (Olivotto et al., 2025).
- **Adaptive management / Cost-benefit analysis:** No clear direct evidence of formal adaptive management protocols or CBA being applied specifically to the Edgemere buyout decisions in the reviewed sources. The Walker et al. (2024) Catskills case describes a parallel NYC watershed buyout program that recently discontinued using monetary CBA as an eligibility criterion, but this refers to a different program. Not coded for Edgemere without direct evidence.

**Coding rationale:** Top-down, Multi-sectoral, Coordination, and Degree of transparency are clearly supported. Participatory/collaborative is coded as partial, given documented workshops but also documented community criticism. Multi-stage retreat, Adaptive management, and CBA are not coded as these are not clearly and directly evidenced for Edgemere in the reviewed

Case study: Auckland (Auckland, Aukland Region, New Zealand)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Project Twin Streams (PTS), former Waitakere City (now part of Auckland Council), Auckland Region, Aotearoa New Zealand.

**Hazard(s):** Riverine and pluvial flooding. The project was developed in response to escalating flooding and stormwater management issues within the Twin Streams catchment (Opanuku and Waitītī streams).

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout as part of a broader environmental restoration and stormwater management programme. The retreat component involved purchasing all or part of properties in the 100-year flood plain and removing houses to create stormwater reserves and management parks.

**Scale:** Approximately 156 property purchases were successfully negotiated (approximately half full purchases, half partial purchases such as land only). Approximately NZD $25 million was allocated to the property purchase phase, funded through a grant from Infrastructure Auckland, a public regional infrastructure development body. No population estimate is provided in the reviewed sources.

**Key Actors:** The former Waitakere City Council (now Auckland Council) was the primary implementing body. Funding was provided through Infrastructure Auckland. The Council deliberated chose not to use compulsory acquisition powers available under the Public Works Act 1981. The central government was not the primary funder or lead actor. The Waitakere City Council merged into Auckland Council in 2010; all events described occurred under the former Waitakere City Council.

**Timeline:** Project Twin Streams began in 2002 and was scheduled to run for approximately 10 years. The property purchase component was active throughout this period. At the time of the primary source (Vandenbeld and MacDonald, 2013), 156 property purchases had been successfully negotiated — language suggesting an ongoing or substantially completed acquisition phase rather than a formally closed post-retreat case.

**Key Outcomes:** The literature presents the managed-retreat component as a successful example of voluntary, carefully communicated acquisition. Land acquired was converted into stormwater reserves, management parks, cycle-ways, and walkways. Flood risk to residents was reduced and the ecological functioning of local waterways was improved. A small number of property owners chose not to sell; their flood risk was documented in Land Information Memoranda. The approach avoided protracted legal disputes — the voluntary, trust-based model allowed the Council to proceed without compulsory acquisition.

---

### Narrative Summary

Project Twin Streams (PTS) was conceived in response to chronic flooding and deteriorating stormwater management in the Twin Streams catchment of the former Waitakere City, Auckland. Rather than relying on hard engineering protection works, the Waitakere City Council developed a multi-objective programme combining environmental restoration, stormwater management, community development, cultural goals, and local employment creation. A central component was the voluntary purchase of properties within the 100-year flood plain and the removal of houses to create stormwater reserves, ecological parks, cycle-ways, and walkways.

The Council made a deliberate decision not to use compulsory acquisition powers available under the Public Works Act 1981. Instead, 156 property purchases were successfully negotiated on a voluntary basis. Properties were acquired at pre-announcement market valuations — used as a starting point for negotiation to prevent the Council from leveraging its interest in the property to depress the price — and the Council paid for moving costs and legal fees. The engagement process was carefully designed: nine months were spent developing consistent messaging and support materials before any contact was made with property owners. Council teams paired engineers who could explain flood risk with staff who had strong interpersonal skills, addressing both technical and emotional dimensions. Individual circumstances were recognised: for example, the Council agreed to purchase both houses in a case where a family lived in adjacent properties, and facilitated the relocation of special trees and the erection of plaques where properties had multi-generational significance.

The project framed the property acquisition positively — as an opportunity to help owners relocate away from flood hazard while improving the environmental, economic, social, and cultural wellbeing of the wider community through PTS. Those who relocated elsewhere in the area could still benefit from the parks and walkways created on vacated land, as well as the wider benefits of PTS. A small number of owners chose not to sell; flood risk was documented on their Land Information Memoranda. The literature presents this case as a notable example of how voluntary, carefully designed community engagement can achieve community acceptance of managed retreat without resorting to compulsion or protracted legal processes. Lawrence et al. (2020) cite Twin Streams alongside the Netherlands Delta Programme as a notable example of publicly funded pre-emptive managed retreat with dedicated funding and significant community engagement.
