Case study: Madoi County (Madoi County, Qinghai, China)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** Community buyout/retreat; Individual buyout/retreat; Other acquisition tools.

**Narrative:** The program operated at both scales. "Village Group Resettlement" (VGR) involved the collective relocation of entire communities through coordinated government planning — qualifying as community buyout/retreat. "Individual Resettlement" (IR) involved household-level relocations within the same county — qualifying as individual buyout/retreat (Du 2012, pp. 124–125).

The government did not purchase properties in the conventional buyout sense; rather, it acquired grassland use rights from herders in exchange for housing, subsidies, and annual compensation. Grassland use rights were surrendered either permanently (VGR) or temporarily (IR, 10-year ban) (Du 2012, p. 125, Table 4). This mechanism is better captured under "Other acquisition tools" — the acquisition of grassland usufruct rights rather than conventional property ownership titles.

**Coding rationale:** Both "Community buyout/retreat" and "Individual buyout/retreat" apply. "Other acquisition tools" is also relevant given the grassland use rights mechanism. This is a government resettlement program, not a market-based property buyout.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? (Litigation), (Legal authority over retreat), (Relevant regulations/acts), (Home acquisition), (Land acquisition), (Title(s) transfer), (Land rezoning), (Retreat land development), (Compliance & enforcement), (Other)

**Answer:** Relevant regulations/acts; Legal authority over retreat; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer (grassland use rights); Land rezoning; Compliance & enforcement.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** The Sanjiangyuan General Plan was approved by the State Council in 2004 as the governing policy framework. The establishment of the Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve in 2003 created the legal basis for the grazing bans and resettlement (Du 2012, pp. 120, 122).

- **Legal authority over retreat:** The State Council, provincial, and county governments held legal authority. In 2003, resettlement in Gyaringhu was effectively compulsory; in 2004 a new policy reframed the program as voluntary with government guidance. Questions about the authenticity of voluntary consent are raised by the article (Du 2012, pp. 123–124).

- **Land acquisition:** Grassland use rights were acquired from herding households. Under the Household Contracted Responsibility System (HCRS), individual household grassland certificates had been issued from 1983–1992. These were surrendered as part of resettlement — permanently in VGR and temporarily (10-year ban) in IR (Du 2012, pp. 120–121, 125).

- **Title(s) transfer:** Grassland user right certificates were returned to the state or placed under grazing ban conditions. The distinction between permanent and temporary surrender created different compensation structures (Du 2012, p. 125, Table 4). Note: these are usufruct/use-right certificates, not ownership titles (all land in China is state-owned).

- **Land rezoning:** The Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve designation placed vacated lands under conservation protection, divided into core, buffer, and experimental zones with different use restrictions. The General Plan called for "returning grazing land to grassland" — effectively rezoning pastoral land to conservation use (Du 2012, pp. 117, 122).

- **Compliance & enforcement:** A grazing ban was legally imposed. However, enforcement was weak: insufficient funds were allocated, retired pastures were scattered over large areas, and some herders continued grazing illegally. Fencing was installed to keep livestock away from banned pastures, though this created new grassland management problems (Du 2012, pp. 129–130).

- **Home acquisition:** Not applicable. The government constructed new housing and provided it free to resettled households; it did not purchase existing homes from herders. This code is not selected.

- **Litigation:** No evidence of legal disputes found in the reviewed source.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project? (Local/Municipal only), (Provincial/State only), (Federal only), (Multiple funders), (International aid), (Local/Municipal), (Provincial/State), (Federal), (Individual), (NGOs), (Lenders), (Insurance)

**Answer:** Multiple funders — Federal (dominant) and Provincial/State, with County/Local contribution.

**Narrative:** The Sanjiangyuan General Plan received approximately RMB 7.5 billion from the Chinese central (federal) government and Qinghai Provincial government combined (Du 2012, p. 117). The State Council approved and funded the plan at the national level. Data from the Ecological Resettlement Management Office of the Qinghai Development and Reform Commission indicates that 86 new settlement villages were built between 2004 and 2010, indicating provincial-level administrative management of funds (Du 2012, p. 122). Madoi County government invested RMB 74.42 million in local resettlement by 2007 (Du 2012, p. 124), representing a local/municipal contribution. The Qinghai Provincial Poverty Alleviation Office also provided support for one livelihood enterprise (the Tibetan blanket factory in Heyuan Xincun) (Du 2012, p. 127). No evidence of international aid, NGO funding, individual self-funding, insurance, or private lender involvement was found.

The Ford Foundation funded the research article itself (Du 2012, Acknowledgements, p. 131), not the resettlement program.

**Coding rationale:** "Multiple funders" (Federal, Provincial/State, and Local/Municipal) is the appropriate category. Federal funding was dominant given State Council approval and the RMB 7.5 billion investment figure.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Livelihoods supports (attempted but largely unsuccessful); no clear evidence of tax base strategy.

**Narrative:** The reviewed source does not explicitly address tax base considerations, consistent with this being a rural poverty-alleviation and ecological protection program in a remote area with a limited formal tax base. The government attempted livelihood support through: (a) construction of dual-purpose livestock enclosures for feed-lot cattle raising and vegetable cultivation; (b) a Tibetan blanket manufacturing enterprise in Heyuan Xincun (supported by the Qinghai Provincial Poverty Alleviation Office, but it went bankrupt in October 2010); and (c) technical training for resettled herders. These efforts failed to generate sustainable livelihoods (Du 2012, pp. 122–123, 127–128).

Basic urban living allowances (approximately RMB 200/person/month) were provided to about half of resettled households in the VGR villages (Du 2012, p. 125, Table 4); these are transfer payments, not tax-generating activities.

**Coding rationale:** "Livelihoods supports" is partially applicable but with a contradictory note — the supports were attempted but largely unsuccessful. No evidence of new industry attraction, redevelopment of retreat lands for revenue, or systematic tax base strategy is found in the reviewed source.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process? (Market value), (Tax value), (Post-disaster value), (Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups), (Free supports and services - demolition, moving, advice, etc.), (Other)

**Answer:** Free supports and services (housing, education); Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups (annual subsidies, moving allowance); Other (grassland use rights compensation; urban living allowances for some households).

**Narrative:**

- **Free housing (in-kind provision):** Each resettled household received a free 45 sq m house (valued at RMB 800/sq m) plus a 120 sq m barn. VGR households received accommodation valued at approximately RMB 80,000; IR households with own grassland certificates received accommodation valued at approximately RMB 40,000; IR households sharing certificates received approximately RMB 30,000 (Du 2012, p. 123, Table 4).

- **Moving allowance:** RMB 400 one-off taxi fare per family (Du 2012, p. 123).

- **Annual subsidy:** RMB 8,000/household/year for 10 years for VGR households complying with the permanent grazing ban; RMB 6,000/year for IR households holding their own grassland user right certificates; RMB 3,000/year for IR households sharing certificates (Du 2012, Table 4).

- **Urban living allowances:** Approximately RMB 200/person/month for approximately half of resettled herders in VGR villages (Du 2012, p. 125, Table 4).

- **Education:** Free primary school education and boarding accommodation for children in resettlement villages (Du 2012, p. 125).

- **Medical care:** Access to basic medical insurance was referenced as part of possible solutions for migrants over 50 who registered as urban residents (Du 2012, p. 130); basic medical care access is referenced among interviewee perspectives (Du 2012, p. 119, interview list).

Compensation was not based on market value, tax value, or post-disaster value of property — it was structured as a package of in-kind housing, fixed subsidies, and services in exchange for grassland use rights. Herders consistently reported that subsidies were insufficient to cover living costs in towns, particularly as inflation rose (Du 2012, pp. 127–128).

**Coding rationale:** "Free supports and services" (housing, education) and "Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups" (annual subsidies, moving allowance) are the applicable categories. "Other" captures the grassland use rights compensation mechanism and the partial urban living allowances, which do not fit standard property market value categories.

---

Case study: Madoi County (Madoi County, Qinghai, China)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process? (Pre-retreat planning), (Immediate risks: 1-5 years), (Emerging risks: 5-10), (Anticipated future risks: 10-100), (Post-retreat follow-up)

**Answer:** Pre-retreat planning; Immediate risks (1–5 years); Anticipated future risks (10–100 years); Post-retreat follow-up (limited and inadequate).

**Narrative:**

- **Pre-retreat planning:** The Sanjiangyuan General Plan involved extensive pre-retreat planning — establishing the nature reserve (2003), designing resettlement village layouts, planning infrastructure, designating grazing ban zones, and developing compensation structures before relocation commenced at scale (Du 2012, pp. 120–122).

- **Immediate risks (1–5 years):** The Gyaringhu pilot (September 2003) responded to immediate and severe degradation in the core zone of the nature reserve, designated as a depopulated zone (Du 2012, pp. 123–124).

- **Anticipated future risks (10–100 years):** The program was designed to prevent long-term ecological collapse of the Sanjiangyuan — protecting the hydrological function of the "Water Tower of Asia" for future generations. The 10-year grazing ban was designed as a medium-term ecosystem recovery window (Du 2012, pp. 120–122).

- **Post-retreat follow-up:** Limited and inadequate. The article documents failures in post-resettlement support: bankruptcy of livelihood enterprises, insufficient subsidies, poor enforcement of grazing bans, and no housing provision for newly formed nuclear families. The article proposes solutions (minimum subsidy for elderly, grassland management employment for young people, better education and training) that were not yet implemented at time of writing (Du 2012, pp. 129–130).

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process? (Multi-criteria decision analysis - MCDA), (Adaptive management), (Bottom-up), (Top down), (Multi-sectoral), (Single stage retreat), (Multi-stage retreat), (Degree of transparency), (Public private partnerships), (Coordination w/ other sectors and jurisdictions), (Bureaucracy reduction), (Cost-benefit analysis - CBA), (Participatory/collaborative)

**Answer:** Top-down; Multi-sectoral; Multi-stage retreat (phased rollout); Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions; Degree of transparency (low).

**Narrative:**

- **Top-down:** The program was unambiguously top-down: designed by the State Council and provincial government, implemented through county governments, with herders as recipients rather than co-designers. The General Plan stated the program should be implemented on "governmental guidance and voluntary participation" terms, but government guidance was dominant (Du 2012, pp. 121–124).

- **Multi-sectoral:** Multiple government bureaus were involved: Development and Reform Commission, Animal Husbandry, Land Resources, Religious and Ethnic Affairs, Medical Care, and Poverty Alleviation Office. This constitutes multi-sectoral coordination (Du 2012, p. 119, interview list).

- **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** The General Plan coordinated across Qinghai Province, multiple prefectures, and counties. Relocations crossed prefectural boundaries (e.g., Madoi County herders resettled to Tongde County of Hainan TAP, approximately 450 km away) (Du 2012, pp. 122–124, Table 2).

- **Multi-stage retreat:** The program began with a pilot in Gyaringhu township (September 2003), shifted to a voluntary framework from 2004, and continued phased implementation through 2010 across 86 resettlement villages. Within communities, relocation sometimes unfolded over several years (e.g., not completed in Gyaringhu until the first half of 2007) (Du 2012, pp. 123–124).

- **Degree of transparency:** Low. The program was presented to herders through advertising campaigns emphasizing ecological protection and ideological framing ("sacrifice small families for our great country"), not through transparent deliberative processes (Du 2012, pp. 122–123).

Case study: Charlotte (Charlotte, North Carolina, United States)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Charlotte-Mecklenburg County Floodplain Buyout Program, Charlotte, Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, United States.

**Hazard(s):** Riverine and pluvial (urban) flooding. Mecklenburg County sits within the Catawba River Basin, with a network of urban creeks and lakes that flash flood regularly, particularly during hurricane season. Shi et al. (2022) note that Climate Central (2015) estimated heavy downpours in Charlotte increased by 86% since 1950, indicating climate change may be exacerbating flooding risk. The flooding is driven by the county's hydrological character combined with historical land-use decisions including stream channelization and floodplain development.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout program. Acquired properties are demolished and converted to permanent open space. The program operates through three sub-mechanisms: (1) FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) buyouts; (2) locally funded, risk-based buyouts; and (3) "Quick Buys" using reserve funds for immediate post-disaster acquisition. Leaseback arrangements are also used on a case-by-case basis.

**Scale:** As reported by Spidalieri et al. (2020), the program had purchased more than 400 flood-prone homes and businesses and enabled over 700 families and businesses to relocate, creating approximately 185 acres of open space. Cardwell (2021) confirms over 450 properties acquired and demolished. More than 5,000 individual properties are located within Mecklenburg County's regulated floodplain (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

**Key Actors:** Charlotte-Mecklenburg Storm Water Services (CMSS) — a joint county-municipal stormwater utility — is the primary implementing body. Federal funding is provided through FEMA's HMGP. The Mecklenburg Board of County Commissioners allocates "rainy day" Quick Buy reserve funds. At specific sites, non-profit partners such as the Charlotte Public Tree Fund have supported post-buyout ecological restoration (Cardwell 2021). Community organizations and neighborhood associations have shaped post-buyout land use at some sites, with notably variable outcomes.

**Timeline:** Program initiated in 1999, following two devastating 100-year flood events in the 1990s causing over $60 million in property damage (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020). Key milestones:
- 1999: Program established; FEMA HMGP buyouts begin.
- 2003: Quick Buy mechanism introduced (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- 2008: Leaseback arrangements introduced (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- 2012–present: Local Risk-Based Buyouts funded through local stormwater fee (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- As of 2019: Program invests approximately $4 million annually; total program investment exceeds $67 million (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- Content current as of early 2020 (Spidalieri et al. 2020); program ongoing.

**Key Outcomes:** Over 400–450 flood-prone properties acquired and demolished; approximately 185 acres converted to open space including community gardens, ecological preserves, and planned greenway corridors (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Cardwell 2021). Spidalieri et al. (2020) report the county estimates it has avoided approximately $25 million in property damage and prevented $300 million in future losses (reported as county estimates, not independently verified in the reviewed sources). Spidalieri et al. (2020) report approximately 85% participation among property owners in priority flood-risk reduction areas. However, significant equity concerns persist: renters were displaced without compensation; socially vulnerable communities received less post-buyout land use investment; the program had not adopted explicit social equity goals or social vulnerability metrics at the time studied (Shi et al. 2022); and greenway implementation has been inequitable, prioritizing wealthier areas (Cardwell 2021).

---

**Narrative Summary**

In 1999, following two devastating 100-year flood events in the 1990s that caused over $60 million in property damage, Charlotte-Mecklenburg Storm Water Services (CMSS) launched a voluntary floodplain buyout program. According to Shi et al. (2022), the flooding prompted 30 to 40 exasperated residents to show up to a county commissioner's meeting with mops and buckets, demanding better stormwater protection. The program purchases flood-prone properties at their pre-disaster fair-market value, demolishes all structures, and converts the land permanently to open space. As of the time of the Spidalieri et al. (2020) report, CMSS had purchased more than 400 flood-prone homes and businesses and enabled over 700 families and businesses to relocate, creating approximately 185 acres of open space. The program combines FEMA HMGP funds with local stormwater-fee and county reserve funding, which allows acquisitions outside strict FEMA disaster timing and eligibility limits, enabling CMSS to buy out properties proactively and in non-disaster contexts (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020).

Despite its widely recognized effectiveness in reducing flood risk — a finding consistent across all interview respondents in Cardwell (2021) — the program has been critiqued for inequitable outcomes. Renters, present in significant numbers in several buyout areas including the former Cavalier and Doral Apartment Complexes, received no compensation when property owners accepted buyouts, resulting in displacement from affordable housing (Cardwell 2021). For lower-income homeowners, the financial pressure of flood-damaged property and the difficulty of refusing an offer effectively limited genuine voluntary choice, in contrast to wealthier homeowners who had the financial resources to decline (Cardwell 2021). Shi et al. (2022) confirm that the program had not adopted explicit social equity goals or social vulnerability metrics at the time studied.

Post-buyout land use outcomes have varied markedly by neighborhood. Communities with strong social capital and political connections — notably Country Club Heights — successfully shaped vacant land into valued community assets such as the Country Club Heights Community Garden. By contrast, socially vulnerable communities such as Hidden Valley were left with poorly maintained or underutilized ecological sites that failed to deliver promised benefits (Cardwell 2021). CMSS does not track where buyout households relocate, and greenway funding has been inequitably distributed, prioritizing wealthier areas of the city (Cardwell 2021). The program offers important lessons about institutional continuity, dedicated local funding, and multi-criteria prioritization as enablers of effective managed retreat, while also illustrating persistent tensions between a program's flood-risk mandate and broader housing equity obligations.

Case study: Charlotte (Charlotte, North Carolina, United States)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Both Reactive and Proactive.

**Narrative:** The program was established reactively, founded in 1999 following two devastating 100-year flood events in the 1990s that caused over $60 million in property damage and prompted strong public pressure for county action, including residents appearing at county commissioner meetings with mops and buckets (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020).

The program subsequently evolved in a notably proactive direction. As Shi et al. (2022) explain, CMSS grew frustrated with FEMA's post-disaster model — local floods were often not large enough to trigger federal disaster declarations, most flooded properties did not meet FEMA eligibility criteria, and buyout times were so long that residents opted to rebuild. In response, CMSS established a local stormwater fee (2012–present) to fund risk-based buyouts independent of disaster declarations (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Shi et al. (2022) explicitly note that "all five programs proactively buy out properties based on established plans rather than solely reactive, post-disaster efforts." CMSS also uses a Flood Risk Assessment and Risk Reduction Plan to score, rank, and prioritize properties (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

At the household level, however, Cardwell (2021) documents that "the majority of houses in Charlotte were acquired after a major flood event where there was significant flood damage to the property," consistent with a reactive pattern. The Quick Buy mechanism (2003–present) also captures properties reactively in the immediate aftermath of a flood, before substantial repairs are made (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

**Categories selected:** Both **Reactive** (founding context; Quick Buy mechanism; majority of household-level decisions post-disaster) and **Proactive** (program's evolved model with local stormwater-fee-funded, risk-based, non-disaster-triggered buyouts).

---

### Date, Number of Households Affected, Number of Population Affected, Total Funding

**Direct Answer:**
- **Program start date:** 1999 (Cardwell 2021; Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Number of properties acquired:** Over 450 (Cardwell 2021); more than 400 (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022). The slight variation reflects different data download dates across studies.
- **Families and businesses relocated:** Over 700 (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Spidalieri et al. 2020 executive summary). This figure is reported by Spidalieri et al. (2020) and may include both residential and commercial relocations.
- **Properties in regulated floodplain:** Over 5,000 (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Total program investment:** More than $67 million (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Annual investment:** Approximately $4 million as of 2019 (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022).
- **Open space created:** Approximately 185 acres (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Individual population affected:** Not directly stated in sources; sources report properties and households, not total individuals.

**Note on sources:** The 700 families/businesses figure and the $67 million total investment come from Spidalieri et al. (2020). Cardwell (2021) provides the "over 450 properties" figure based on a geodatabase downloaded in September 2018. These are consistent but reflect different snapshot dates.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Single Hazard.

**Narrative:** All three sources consistently identify flooding (riverine and pluvial) as the single hazard driving the buyout program. Shi et al. (2022) describe "urban creeks and lakes that flash flood regularly during hurricane season." Spidalieri et al. (2020) describe the program as responding to "repetitive loss structures" in Mecklenburg County's floodplain. Cardwell (2021) focuses exclusively on floodplain flooding risk. No second distinct hazard type is mentioned in any source.

**Category selected:** Single Hazard.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Natural Hazard, with climate change noted as a contextual exacerbator.

**Narrative:** The primary driver is riverine and pluvial flooding — a natural hazard. Shi et al. (2022) note that "climate change has increased heavy downpours in Charlotte, the county's largest city, by 86% since 1950 (Climate Central 2015)" as cited contextual background, and state that "climate change-exacerbated flooding has renewed interest in property buyouts." The hazard is natural in origin; the program was not triggered by a technological accident or industrial event. Climate change is treated in the sources as an exacerbating factor, not the sole cause, of flooding risk.

**Category selected:** Natural Hazard. Climate change is noted as a contextual exacerbator but is not the standalone driver in the program's founding narrative.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Riverine/Pluvial Flooding.

**Narrative:** The program explicitly targets properties in the regulated floodplain subject to riverine and pluvial flash flooding. Spidalieri et al. (2020) describe the county's network of "urban creeks and lakes that flash flood regularly." Cardwell (2021) and Shi et al. (2022) also focus exclusively on floodplain flooding. The program addresses inland riverine and pluvial flooding rather than coastal inundation; no coastal flooding hazard is discussed in any source.

**Category selected:** Riverine/Pluvial Flooding.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project?

**Answer:** Individual Homes and Neighbourhood.

**Narrative:** The program operates primarily at the individual property (parcel) level: CMSS identifies, appraises, and acquires individual flood-prone properties through voluntary sales (Spidalieri et al. 2020). However, CMSS prioritizes and groups properties into clusters, with acquisition strategies designed to aggregate buyouts within neighborhoods to restore floodplain functions over larger contiguous areas. The orphan property program specifically incentivizes the last homeowners in a high-risk neighborhood to sell so the entire site can be restored (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Cardwell (2021) identifies 13 cluster sites studied at the neighborhood level. Spidalieri et al. (2020) note that "CMSS works with community members to design and realize a vision for each large-scale bought-out area once all homes are purchased and demolished."

**Categories selected:** Individual Homes (operational unit of acquisition) and Neighbourhood (strategic clustering and aggregation target).

---

### Who or what was retreated?

**Answer:** Individuals (homeowners and, indirectly, renters and some commercial operators).

**Narrative:** The program retreats individual residents and businesses from flood-prone properties. Spidalieri et al. (2020) state the program enabled "over 700 families and businesses to relocate." The program focuses on residential properties, with the primary targets being homeowners. Renters were affected — often displaced — when landlords accepted buyouts, but renters were not formal participants in the buyout process and received no direct compensation (Cardwell 2021). Some commercial properties were also acquired (Spidalieri et al. 2020 refers to "homes and businesses"). No evidence of retreat of critical infrastructure or industrial assets in the reviewed sources.

**Category selected:** Individuals (and Groups/Neighbourhoods to a secondary degree, given neighborhood-level clustering strategy).

---

### Other notes (General Information)

The program specifically addresses "repetitive loss structures" — properties that have flooded multiple times (Spidalieri et al. 2020). The Quick Buy mechanism captures properties immediately following flood events before substantial repairs are made, preventing the cycle of damage and rebuild (Spidalieri et al. 2020). The program addresses inland riverine and pluvial flooding; no coastal or sea-level-rise hazard context is discussed in the sources.

Case study: Charlotte (Charlotte, North Carolina, United States)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project?

**Answer:** Individual buyout/retreat (primary); Leasebacks, easements and buffers (secondary).

**Narrative:** The core mechanism is individual property acquisition through voluntary buyouts (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Cardwell 2021; Shi et al. 2022). Properties are acquired one at a time through negotiated sales at pre-disaster fair-market value.

CMSS has also implemented leaseback arrangements — specifically triple net leasebacks and orphan parcel leasebacks — as supplementary tools (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Spidalieri et al. (2020) note that CMSS has implemented leasebacks since 2008, and as of 2019 approximately a dozen have been used (around one per year). These are used to manage timing, reduce holdouts, support elderly or financially constrained owners, and reduce property maintenance costs.

Post-buyout, acquired lands are deed-restricted as permanent open space, preventing future development — a functional restriction analogous to an easement in effect (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022).

**Categories selected:** Individual buyout/retreat (primary); Leasebacks, easements and buffers (secondary, for leaseback tool). Deed restrictions function as a form of open-space constraint, though the sources do not explicitly label them as "easements."

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Relevant regulations/acts; Home acquisition; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer; Retreat land development; Compliance & enforcement.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** FEMA's HMGP rules govern eligibility, cost-benefit analysis, and permanent deed-restriction requirements for federally funded buyouts (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022). The program is described as requiring properties to "meet eligibility and priority criteria set by the federal and/or state governments" (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

- **Home acquisition:** Properties are acquired voluntarily; eminent domain is explicitly not used (Spidalieri et al. 2020). FEMA's HMGP requires voluntary participation. The program uses appraisals to determine pre-disaster fair-market value (Cardwell 2021).

- **Land acquisition:** CMSS operates three distinct legal funding and acquisition pathways: FEMA grants, local stormwater-fee-funded buyouts, and Quick Buys (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Local risk-based buyouts fund properties that do not meet federal grant criteria.

- **Title(s) transfer:** Upon completion, title transfers to CMSS/Mecklenburg County. Properties are then deed-restricted as permanent open space (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

- **Retreat land development:** FEMA requirements govern allowable post-buyout uses (open space only; no development). Local uses such as community gardens, greenway trails, and ecological preserves are planned and implemented at the local level (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Cardwell 2021). In certain circumstances, after buyouts within a given area are completed, streets and utilities may also be removed or left unmaintained to further restore the floodplain (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

- **Compliance & enforcement:** Orphan parcel leaseback lessees are subject to periodic inspections by CMSS to ensure compliance with lease terms and, for federally funded properties, FEMA requirements (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Triple net leasebacks include "triggers" that can terminate the lease (e.g., a major flooding event or death of the homeowner). Leases are not transferable and do not allow substantial improvements or acceptance of government repair funds (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

**Note on land rezoning:** No source explicitly describes formal land rezoning as part of the program process. Deed restrictions to open space are the primary land-use control mechanism described. This category is therefore not selected.

**No evidence of litigation** arising from the buyout program in the reviewed sources.

**Categories selected:** Relevant regulations/acts; Home acquisition; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer; Retreat land development; Compliance & enforcement.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** Multiple funders — Federal (FEMA HMGP) and Local/Municipal (stormwater utility fee, county reserve funds).

**Narrative:** The program relies on three funding streams (Spidalieri et al. 2020):
1. **FEMA HMGP grants** — federal funding; local governments provide a 25% match (Cardwell 2021; Shi et al. 2022). CMSS has used FEMA grants less frequently since the program's founding as more local buyouts are completed and fewer properties meet federal eligibility criteria (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
2. **Local stormwater utility fee** — a fee that generates most of the approximately $4 million annual budget for non-FEMA-eligible, risk-based buyouts (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020). Charlotte and Austin "raise funds through a stormwater utility tax on impervious surface" (Shi et al. 2022).
3. **Mecklenburg Board of County Commissioners "rainy day" funds** — used for Quick Buys immediately after flood events (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

As of 2019, most buyouts are funded completely by local government funds (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Total program investment exceeds $67 million (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Leaseback arrangements also generate some rental income (in-kind or monetary), partially offsetting property maintenance costs (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

**Categories selected:** Multiple funders — Federal (FEMA HMGP) and Local/Municipal (stormwater utility fee and county reserve funds).

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Limited evidence. Some indirect reference to encouraging resilient redevelopment elsewhere in the county.

**Narrative:** The sources do not explicitly identify tax base maintenance as a stated goal of the CMSS program. Shi et al. (2022) note that "local tax rolls may be permanently reduced when valuable real estate is removed from the city's building stock" as a general concern about buyout programs, but do not identify specific CMSS measures to address this. Spidalieri et al. (2020) note the program "encouraged the development of newer, more resilient buildings in less vulnerable locations within Mecklenburg County" — implying an indirect expectation that displaced households' economic contributions relocate within the county. Post-buyout land uses (community gardens, greenways, ecological preserves) are described as community assets, not as explicit tax-base maintenance strategies.

**Category with limited evidence:** Redevelopment of retreat lands — partial and implicit only (community amenities created on vacated land). No evidence for new industry, new housing for buyout recipients as a tax-base strategy, or explicit livelihood supports for this purpose.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Market value; Free supports and services (demolition).

**Narrative:**
- **Market value:** Homeowners are offered the pre-disaster fair-market value of their home — "calculated as if the house hadn't sustained flood damage" (Cardwell 2021). This was described as the "tipping point" for many homeowners. Under FEMA's HMGP, "homeowners receive funding equal to their home's pre-disaster fair-market value" (Shi et al. 2022).
- **Free supports and services:** All structures are demolished at CMSS's expense upon acquisition (Spidalieri et al. 2020). In some circumstances, streets and utilities may also be removed (Spidalieri et al. 2020).

**What is not provided:** FEMA's HMGP does not fund relocation assistance, financial counseling, or real estate services (Shi et al. 2022). The sources do not indicate that CMSS independently funds these services for buyout participants. This is explicitly contrasted with Austin's program, which models benefits after the federal Uniform Relocation Assistance Act (Shi et al. 2022). No direct financial top-ups, relocation bonuses, or bridging payments to buyout participants are documented for CMSS. Renters receive no compensation mechanism (Cardwell 2021; Shi et al. 2022).

**Note on leasebacks as compensation:** Leaseback arrangements allow continued residence for a period post-sale, which provides practical benefit to participants. However, this is a program management tool rather than a direct compensation payment. Accordingly, "Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups" is not selected as a category for this program based on the available evidence.

**Categories selected:** Market value; Free supports and services (demolition and, in some cases, infrastructure removal).

Case study: Charlotte (Charlotte, North Carolina, United States)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Pre-retreat planning; Immediate risks (1–5 years); Anticipated future risks (10–100 years); Post-retreat follow-up.

**Narrative:**
- **Pre-retreat planning:** CMSS uses a Flood Risk Assessment and Risk Reduction Plan to score, rank, and prioritize properties for acquisition (Spidalieri et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022). This constitutes explicit pre-retreat planning independent of disaster events.
- **Immediate risks (1–5 years):** The Quick Buy mechanism responds within days to weeks of a flood event (Spidalieri et al. 2020), addressing immediate risks from a just-occurred event.
- **Anticipated future risks (10–100 years):** CMSS estimates avoided future losses of $300 million (Spidalieri et al. 2020), and Shi et al. (2022) reference climate change projections for future rainfall increases. The locally funded buyout stream explicitly targets future risk reduction.
- **Post-retreat follow-up:** Spidalieri et al. (2020) describe CMSS working with communities to design post-buyout uses and maintaining properties (directly or via orphan parcel leasebacks). However, Cardwell (2021) documents significant failures of post-retreat follow-up engagement at several sites, particularly socially vulnerable communities such as Hidden Valley, where promised uses were not delivered and maintenance deteriorated.

**Categories selected:** Pre-retreat planning; Immediate risks (1–5 years) (Quick Buy mechanism); Anticipated future risks (10–100 years) (proactive, data-driven prioritization; avoided future loss estimates); Post-retreat follow-up (acknowledged as an objective, but documented by Cardwell 2021 as unevenly and sometimes poorly achieved).

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Top-down; Participatory/collaborative (variably, site-specific); Cost-benefit analysis (CBA); Multi-criteria decision analysis (elements of); Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions (limited); Degree of transparency; Multi-stage retreat; Adaptive management.

**Narrative:**
- **Top-down:** CMSS, as a governmental utility, unilaterally scores, ranks, and prioritizes properties and determines where and when buyouts occur. County commissioners allocate Quick Buy funds. Federal FEMA rules set eligibility criteria (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Participatory/collaborative:** CMSS engages residents through peer-to-peer programs (past buyout participants share experiences), participatory budgeting exercises ("monopoly money" workshops), and public outreach (Shi et al. 2022). Community engagement quality varies significantly across sites: effective in Country Club Heights and Chantilly; absent or inadequate in Biddleville-Smallwood and Hidden Valley (Cardwell 2021).
- **CBA:** Properties are prioritized partly based on cost-effectiveness, and FEMA's benefit-cost analysis is applied where federal funding is used (Spidalieri et al. 2020). Shi et al. (2022) note CMSS has broadened CBA criteria to include community-level benefits.
- **MCDA (elements of):** CMSS uses "a holistic scoring system that captures local risks, land use priorities, and vulnerabilities" and considers community value (greenway connections, historic sites, civic centers) alongside cost-effectiveness (Shi et al. 2022). The sources describe elements consistent with MCDA, though no formal named MCDA framework is cited.
- **Coordination with other sectors:** Shi et al. (2022) note that in Charlotte-Mecklenburg, CMSS "had formed a coalition with watershed, recreation, stewardship, and flood monitoring groups, not housing and community development." Coordination with housing agencies is notably absent. The program does not coordinate with agencies responsible for affordable housing or receiving communities.
- **Degree of transparency:** CMSS publishes a Flood Risk Assessment and Risk Reduction Community Guidebook (CMSS 2020) and offers an interactive flood risk mapping tool (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020). However, Cardwell (2021) documents that community members in some neighborhoods expressed confusion about who owned vacant land and what uses were permitted, suggesting transparency is uneven in practice.
- **Multi-stage retreat:** The program is ongoing over 20+ years, with properties acquired in stages. The orphan property program encourages last holdouts to sell once adjacent properties are acquired, enabling phased neighborhood-scale restoration (Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **Adaptive management:** The program has evolved significantly over time, shifting from reliance primarily on FEMA grants (1999) to establishing a local stormwater fee for non-FEMA-eligible buyouts (2012) and adding leaseback tools (2008). Shi et al. (2022) describe this institutional learning as a key advantage of standing programs. Internally, CMSS recognized that its "neighborhood change score" could have exclusionary effects, prompting it to hire a facilitator to address distributive injustice (Shi et al. 2022).

**Note:** "Bottom-up" is not selected as a primary category. While some neighborhoods successfully shaped outcomes through strong social capital (Country Club Heights), the program's decision-making authority remains with CMSS.

**Categories selected:** Top-down; Participatory/collaborative (variable and site-specific); CBA; MCDA (elements of); Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions (limited, primarily within environmental/watershed sector); Degree of transparency (published guidebook and mapping tool, though uneven in practice); Multi-stage retreat; Adaptive management.

---

### What decision support tools were used in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** CBA; MCDA (elements of); Hazard maps & models; Process guidance; Social vulnerability assessments (emerging/research-only in practice).

**Narrative:**
- **CBA:** FEMA's benefit-cost analysis methodology is applied for federally funded buyouts. CMSS has also diversified CBA criteria beyond property value to include community benefits (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020).
- **MCDA (elements of):** CMSS uses a holistic scoring system incorporating multiple criteria — flood risk, cost-effectiveness, land use priorities, community value — when prioritizing properties (Shi et al. 2022; Spidalieri et al. 2020). No formally named MCDA model is cited in the sources.

Case study: Kinston (Kinston, North Carolina, United States)
Section: Case Study Overview

**Case Name and Location:** Kinston-Lenoir County Floodplain Acquisition and Relocation Program, City of Kinston, Lenoir County, North Carolina, United States of America.

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding of the Neuse River floodplain, triggered by hurricanes and tropical storms. Hurricane Fran (September 1996) and Hurricane Floyd (September 1999) were the primary triggering events. Hurricane Bertha (July 1996) preceded Fran and caused minor wind damage and localized flooding; Hurricane Dennis (September 1999) saturated the drainage basin in the days before Floyd and contributed to the severity of that flood. Flooding was compounded by a technological hazard dimension: the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant adjacent to Lincoln City flooded during both storms, releasing raw and partially treated sewage into the Neuse River, and six junkyards in the floodplain spilled oils, chemicals, and other toxic compounds into floodwaters.

**Type of Retreat:** Voluntary individual property buyout and relocation program. Individual homeowners in the 100-year floodplain were offered pre-disaster fair market value for their homes, primarily through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), supplemented by North Carolina's State Acquisition and Relocation Fund (SARF) to assist residents in purchasing replacement housing within city limits. The program operated as voluntary acquisition; officials did not pursue eminent domain, noting it was not a viable option and would have disqualified the city from HMGP funds.

**Scale:** Approximately 775 individual property acquisitions within the city of Kinston, totaling an estimated 1,500–2,000 people displaced from the floodplain, representing approximately 7% of Kinston's total population at the time. The FEMA case study reports that Kinston and Lenoir County together acquired over 1,000 properties with HMGP funds, with approximately 225 remaining to be acquired at the time of that publication. The buyout area was concentrated in the southern portion of Kinston, including Lincoln City and adjacent floodplain neighborhoods. Virtually all of the residents bought out were African American, with large concentrations of low-income and elderly populations.

**Key Actors:** City of Kinston planning department (led by Floodplain Administrator Tommy Lee); Lenoir County government; the County Hazard Mitigation Planning Team (COHMIT); North Carolina Division of Emergency Management (administering HMGP); North Carolina Division of Community Assistance (administering SARF and Community Development Block Grants); U.S. FEMA; U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD, via CDBG); the Greater Kinston Community Development Corporation (GKCDC), a local non-profit; the Conservation Fund; the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; the Kinston Area Recovery Effort (KARE) volunteer organization; and real estate professionals who helped residents find replacement housing.

**Timeline:** Hurricane Fran struck September 1996. COHMIT was formed within 30 days. HMGP applications were submitted December 1996, but the first grant was not processed until 14 months later. The first property acquisition occurred April 1998. Hurricane Floyd struck September 1999. The Greater Kinston Urban Growth Plan was formally adopted October 1999. After Floyd, a pre-disaster application package was submitted and approved within one week. The buyout program continued through approximately 2004. A Clean Water Management Trust Fund grant to acquire remaining vacant lots in the floodplain was received around 2005. Green infrastructure planning continued through at least 2005–2006. By the time of the reviewed sources, the bulk of acquisitions were complete, though vacant-lot acquisition and Green Infrastructure Plan implementation were still ongoing.

**Key Outcomes:** The program achieved a 97% participation rate among eligible homeowners. Approximately 90% of participants relocated within Kinston city limits; according to McCann (2006), this created a net tax gain for the city because equity on new homes was generally substantially higher than on the flooded properties. The first 101 acquired buildings avoided an estimated $6,387,000 in flood losses during Hurricane Floyd (McCann 2006, Table 1). Over $100 million in grant money was administered overall (McCann 2006), though the precise breakdown across funding streams is not fully reconciled in the available sources. Beyond the buyout itself, the city used disaster recovery funding to advance broader smart-growth goals: construction of 170 single-family homes on infill lots; rehabilitation of an abandoned high school into 57 units of senior housing (Grainger Place) plus 100 additional multi-family units; a downtown business incubator (Kinston Enterprise Center); removal of five of six floodplain junkyards; and decommissioning of the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant. A Green Infrastructure Plan was developed for the acquired open space in partnership with Lenoir County, the Conservation Fund, and UNC Chapel Hill. However, the program carries critical equity dimensions: buyouts were concentrated almost entirely in historically Black, low-income neighborhoods. A post-buyout episode — in which some homes acquired after Floyd were refurbished and relocated into other African-American neighborhoods without notifying original homeowners or, according to the Johnsons, nearby residents — revealed major gaps in notification, accountability, and care in the program's devolved governance structure (de Vries and Fraser 2017).

---

**Narrative Summary**

Kinston, North Carolina, a small city of approximately 20,000 people in Lenoir County, experienced two devastating hurricanes within three years — Fran in 1996 and Floyd in 1999. Both storms caused the Neuse River to overflow its banks and flood significant portions of the city's southern neighborhoods, which were predominantly low-income, African-American areas located in the floodplain. Floyd, which deposited over 13 inches of rain in 24 hours and caused the Neuse to crest more than 10 feet above flood stage, compounded damage from a still-incomplete recovery from Fran. A key factor in both floods was a compound hazard: the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant, located adjacent to the Lincoln City neighborhood, flooded during both storms, releasing raw and partially treated sewage, and six junkyards in the floodplain spilled oils and other toxic compounds into floodwaters. The fecal contamination that entered Lincoln City homes during Floyd was described by de Vries and Fraser (2017) as a defining factor in residents' willingness to participate in the buyout.

In response, the City of Kinston — with state and federal partners — implemented a voluntary floodplain buyout and relocation program funded primarily through FEMA's HMGP (75% of acquisition costs), Community Development Block Grants (HUD), and North Carolina's SARF. The program achieved a 97% participation rate among eligible homeowners, moving approximately 1,500–2,000 residents out of the floodplain, approximately 90% of whom relocated within the city. Kinston distinguished itself from comparable communities by integrating the buyout not merely as a risk-reduction measure but as the implementation vehicle for a broader urban growth plan, incorporating affordable housing, downtown revitalization, environmental hazard removal, and green infrastructure planning. The acquired floodplain is now largely open space, with forest regrowth across much of the area, though some vacant lots, remaining structures, and utilities are still present.

Despite these widely cited achievements, the case carries important critical dimensions. The buyout was concentrated almost entirely in historically Black, low-income neighborhoods that had been confined to flood-prone land since the early twentieth century due to racial segregation. De Vries and Fraser (2017) document a post-buyout episode in which some homes acquired after Floyd — which had been contaminated with sewage — were refurbished by the Greater Kinston Community Development Corporation and relocated into other African-American neighborhoods in Kinston, without notifying the original homeowners or, according to the Johnsons, nearby residents in receiving areas. Residents who raised concerns found no accountability at the city, state, or federal level, with FEMA indicating the matter was outside its jurisdiction. This episode illustrates how the program's devolved governance structure and its "logic of choice" — where responsibilities were demarcated contractually — perpetuated rather than remedied the discriminatory waterscape dynamics that originally produced the hazard conditions in Lincoln City. The Kinston case thus stands simultaneously as a frequently cited model of successful floodplain acquisition and as a critical case study in the equity limitations of devolved managed retreat governance.

Case study: Kinston (Kinston, North Carolina, United States)
Section: Coding Questions

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Primarily **Reactive**, with elements of **Proactive** planning that developed after the first hurricane.

**Narrative:** The acquisition and relocation program was initiated in direct response to Hurricane Fran (September 1996), a post-disaster reactive trigger. Prior to Fran, Kinston had no meaningful hazard mitigation planning, had not implemented a significant buyout program, and had been denied prior funding for floodplain structure elevation (McCann 2006). The program was therefore fundamentally reactive in its origins.

However, proactive elements emerged over the course of the program. Within 30 days of Fran, COHMIT was formed and had a strategy in place. HMGP applications were submitted within 90 days. Most significantly, after Floyd struck in 1999, Kinston's experience with the Fran-era program enabled rapid response: the NOAA Digital Coast source notes that a pre-disaster project application package had been developed and was submitted and approved within one week of Floyd. The Greater Kinston Urban Growth Plan was formally adopted October 1999, integrating mitigation as the implementation tool for broader smart-growth objectives — evidence of proactive strategic framing. After Floyd, the city also used access restrictions and a six-month moratorium to reduce re-occupation and rebuilding before buyouts could be completed (McCann 2006), reflecting deliberate proactive governance to manage the transition.

Both codes are appropriate: the trigger was reactive (post-disaster), but Kinston's subsequent approach incorporated proactive planning that went beyond conventional disaster response.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date of initiation:** September 1996 (Hurricane Fran); formal program underway from December 1996 (HMGP applications submitted); first acquisition April 1998; program expanded after Hurricane Floyd, September 1999; buyout program continued through approximately 2004; vacant-lot acquisition and green infrastructure planning ongoing through at least 2005–2006.

- **Number of households/properties:** Approximately 775 direct buyout acquisitions within the City of Kinston (McCann 2006; Siders 2019). The FEMA case study reports that Kinston and Lenoir County together had acquired over 1,000 properties with HMGP funds, with approximately 225 remaining at the time of that publication.

- **Number of population affected:** Approximately 1,500–2,000 people (McCann 2006), representing approximately 7% of Kinston's total population of about 20,000 (NOAA Digital Coast; McCann 2006).

- **Total funding:** McCann (2006) reports over $100 million in grant money administered overall, but the precise breakdown across HMGP, CDBG, SARF, and other streams is not fully reconciled in the available sources and different figures refer to different scopes (city vs. county), different purposes (acquisition vs. relocation vs. housing construction), and different stages (applications vs. funds disbursed). Key figures that are individually supported: the largest HMGP housing application sought over $23.5 million (state responsible for $7.8 million of this; McCann 2006); total HMGP applications from Kinston after Fran totalled over $36.5 million (McCann 2006); CDBG funding was approximately $24.9 million (McCann 2006); HMGP contributed approximately $30 million county-wide, with the state balance approximately $10 million (FEMA case study); the Governor's relief fund provided $1.5 million for housing construction materials; and a $1.05 million EDA grant funded the business incubator (McCann 2006). These figures should not be simply added together as they describe different components at different scales.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Multiple Hazards.**

**Narrative:** The primary hazard was riverine flooding from the Neuse River triggered by hurricanes and tropical storms. However, multiple hazard dimensions are documented: (1) flooding from multiple successive storms — Bertha (July 1996, minor), Fran (September 1996, major), Dennis (September 1999, contributed to basin saturation before Floyd), and Floyd (September 1999, catastrophic); (2) contaminated floodwaters from the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant, which flooded during both Fran and Floyd, releasing raw and partially treated sewage into the Neuse River (McCann 2006); and (3) flooding of six junkyards in the floodplain, which spilled oils and chemicals into floodwaters (McCann 2006). De Vries and Fraser (2017) characterize the hazard as a compound toxic event — not purely hydrological — noting that fecal contamination entering homes during Floyd was a defining factor in participation decisions. These compound hazard conditions were relevant to both the retreat decision process and the scale of resident participation.

The "Multiple Hazards" code applies because two or more hazards (riverine flooding plus technological/contamination hazard) impacted the same area in a cascading fashion.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard** (primary) and **Technological Hazard** (secondary/compound).

**Narrative:** The flooding itself was a natural hazard driven by hurricane activity and riverine dynamics. However, the technological hazard component — the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant and floodplain junkyards — substantially exacerbated harm to residents and was explicitly part of the rationale for retreat (both to move people out and to remove the environmental hazards). McCann (2006) and de Vries and Fraser (2017) both describe the toxic contamination of floodwaters as integral to the case. The decommissioning of the wastewater plant and removal of five junkyards were direct outcomes of the buyout program. Both origins are therefore coded.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), (Lake Flooding/Erosion), (Wildfire), (Volcano), (Land Subsidence), (Landslide/Debris Flow), (Earthquake), (Tsunami), (Hurricane), (Other)

**Answer:** **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding** and **Hurricane** (as the triggering mechanism). **Other** may also apply for the compound toxic contamination hazard.

**Narrative:** The primary hazard was riverine flooding of the Neuse River floodplain, which is clearly the central driver of the buyout. Hurricanes (Fran and Floyd primarily, with Bertha and Dennis as contributing factors) were the proximate causes of the flooding and are accordingly relevant. The flooding described is riverine/floodplain flooding, not direct coastal storm surge — Kinston is an inland city. The toxic contamination from the wastewater plant and junkyards constitutes an "Other" compound hazard dimension, though it is not a standard separate hazard category in the codebook.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Individual homes** (mechanism) and **Neighbourhood** (geographic outcome), with community-scale impacts.

**Narrative:** The program operated through individual property acquisitions — each buyout was negotiated separately with individual homeowners on a parcel-by-parcel basis (McCann 2006; FEMA case study). However, acquisitions were geographically concentrated in specific neighborhoods — most notably Lincoln City and adjacent southern Kinston floodplain neighborhoods — and the city's explicit goal was to remove all residential structures from the 100-year floodplain (FEMA case study). The 97% participation rate and the access restrictions and construction moratorium effectively transformed entire neighborhoods into open space. "Entire community" is not selected because the buyout affected approximately 7% of the city's population and did not relocate the entire city.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Individuals**, **Groups/Neighbourhoods**, **Critical infrastructure**, and **Industrial assets**.

**Narrative:** The core of the program was individual homeowners participating in voluntary buyouts (McCann 2006). The geographic concentration of buyouts in Lincoln City and surrounding floodplain neighborhoods effectively resulted in the retreat of entire neighborhoods. Additionally, the city explicitly used the disaster recovery process to remove industrial hazards: five of six floodplain junkyards were bought out, and the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant was decommissioned — the latter falling under both "Critical infrastructure" and "Industrial assets" (McCann 2006). The FEMA case study also mentions mobile home parks among acquired properties.

### Other notes (General Information)

Siders (2019) includes the Kinston program among eight well-documented US buyout programs analyzed for social justice implications, noting approximately 775 buyouts with a 97% participation rate and that major participants were low-income minorities. The Siders paper uses McCann (2006) and other UNC Chapel Hill research as its primary source for the Kinston case. Note that Siders (2019) is included in the provided source documents (the paper "Social justice implications of US managed retreat buyout programs," Climatic Change), so this citation is verifiable.

The NOAA Digital Coast source states "A total of 1,600 homes have been purchased, leaving 73 percent of the city's floodplain as open space." These figures (1,600 homes and 73% of floodplain) are not corroborated by the McCann thesis or FEMA case study provided, and may refer to a broader or later scope than the primary sources cover. These figures are noted here for completeness but are not used in factual claims elsewhere in this memo, as their basis cannot be independently verified from the other provided sources.

Section: Institutional Environment

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (primary mechanism) and **Managed realignment of infrastructure** (secondary outcome).

**Narrative:** The program operated through individual voluntary property acquisitions — homeowners each made individual decisions to participate (McCann 2006; FEMA case study). This is the standard HMGP acquisition model. However, the density and geographic concentration of buyouts in specific neighborhoods produced community-scale outcomes in practice. Additionally, the decommissioning of the Peachtree Wastewater Treatment Plant and the removal of five junkyards constitute managed realignment of infrastructure out of the floodplain; these were explicitly pursued through the same disaster recovery funding framework (McCann 2006). "Managed realignment of infrastructure" is therefore coded as a secondary element.

"Community buyout/retreat" is not selected as the primary code, as the program operated through individual voluntary agreements rather than a coordinated community relocation process with collective decision-making.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Legal authority over retreat**, **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Compliance & enforcement**, and **Other** (heir property complications; duplication of benefits rule; House Bill 1783 controversy).

**Narrative:**

- **Legal authority over retreat:** FEMA's HMGP program prohibits use of eminent domain; acquisitions must be voluntary and communities must notify property owners in writing that eminent domain will not be used if a voluntary agreement is not reached (McCann 2006, citing FEMA 1998). Kinston officials acknowledged they could theoretically have used eminent domain but did not see it as a viable option, particularly given it would disqualify the city from HMGP funds (McCann 2006).

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** HMGP regulations required that acquired land be maintained as open space in perpetuity and that structures be demolished within 90 days of closing (McCann 2006). FEMA's 100-year floodplain mapping determined eligibility, but inaccurate floodplain maps created obstacles when homes outside the mapped floodplain were flooded (McCann 2006). The Bunning-Bereuter-Blumenauer Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004 (cited in de Vries and Fraser 2017) mandated that property owners with repetitive losses were held responsible for damage if they chose not to leave the 100-year floodplain.

- **Home acquisition / Land acquisition / Title(s) transfer:** The process required property appraisals, title searches, legal surveys, and deed transactions. "Heir property" — properties passed down without legal wills — was among the most time-consuming tasks; in some cases requiring sign-off from up to 30–40 heirs for a single property (McCann 2006).

- **Compliance & enforcement:** After Floyd, the city used security checkpoints to restrict access to flooded areas for over a month, and then passed a six-month moratorium on any new construction or additions — an act that was never officially rescinded — to reduce re-occupation and rebuilding before buyouts could be completed (McCann 2006).

- **Other (duplication of benefits):** FEMA's "duplication of benefits" rule required that flood insurance payouts be subtracted from buyout compensation, which insured owners perceived as a penalty and which generated resistance among some participants (McCann 2006).

- **Other (House Bill 1783):** De Vries and Fraser (2017) document that the City Attorney invoked House Bill 1783 of the 1999 NC General Assembly (Section 2.2) to permit rehabilitation of condemned homes for flood victims, creating a legal ambiguity about the meaning of "condemnation" that was central to the refurbished-homes controversy.

"Land rezoning" is not coded because the sources do not document formal rezoning of floodplain parcels. The construction moratorium restricted new development but is not the same as a rezoning of land use classifications.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Multiple funders** — **Federal**, **State/Provincial**, **Local/Municipal**, and **NGOs**.

**Narrative:**

- **Federal (FEMA HMGP):** Provided 75% of acquisition costs; approximately $30 million county-wide per the FEMA case study; largest single HMGP housing application sought over $23.5 million (McCann 2006).
- **Federal (HUD CDBG):** Community Development Block Grants, approximately $24.9 million, for relocation housing and community development components (McCann 2006).
- **State (NC — SARF):** State Acquisition and Relocation Fund provided supplemental relocation assistance (~$35,000 per household), enabling residents to purchase replacement homes; administered by NC Division of Community Assistance (McCann 2006).
- **State (NC Division of Emergency Management):** Administered HMGP at the state level; provided the balance of HMGP match (~$10 million county-wide, FEMA case study).
- **State (Governor's relief fund):** $1.5 million for construction materials for replacement housing under the NC Permanent Housing Initiative (McCann 2006; FEMA case study).
- **Local/Municipal:** Kinston advanced funds for the program and was later reimbursed — a critical flexibility that distinguished it from other communities (McCann 2006).
- **Clean Water Management Trust Fund:** Grant for acquiring remaining vacant lots post-2005 (McCann 2006).
- **NGOs / non-profit:** GKCDC received land grants from the NC Community Development Initiative for the refurbishment initiative (de Vries and Fraser 2017). Conservation Fund partnered on the Green Infrastructure Plan. EDA grant ($1.05 million) funded the Kinston Enterprise Center (McCann 2006).
- **Private sector (tax credits):** Low-income housing tax credits and historic preservation tax credits used for Grainger Place (McCann 2006).

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Assisting BO recipients to find housing in community**, **New housing for BO recipients**, **Redevelopment of retreat lands** (partially), and **New industry**.

**Narrative:**

- **Assisting BO recipients to find housing in community:** A central explicit objective. SARF funds were conditioned on residents relocating within Kinston city limits. Approximately 90% of participants relocated within city limits; McCann (2006) describes this as creating a net tax gain because equity on new homes was generally substantially higher than on the flooded homes. Simultaneous closings ensured smooth transitions. The FEMA case study states that "97 percent of those residents" relocated within the tax district.

- **New housing for BO recipients:** The "Call Kinston Home" initiative and NC Permanent Housing Initiative built 170 single-family homes on infill lots and approximately 100 homes through the inmate-panel program (McCann 2006; FEMA case study). Grainger Place created 57 units of senior housing and 100 additional multi-family units.

- **Redevelopment of retreat lands:** The acquired floodplain was maintained as open space per FEMA requirements; the Green Infrastructure Plan proposed recreational, educational, and economic uses that could generate future value, though this remained in early implementation stages at the time of the sources. This element is therefore partial.

- **New industry:** The Kinston Enterprise Center (business incubator, $1.05 million EDA grant) was explicitly framed as economic development to stimulate entrepreneurship and revitalize the downtown tax base (McCann 2006).

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Market value** (pre-disaster), **Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups**, and **Free supports and services**.

**Narrative:**

- **Market value (pre-disaster):** HMGP requires pre-disaster fair market value as determined by a licensed appraiser; this was the base compensation offered (McCann 2006; FEMA case study).

- **Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups:** A relocation allowance of approximately $35,000 (SARF) was provided on top of the home purchase price, conditioned on purchasing replacement housing within Kinston city limits (McCann 2006).

- **Free supports and services:** The city paid all closing costs and real estate transaction costs (appraisals, title searches, surveys). A real estate agent helped relocated families find new homes. The city administered simultaneous closings to facilitate smooth transitions. A video was produced explaining the entire process to residents. Counseling sessions were held to prepare residents for higher bills in new homes and to advise against home equity loan risk (McCann 2006).

- **Note on duplication of benefits:** Residents who had flood insurance had the insurance payment subtracted from their purchase price under FEMA's "duplication of benefits" rule, which was a source of conflict and perceived inequity (McCann 2006). Post-disaster value was not used; the program maintained pre-disaster FMV.

Case study: Kinston (Kinston, North Carolina, United States)
Section: Planning Processes

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Pre-retreat planning**, **Immediate risks: 1–5 years**, **Anticipated future risks: 10–100 years**, and **Post-retreat follow-up**.

**Narrative:**

- **Pre-retreat planning:** COHMIT was created within 30 days of Fran to develop a hazard mitigation plan (McCann 2006). After Floyd, Kinston's experience allowed preparation and submission of a pre-disaster application package that was approved within one week (NOAA Digital Coast). The Greater Kinston Urban Growth Plan was adopted to guide long-term recovery.

- **Immediate risks (1–5 years):** Given repeated hurricane strikes, the city treated flood risk as immediate and acted urgently to move residents out quickly, in part to prevent re-occupation (McCann 2006).

- **Anticipated future risks (10–100 years):** The goal of permanently removing all residential structures from the 100-year floodplain, and the FEMA requirement that acquired land remain open space in perpetuity, reflect a multi-generational time horizon. GIS was used to map 100- and 500-year floodplains (FEMA case study; McCann 2006).

- **Post-retreat follow-up:** Ongoing maintenance of acquired open space, continued acquisition of remaining vacant lots (Clean Water Management Trust Fund grant, ~2005), Green Infrastructure Plan development, and housing counseling for relocated residents all reflect post-retreat follow-up (McCann 2006).

"Emerging risks: 5–10 years" is not separately coded as the sources do not explicitly discuss a distinct 5–10 year horizon; the planning addressed both immediate and long-term timeframes.

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Top-down** (primary governance structure), with elements of **Multi-sectoral**, **Participatory/collaborative**, **Adaptive management**, **Cost-benefit analysis**, **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions**, **Bureaucracy reduction** (as implementation strategy), and **Multi-stage retreat**.

**Narrative:**

- **Top-down:** The program was initiated and administered by city and county government in coordination with state and federal agencies. Decisions were government-led (McCann 2006).

- **Multi-sectoral:** The recovery integrated housing, environmental, economic development, and infrastructure sectors. COHMIT brought together city, county, emergency management, community development, and other agencies (McCann 2006).

- **Participatory/collaborative:** Community meetings were held; a video was produced to educate residents; the KARE volunteer network mobilized community support; the Conservation Fund and UNC Chapel Hill participated in green infrastructure planning (McCann 2006; FEMA case study). However, de Vries and Fraser (2017) note significant gaps in genuine community participation — notably, no community notification or input regarding the refurbishment and relocation of flood-contaminated homes into receiving neighborhoods.

- **Adaptive management:** After Fran, the city learned from mistakes (e.g., failure to prevent re-occupation) and implemented more effective strategies after Floyd, including the construction moratorium and access restrictions (McCann 2006).

- **CBA:** HMGP eligibility required a FEMA-approved cost-benefit analysis. Losses avoided ($6,387,000 from the first 101 acquisitions) were explicitly calculated (McCann 2006, Table 1).

- **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** Extensive coordination between city, county, state, and federal levels; GIS used to manage information across levels (McCann 2006; FEMA case study).

- **Bureaucracy reduction:** Kinston advanced funds locally rather than waiting for federal reimbursement — a deliberate strategy to cut through bureaucratic delays (McCann 2006). This is better characterized as an implementation tactic than a formal planning element, but it was intentional and significant.

- **Multi-stage retreat:** The program operated in phases: Fran-era acquisitions began in 1998, Floyd-era acquisitions were rolled into the same program in 1999, and vacant lot acquisition continued through 2005+ (McCann 2006).

"Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)" and "Bottom-up" are not coded as the sources do not clearly document use of formal MCDA tools or a community-led bottom-up planning process.

---

### What decision support tools were used in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Hazard maps and models**, **CBA**, **Housing assessment**, **Social vulnerability assessments**, **Demographic projections**, and **Process guidance**.

**Narrative:**

- **Hazard maps and models:** GIS was central to the program. Kinston used GIS to display 100- and 500-year floodplains, track acquisitions, and illustrate flood risk. Existing floodplain maps were found to be inaccurate — homes outside the mapped 100-year floodplain were flooded — creating eligibility complications; GIS was used to remap (McCann 2006; FEMA case study).

- **CBA:** Required for HMGP eligibility; losses-avoided calculations were documented (McCann 2006, Table 1).

- **Housing assessment:** GIS was used to develop a demographic profile of the floodplain and determine how many homes were needed and at what price ranges to enable relocation within city limits (FEMA case study; McCann 2006).

- **Social vulnerability assessments:** GIS databases included information on special needs populations (elderly, infants, handicapped), socio-economic data (renters, homeowners, annual incomes), and repetitive loss data (FEMA case study).

- **Demographic projections:** GIS was used to develop relocation needs projections (FEMA case study; McCann 2006).

- **Process guidance:** FEMA's Property Acquisition Handbook for Local Communities (FEMA 1998) provided guidance; COHMIT workshops brought state and federal guidance to local planners (McCann 2006).
