Case study: Matata Managed Retreat (Matata, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case name and location:** Awatarariki Fanhead Voluntary Managed Retreat, Matatā, Bay of Plenty, North Island, New Zealand.

**Hazard(s):** Debris flow / landslide, triggered by extreme rainfall in the Awatarariki stream catchment. The managed retreat decision was driven specifically by this debris flow risk. Separately, Matatā as a community is exposed to a broader range of natural hazards — including earthquakes, landslides, floods, coastal erosion and inundation, and far-sourced hazards such as tsunami and volcanic eruption from the Taupō Volcanic Zone — but these broader hazards did not drive the specific managed retreat decision at Awatarariki fanhead [2].

**Type of retreat:** Voluntary property buyout (land acquisition package) offered to individual property owners in the high-risk zone (HRZ), developed using general competency powers under the Local Government Act 2002 s12(2)(a) rather than the Public Works Act 1981. The buyout was supported by two regulatory plan changes: a District Plan Change proposed to rezone the land from Residential to Coastal Protection Zone; and a Regional Plan Change (Bay of Plenty Regional Natural Resources Plan, Plan Change 17) proposed to extinguish existing use rights in the HRZ [2, 3].

**Scale:** The Awatarariki fanhead area contained 45 properties (sections and developed sites), 34 in private ownership, with 16 homes permanently occupied and 18 vacant sections [2]. Matatā's total population was approximately 645 (2013 census); however, the retreat targeted the fanhead properties specifically, not the whole town [2].

**Key actors:** Whakatāne District Council (WDC) — primary implementation body; Bay of Plenty Regional Council (BOPRC) — regional regulatory authority; Central Government (Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management and other agencies) — funding contributor; Tonkin and Taylor (T&T) — specialist engineering consultants; Stimpson & Co. — workshop facilitators; The Property Group Ltd — land acquisition advisors; GNS Science — technical risk research; affected property owners; iwi (Ngāti Rangitihi, Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau, and the Mataatua District Māori Council) [2].

**Timeline:** The triggering debris flow occurred in May 2005. Engineering mitigation was pursued from 2005; by December 2012, WDC concluded no viable engineering solutions remained, after which managed retreat was developed over several years. A Consensus Development Group (CDG) was convened March–May 2015. Preliminary buyout offers were made in December 2016. Plan Change 17 was publicly notified in June 2018. Regional and central government agreed to co-fund the buyout in 2019 [2, 3]. The process spans at least 14 years (2005–2019).

**Key outcomes:** By February 2017, 23 landowners had provided registrations of interest: 21 in support of continuing, 2 declining, and 11 non-responses [2]. In 2019, regional and central government agreed to co-fund the buyout through a tripartite model (central government, BOPRC, and WDC each contributing approximately one-third) [3]. Regulatory plan changes were publicly notified and progressed. The case contributed to policy learning on collaborative funding models and risk-based approaches to managed retreat in New Zealand, and the Department of Internal Affairs worked with WDC staff to develop a managed retreat affordability principles framework [2]. The case is also a cautionary example: the protracted timeline, cascading institutional uncertainties, erosion of community trust, and significant and ongoing trauma to residents are extensively documented [2, 3].

---

### Narrative Summary

In May 2005, a severe rainstorm triggered catastrophic debris flows in the Awatarariki stream catchment near the small coastal township of Matatā in the Bay of Plenty, New Zealand. Rocks up to seven metres in diameter were transported at 15–30 km/hr, releasing an estimated 300,000+ cubic metres of rock, wood debris, silt, and slurry onto fanhead properties [2]. The debris flow destroyed 27 homes and damaged a further 87 properties [3]. No lives were lost, although risk assessment modelling later estimated that a repeat event of the same scale could cause five fatalities [2].

In the immediate aftermath, both the community and WDC focused on recovery and selected a debris dam engineering solution. Over the following seven years, engineering designs were repeatedly revised as peer reviews raised concerns about the unprecedented scale, viability, and mounting costs — eventually estimated at $5–7 million or more. By December 2012, WDC concluded no viable engineering solutions remained, after which managed retreat was developed over several further years [2]. Between 2013 and 2016, risk assessments confirmed an intolerable level of loss-of-life risk; a CDG was formed and conducted four full-day workshops considering eight options; cost-benefit and multi-criteria analyses were conducted; and a voluntary acquisition package was developed. The preferred option (Option 2) was costed at between $12.2 million and $14.2 million to acquire 75–100% of the 16 properties with dwellings, the 18 vacant sections, and to cover reserve development costs [2]. Preliminary indicative buyout offers based on current market value were made in December 2016. In parallel, WDC and BOPRC progressed plan changes, creating a perception among many residents that the buyout was not truly voluntary and contributing to mistrust [2, 3]. Residents reported sustained trauma, stress, financial anxiety, and a sense of being trapped. Some residents reported ongoing trauma 13–14 years after the original event; one participant stated they had post-traumatic stress disorder [3]. Funding was agreed in 2019 through a tripartite co-funding model [3].

The Matatā case is instructive at multiple levels. It demonstrates the long-term human costs of short-term post-disaster decision-making, the institutional gaps in New Zealand's managed retreat governance framework, the challenges of implementing voluntary retreat without national policy guidance and confirmed funding, and the cascading nature of uncertainties — technical, financial, legal, political, and social — that compound and reinforce each other. Māori cultural concerns were also significant: the Awatarariki fanhead contains a historically significant burial ground (urupā) whose disturbance had been opposed by local iwi before original development was permitted. The case contributed to New Zealand policy learning on managed retreat and prompted development of national managed retreat affordability principles [2].

Case study: Matata Managed Retreat (Matata, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Reactive.

**Narrative:** The managed retreat process in Matatā was initiated directly in response to the May 2005 debris flow disaster, which destroyed 27 homes and damaged 87 more [3]. The decision to pursue managed retreat was not made immediately after the event — WDC initially pursued engineering solutions — but the entire trajectory of events was triggered by the disaster. Sources consistently describe managed retreat as a last resort arrived at after engineering options were ruled out. Hanna et al. (2018) state explicitly: "In this case, overcoming this dependency and arriving at managed retreat was not enabled by a specific action or tool, but the fact that there were no other options left, it was a last resort" [2]. Hanna (2020) similarly notes that managed retreat "became necessary as other options were ruled out" [3].

There is no evidence that managed retreat was proactively planned before the disaster or as part of any anticipatory hazard management strategy. Hanna et al. (2018) note in hindsight that "immediate post-disaster retreat would have been more efficient and effective and less harmful to the long-term resilience of the community," but this did not occur [2]. Hanna et al. (2017) confirm that proactive managed retreat remains rare across New Zealand, with Matatā being an example of reactive, post-disaster retreat [1].

**Category selected:** Reactive. Proactive is not applicable.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date of triggering event:** May 2005 (debris flow) [2, 3].
- **Key dates in retreat process:** December 2012 — WDC confirms no viable engineering solutions remain; March–May 2015 — CDG workshops; December 2016 — preliminary buyout offers made; June 2018 — Plan Change 17 publicly notified; 2019 — regional and central government agree to co-fund the buyout [2, 3].
- **Number of properties/households affected:** The fanhead area contained 45 properties (sections and developed sites), 34 in private ownership. The preferred buyout option (Option 2) was costed to acquire 75–100% of the 16 properties with dwellings and the 18 vacant sections [2].
- **Number of population affected:** Matatā's total population was approximately 645 (2013 census) [2]. The retreat targeted the fanhead properties specifically; the number of people directly affected by the buyout is not specified beyond the 16 permanently occupied dwellings.
- **Total funding:** Option 2 was costed between $12.2 million and $14.2 million to acquire 75–100% of the identified properties and cover reserve development costs [2]. A tripartite funding model was proposed and agreed in principle, with central government, BOPRC, and WDC each contributing approximately one-third [2, 3]. Final confirmed funding amounts are not specified in the reviewed sources; the $12.2–14.2 million figure is the indicative business case estimate from 2017. Prior to the managed retreat phase, the Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management provided a grant of $2.890 million and WDC approved a budget of $3.558 million for the failed engineering phase [2].

**Uncertainty:** The final confirmed total funding amount for the buyout is not provided in the reviewed sources.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** Single Hazard (for the purpose of the managed retreat decision).

**Narrative:** The managed retreat decision was specifically and exclusively driven by the debris flow / landslide risk on the Awatarariki fanhead, assessed as posing an intolerable level of loss-of-life risk [2, 3]. The Quantitative Landslide Risk Assessment concluded intolerable risk from future debris flows specifically [2]. Plan Change 17 and the District Plan Change were both designed to address this specific hazard.

Matatā is described as being exposed to "a range of natural hazards including earthquakes, landslides, debris flows, floods, coastal erosion and inundation, with far-sourced hazards including tsunami and volcanic eruption from the Taupō Volcanic Zone" [2], but these broader hazards are contextual only and did not drive the specific managed retreat decision.

**Category selected:** Single Hazard (debris flow/landslide, for the MR decision process). The broader multiple-hazard context is noted but is not the basis for the retreat.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** Natural Hazard.

**Narrative:** The 2005 debris flow was triggered by a natural geophysical process — extreme rainfall in the Awatarariki catchment causing severe flooding and a major debris flow [2]. Sources consistently describe the event as a natural hazard [1, 2, 3]. There is no evidence of a technological or human-caused origin for the hazard itself. While land development on the fanhead increased exposure, the hazard origin is natural.

**Category selected:** Natural Hazard.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), (Lake Flooding/Erosion), (Wildfire), (Volcano), (Land Subsidence), (Landslide/Debris Flow), (Earthquake), (Tsunami), (Hurricane), (Other)

**Answer:** Landslide/Debris Flow.

**Narrative:** All sources confirm the primary and only hazard driving the managed retreat decision was debris flow on the Awatarariki fanhead [1, 2, 3]. Hanna et al. (2018) describe the 2005 event: "The 2005 debris flow in the Awatarariki stream was catalysed by a significant amount of rainfall in the catchment resulting in severe flooding and a major debris flow" [2]. The Quantitative Landslide Risk Assessment was specifically commissioned to assess debris flow risk and concluded an intolerable level of loss-of-life risk [2]. Plan Change 17 specifically addresses natural hazard risk on the fanhead from this hazard type.

While coastal erosion, coastal inundation, and other hazards are mentioned as part of Matatā's broader multi-hazard context [2], these were not part of the managed retreat decision process for the Awatarariki fanhead.

**Category selected:** Landslide/Debris Flow only.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** Neighbourhood and Individual Homes.

**Narrative:** The retreat affected a specific sub-area of Matatā — the Awatarariki fanhead, described as "located towards the western end of the township" — comprising 45 properties (34 in private ownership, 16 occupied dwellings, 18 vacant sections) [2]. This is clearly a sub-community or neighbourhood-scale area, not the entire community of Matatā (population ~645). The acquisition strategy operated at the individual property level, with offers made at individual meetings based on independent property valuations [2]. Both Neighbourhood (the Awatarariki fanhead area) and Individual Homes (parcel-by-parcel property acquisition) are therefore applicable.

**Categories selected:** Neighbourhood (Awatarariki fanhead sub-area of Matatā) and Individual Homes (individual property acquisition offers).

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** Individuals and Groups/Neighbourhoods.

**Narrative:** The retreat targeted individual property owners and residents on the fanhead. Preliminary offers were made to individual property owners at individual meetings, and registrations of interest were collected individually [2]. However, the overall strategy sought retreat of a defined neighbourhood cluster — the entire Awatarariki fanhead HRZ — rather than scattered individuals across the wider community. The CDG process and plan changes were designed to achieve collective retreat of this neighbourhood [2, 3]. Critical infrastructure, hazard protection structures, and industrial assets are not identified as subjects of retreat in the reviewed sources.

**Categories selected:** Individuals and Groups/Neighbourhoods.

---

### Other notes (General Information)

Matatā's socioeconomic status is low — a deprivation index of 9 out of 10, with unemployment at 13.7%, almost double the national average — and 60% of residents identify as Māori [2]. These characteristics are relevant to equity and cultural dimensions discussed in subsequent sections. The extraordinary duration of the process (at least 14 years from triggering event to funding agreement) was itself a significant and documented source of harm to the community [2, 3].

Case study: Matata Managed Retreat (Matata, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** Individual buyout/retreat, with elements of Community buyout/retreat.

**Narrative:** The primary mechanism was a voluntary individual property acquisition package. WDC adopted an Acquisition Strategy developed by The Property Group Ltd reflecting key principles of land acquisition under the Public Works Act 1981, offering indicative prices to each of the 34 property owners in the HRZ at individual meetings [2]. The strategy was developed using general competency powers under the LGA s12(2)(a) rather than the PWA, as WDC received legal advice that the PWA could not be used for managed retreat and subsequent reserve conversion [3].

The strategy also had community-scale dimensions: the CDG process was collective; the plan changes applied to the entire fanhead zone; and the strategy aimed at achieving near-complete retreat of a defined neighbourhood. Hanna et al. (2017) note that "the voluntary retreat package has been offered to property owners on a one-time basis" for the entire zone [1]. The goal was whole-neighbourhood clearance. Both categories are therefore warranted.

There is no evidence of leasebacks, easements, buffers, or managed realignment of infrastructure as mechanisms in this case.

**Categories selected:** Individual buyout/retreat (primary mechanism) and Community buyout/retreat (intended collective outcome and neighbourhood-scale regulatory approach).

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Legal authority over retreat, Relevant regulations/acts, Home acquisition, Land acquisition, Title(s) transfer, Land rezoning, Compliance & enforcement, Litigation (potential/threatened), Other.

**Narrative:** This case is defined by its legal complexity. Key legal issues identified across the sources include:

**Legal authority over retreat:** A central barrier was the jurisdictional mismatch between territorial authorities (WDC, responsible for land use but lacking power to extinguish existing use rights) and regional councils (BOPRC, which held power to extinguish existing use rights under s20A RMA but was politically reluctant to exercise it) [2, 3]. Participant 2 states: "in terms of an area that's already developed, the tools are pretty weak, they are incredibly weak" [2].

**Relevant regulations/acts:** Multiple pieces of legislation are implicated: the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA, including ss 20A, 30, 31, 62, 85, and 33 regarding transfer of functions); Local Government Act 2002 (s12(2)(a) general competency powers, used by WDC to develop the buyout outside the statutory regime) [3]; Public Works Act 1981 (WDC received legal advice the PWA could not be used for managed retreat and subsequent reserve conversion, though the Resource Legislation Amendment Act 2017 s85(3A)(a)(ii) suggests otherwise) [3]; Building Act 2004 (Determination 11912 in 2006 created difficulties by enabling rebuilding on the fanhead; Determination 2016/034 later supported declining building consents) [2]; New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010 [1]; Bay of Plenty Regional Policy Statement incorporating Change 2 (July 2016), introducing a risk-based approach [2].

**Home and land acquisition:** The acquisition package was developed using LGA general competency powers rather than the PWA [3]. Independent property valuations were used to set indicative offers at current market value without recognition of the hazard [2].

**Title(s) transfer:** Implied in the acquisition process; vacated land was to be converted to Coastal Reserve/Coastal Protection Zone status [2].

**Land rezoning:** A District Plan Change was proposed to rezone the land from Residential to Coastal Protection Zone; BOPRC's proposed Plan Change 17 to the Bay of Plenty Regional Natural Resources Plan introduced new objectives and policies and a rule prohibiting residential activities in the HRZ after 31 March 2021 [2].

**Compliance and enforcement:** Significant uncertainty existed regarding enforcement if voluntary retreat was unsuccessful. Participant 5 states: "nobody's got any appetite to be sending in bulldozers with protesters lying on the road... 'How do you expect me to get these people out?'" [2, 3]. The timing of regulatory measures relative to the voluntary buyout was a major governance challenge [2].

**Litigation (potential/threatened):** Residents threatened civil disobedience, and it was anticipated that case law arising from Bay of Plenty Regional Plan Change 17 would determine the legality of extinguishing existing use rights under s85 RMA [2]. The Supreme Court decision in Quake Outcasts v The Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery [2015] NZSC 27 — which held that offers made under conditions where residents had "no realistic alternative" were not truly voluntary — was referenced as directly relevant to the Matatā situation [2].

**Other:** Building Act Determination 11912 (2006) presented a significant institutional constraint by enabling rebuilding on the fanhead under assumptions of mitigation that did not eventuate, creating path dependencies and complicating later managed retreat [2]. WDC's use of LGA general competency powers as an alternative legal vehicle for the buyout is also notable [3].

**Categories selected:** Legal authority over retreat, Relevant regulations/acts, Home acquisition, Land acquisition, Title(s) transfer, Land rezoning, Compliance & enforcement, Litigation (potential/threatened), Other (Building Act determinations as constraint; LGA general competency as alternative vehicle).

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** Multiple funders — Federal/Central Government, Provincial/State (Regional Council — BOPRC), and Local/Municipal (WDC).

**Narrative:** The proposed and ultimately agreed funding model was a tripartite arrangement: central government, BOPRC, and WDC each contributing approximately one-third of costs [2, 3]. In 2019, regional and central government agreed to co-fund the buyout [3]. This collaborative, multi-agency funding solution was developed at the local level.

Prior to the managed retreat phase, the Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management provided $2.890 million and WDC approved a budget of $3.558 million for the engineering phase — funds that proved to be sunk costs [2].

WDC faced a "chicken and egg" problem: confirmed funding was an essential element of meaningful acquisition, but funding agencies required certainty around financial parameters before committing [2]. The absence of a nationally funded buyout programme or reserve fund was a significant barrier [2, 3].

**Category selected:** Multiple funders — Local/Municipal (WDC), Provincial/State (BOPRC), Federal/Central Government. No evidence of NGO, international aid, insurance, or individual self-funding for the buyout.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Limited evidence. Some consideration of potential growth to the east of Matatā, but no explicit tax base maintenance strategy.

**Narrative:** The sources do not explicitly discuss tax base maintenance as a planning objective. WDC "undertook some research to determine the potential for future growth to the east of Matatā, and the impacts of intensification upon the town sewerage system" [3]. This implies some consideration of where retreating residents might relocate within or near the community, which could indirectly support the local tax base. The proposed rezoning of the fanhead to Coastal Reserve/Coastal Protection Zone indicates the retreat lands would not be redeveloped for revenue-generating purposes. There is no evidence of new industry attraction, new housing programmes for buyout recipients, livelihoods supports, or other explicit tax base measures being considered in the reviewed sources.

**Category selected:** Assisting BO recipients to find housing in community (very limited — some research into growth to east of Matatā). All other tax base categories: No evidence found in reviewed sources.

**Uncertainty:** Tax base maintenance was not a prominent theme in the reviewed sources.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Market value, Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups.

**Narrative:** The acquisition package was based on "the current market value of their property without recognition of the hazard" [2, 3] — a deliberate choice to offer pre-hazard market value rather than any post-disaster or post-risk-disclosure depreciated value. This approach was designed to be fair to owners while avoiding speculative buyers profiting; eligibility conditions were designed so that the buyout was "discreet, based on specific criteria" regarding whether owners knew of risks before purchasing [2].

Additional incentives included: a $1,200 legal fees contribution; a relocation subsidy of $2,500 for fanhead residents; and the potential for deferred settlement of up to three years for special circumstances [2]. These are monetary top-ups to the purchase offer and are best coded as Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups rather than as free supports and services, consistent with the auditor's coding correction.

WDC explicitly stated it had "a moral obligation to compensate owners for their loss of property under voluntary retreat" and that "successful retreat entails financial incentive" [2]. The compensation was not legally required — WDC chose to offer it as a moral and practical necessity [2].

Residents expressed concern that indicative offers were insufficient for relocation, with Participant 16 noting: "The indicative price they offered us might've seemed like a good price, but it would be about $80,000–$90,000 to shift our house... it would probably gobble up absolutely everything" [3].

**Categories selected:** Market value (primary basis); Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups ($1,200 legal fees contribution, $2,500 relocation subsidy, deferred settlement option). Post-disaster value: not selected — the offer was explicitly based on pre-hazard market value. Free supports and services: not selected separately, as the legal fees contribution and relocation subsidy are monetary top-ups more accurately coded as Additional incentives/bonuses/top-ups.

---

Case study: Matata Managed Retreat (Matata, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Pre-retreat planning, and Post-retreat follow-up (partial).

**Narrative:** The process involved extensive pre-retreat planning from approximately 2013–2018, including risk assessment, CDG workshops, CBA/MCA analysis, business case development, acquisition strategy development, and plan change preparation [2, 3].

The Plan Change 17 rule prohibiting residential activities after 31 March 2021 establishes an implementation deadline, but this is best understood as a policy implementation trigger point rather than a hazard time horizon per se. The debris flow hazard was an existing, present risk — not a projected future risk over a defined time horizon. The managed retreat decision was framed around existing intolerable risk to life, not around a 1–5, 5–10, or 10–100 year projected risk horizon [2]. Accordingly, coding Immediate risks: 1–5 years based on the 2021 rule implementation window — as noted by the auditor — is not warranted as a risk horizon code; the 2021 date is an administrative deadline, not a risk emergence horizon.

The Bay of Plenty RPS and NZCPS reference 100-year planning timeframes for coastal hazards [1], but the specific Matatā retreat decision was not framed around a projected future risk within a particular time horizon.

Post-retreat planning (future land use as Coastal Reserve, research into growth east of Matatā) was considered but not well-developed in the reviewed sources [3].

**Categories selected:** Pre-retreat planning (extensive); Post-retreat follow-up (partial — some consideration of land use and receiving areas, but limited). Immediate risks: 1–5 years, Emerging risks: 5–10, and Anticipated future risks: 10–100 are not selected as primary risk horizon codes for this case; the hazard was an existing, present, and intolerable risk, not a projected future one.

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** CBA, MCDA, Top-down, Bottom-up (partial), Multi-sectoral, Multi-stage retreat, Degree of transparency, Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions, Participatory/collaborative (partial).

**Narrative:**

**CBA and MCDA:** Four short-listed options were compared using both CBA and MCA, including net present value calculations and non-monetary benefits/dis-benefits assessment. This is explicitly confirmed: "Cost benefit analysis (CBA) and multi-criteria analysis (MCA) were used to compare the shortlisted options" [2]. The MCA recommended Option 2 as the preferred way forward [2].

**Top-down:** The regulatory framework (plan changes, risk assessments, buyout parameters) was largely developed and driven by WDC and BOPRC, with central government providing direction and funding conditions [2, 3].

**Bottom-up/Participatory:** The CDG process (March–May 2015) involved six landowners alongside council staff, councillors, regional council representatives, expert advisers, and facilitators, attending four full-day workshops considering eight options [2]. Individual meetings were held with property owners at the preliminary offer stage. Community engagement through "drop in days and individual meetings" was conducted for plan change consultations [2]. However, some community members felt the process was not genuinely participatory or voluntary, and WDC's change of uptake threshold from 90% to no threshold further eroded trust [3]. Both bottom-up and participatory elements were present but limited in effect.

**Multi-sectoral:** The process involved WDC, BOPRC, central government, specialist engineers (Tonkin & Taylor), risk assessors, legal advisors, financial advisors (The Property Group Ltd), workshop facilitators (Stimpson & Co.), iwi representatives, and the affected community [2, 3].

**Multi-stage retreat:** The process was designed as multi-stage — voluntary acquisitions first, with regulatory plan changes as a backstop if uptake was insufficient [2, 3]. However, the two tracks ran in parallel rather than sequentially, creating governance and trust problems [2, 3].

**Degree of transparency:** WDC attempted to be transparent. Participant 1 describes staff as having "bent over backwards to do everything they can... in a very thorough and fair manner" [2]. However, changes to uptake thresholds and the parallel regulatory track undermined perceived transparency. The decision to move from limited to public notification of Plan Change 17 was also transparency-relevant [2].

**Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** A central challenge and partial achievement of the case — coordination between WDC, BOPRC, and central government, as well as between planning, engineering, legal, financial, and community engagement functions [2, 3].

**Adaptive management:** The process involved continuous revision — of engineering solutions, of policy approach, of uptake thresholds, of notification strategies. However, as the auditor notes, the sources describe iterative revision and policy learning but do not explicitly frame the Matatā case as adaptive management. This element is noted as implicit/uncertain rather than a primary code.

**Categories selected:** CBA, MCDA, Top-down, Bottom-up (partial), Multi-sectoral, Multi-stage retreat, Degree of transparency, Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions, Participatory/collaborative (partial). Adaptive management: not coded as primary; noted as implicit.

---

### What decision support tools were used in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** CBA, MCDA, Hazard maps and models, Process guidance (partial).

**Narrative:**

**CBA:** Explicitly used to compare four short-listed options, calculating net present values and costs [2].

**MCDA:** Multi-criteria analysis was used alongside CBA; the MCA recommended Option 2 as the preferred way forward [2].

**Hazard maps and models:** T&T's Quantitative Landslide Risk Assessment (QLRA) concluded intolerable loss-of-life risk [2]. Risk mapping was central to defining the HRZ. The BOP RPS established a risk matrix developed through community engagement [2].

**Process guidance:** WDC worked with The Property Group Ltd to develop an acquisition strategy reflecting Public Works Act principles [2]. The Department of Internal Affairs was working with WDC to develop a "managed retreat affordability principles framework" [2]. However, the absence of national process guidance was itself a major barrier — "learning by doing" was the dominant mode [2, 3].

**Social vulnerability assessments:** The sources acknowledge the socioeconomic context (deprivation index 9/10, high Māori population, unemployment) but no formal social vulnerability assessment tool is identified. Per the auditor's correction, this should not be coded as a decision support tool used in the process; it is contextual information only.

**Housing assessment, CC projection models, demographic projections, socioeconomic projections, new site evaluation process:** No formal tools of these types are identified in the reviewed sources.

**Categories selected:** CBA, MCDA, Hazard maps and models, Process guidance (partial). Social vulnerability assessments: not coded as a tool; contextual information only.

---

### What planning measures were taken for receiving areas in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Minimal. Some research into potential for growth east of Matatā, but no comprehensive receiving area planning.

**Narrative:** WDC undertook some research into potential for future growth to the east of Matatā and the impacts of intensification on the town sewerage system [3], but this was not a developed receiving area plan. The "managed retreat to where?" question was largely left for individuals to manage: "the question of 'managed retreat to where?' has been left for individuals to manage, and there are concerns regarding the impacts on social, cultural, and economic vulnerability" [3].

Residents expressed desire for land swap options and certainty about property options [3]. This represents a significant gap in the retreat planning process.

Case study: Pointe-Gatineau Home Buyout Program (Pointe-Gatineau, Quebec, Canada)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Pointe Gatineau Managed Retreat / Quebec Provincial Property Buyout Program — Pointe Gatineau, a municipal electoral district within the City of Gatineau, Quebec, Canada [Source 1, Source 3]. Gatineau is located in the Outaouais region of Quebec at the confluence of the Gatineau and Ottawa Rivers, bordering Ontario and the National Capital Region [Sources 2, 3].

**Hazard(s):** Riverine flooding caused by springtime snowmelt and heavy rainfall in the Ottawa River watershed. Pointe Gatineau has a documented flood history spanning more than 200 years, and portions of the community sit within a 1:20-year floodplain (5% annual exceedance probability) [Source 2]. Major flood events occurred in April 2017 and May 2019; the reviewed literature describes these as record-setting floods and, in some places, as approximately 100-year floods [Sources 2, 3].

**Type of Retreat:** Government-sponsored voluntary property buyouts with significant coercive elements, implemented at the individual household level but geographically concentrated in the Pointe Gatineau district. The buyouts were embedded in Quebec's General Indemnity and Financial Assistance Program Regarding Actual or Imminent Disasters (Flooding) and were accompanied by regulatory tools — including the Special Intervention Zone (ZIS) — that prohibited reconstruction in the 0–20-year floodplain, creating strong coercive pressure for properties in that zone and effectively requiring retreat rather than rebuilding [Sources 1, 2, 3].

**Scale:** Approximately 1,800 homes were affected by flooding across the wider City of Gatineau in the 2017 floods [Source 2]. In 2019, 923 properties were damaged in Pointe Gatineau alone [Source 3]. Province-wide disaster claims and buyouts are summarised in Source 1 Table 1: after the 2017 floods, 3,945 homeowners made provincial claims, resulting in 419 buyouts, of which 126 were in Gatineau; after the 2019 floods, 4,964 homeowner claims resulted in 979 buyouts, of which 45 were in Gatineau. After limited 2023 flooding, 797 homeowner claims resulted in 11 provincial buyouts, none in Gatineau [Source 1]. Three years into the process, 185 properties in Pointe Gatineau had been demolished, of which 148 had been officially transferred to the City of Gatineau, with remaining plots still in transfer at the time of reporting [Source 3]. The reviewed sources document no buyouts for tenants in any program cycle, though tenants were eligible for disaster financial assistance [Source 1, Table 1; Source 3].

**Key Actors:** The Government of Quebec (Ministry of Public Security / Directorate General for Recovery) designed and funded the buyout program [Sources 1, 3]. The City of Gatineau handled local implementation, including identifying properties, assessing damage, processing applications, receiving title transfers, and managing demolitions [Source 3]. Community organisations (CREDDO, Park People), design consultants (Mandaworks), and city councillors contributed to post-buyout land use planning [Sources 1, 2]. The federal government played no direct role in the buyout program itself [Sources 2, 3].

**Timeline:**
- **April–May 2017:** Major spring flooding; ad hoc buyout program introduced under the existing disaster financial assistance framework; 126 Gatineau homeowners and 56 Gatineau businesses received buyouts from this cycle [Source 1, Table 1].
- **April–May 2019:** Second major flood, exceeding 2017 levels; Province announced a revised and expanded buyout program. 45 homeowner buyouts and 27 business buyouts in Gatineau from this cycle [Source 1, Table 1].
- **June 2019:** Special Intervention Zone (ZIS) formally enacted; moratorium on construction/reconstruction in 0–20-year floodplain [Sources 1, 3].
- **2019–2021:** 185 properties demolished; 148 officially transferred to the City [Source 3].
- **2020:** Territorial Protection Plan against Floods (PPTFI) introduced with $479 million budget [Source 1]. City of Gatineau city council allocated $1.4 million for post-buyout revitalisation [Sources 2, 3].
- **2020–2021:** City of Gatineau, CREDDO, Park People, and Mandaworks develop the Master Plan (PDA) for vacant lots in Pointe Gatineau and Lac-Beauchamp districts [Source 1].
- **March 2022:** ZIS replaced by the Transitional Regime for the Management of Flood Zones, Banks and Coastlines (TRMFZBC), which lifted the ZIS and empowered municipalities to authorise development in flood zones, though in practice it imposed additional procedural requirements and costs [Source 1].
- **July 2022:** Compensation caps raised to $325,000 (residence) and $60,000 (land); small businesses eligible for up to $485,000 [Source 1].
- **2023:** Minor flooding; 11 provincial buyouts, none in Gatineau [Source 1].
- **2024:** Province planning new flood maps and regulatory framework (OPI); Master Plan (PDA) funded but largely unimplemented; Gatineau described as "partially retreated" [Source 1].

**Key Outcomes:**
- 185 properties demolished and 148 officially transferred to municipal ownership in Pointe Gatineau, creating a "swiss-cheese" or checkerboard landscape [Sources 1, 2, 3].
- The province achieved partial alignment between buyout programs and regulatory tools (ZIS, then TRMFZBC), restricting rebuilding in high-risk zones — though the policy environment also exhibited significant fragmentation [Source 1].
- A community Master Plan (PDA) for vacant lots was developed but remains largely unimplemented due to funding gaps and absence of provincial direction on updated flood maps [Source 1].
- A municipal official stated that the tax base had been cut by "probably 30%," creating ongoing service delivery challenges [Source 1].
- Significant bureaucratic delays and lack of intergovernmental coordination were widely criticised [Sources 1, 2, 3].
- The reviewed sources report little or no dedicated relocation assistance — including no help for bought-out homeowners in finding safer housing [Sources 1, 2].
- Tenants were eligible for disaster financial assistance but the reviewed sources document no tenants receiving buyouts in any program cycle [Source 1, Table 1].

---

**Narrative Summary**

Pointe Gatineau is a working-class riverine neighbourhood in the City of Gatineau, Quebec, located at the confluence of the Gatineau and Ottawa Rivers [Sources 2, 3]. It has a documented flood history stretching back more than 200 years [Source 2]. After two successive and record-breaking spring flood events in April 2017 and May 2019 — described in the literature as approximately 100-year floods — the Province of Quebec introduced and then expanded a government-sponsored property buyout program enabling homeowners to permanently vacate flood-damaged properties in exchange for financial compensation [Sources 1, 2, 3]. The buyouts were framed as voluntary, but the simultaneous introduction of lifetime limits on disaster assistance and prohibitions on reconstruction in the 0–20-year floodplain created strong coercive pressure on homeowners — and, for those in the ZIS zone, effectively required retreat rather than rebuilding [Sources 1, 3]. Three years after the 2019 floods, 185 properties in Pointe Gatineau had been demolished, of which 148 had been officially transferred to the City of Gatineau [Source 3].

The experience in Pointe Gatineau illustrates both the potential and the limitations of managed retreat implemented reactively in a post-disaster environment. On the positive side, the province partially aligned buyout policy with regulatory tools (the ZIS, and subsequently the TRMFZBC) to restrict rebuilding in high-risk zones, representing a notable evolution in Canadian flood risk governance [Source 1]. On the negative side, the buyout process was widely criticised for excessive bureaucracy, lengthy application delays, insufficient compensation for some homeowners, narrow eligibility criteria, and a near-total absence of support for homeowners in finding alternative housing. Tenants — who filed hundreds of disaster claims — received no buyouts under any program cycle [Source 1, Table 1].

Five years after the 2019 floods, Pointe Gatineau remains in what Source 1 describes as a "partially retreated" state. The vacant lots created by the buyouts present an opportunity for ecological restoration and community revitalisation. The City of Gatineau, with partners including CREDDO, Park People, and Mandaworks, developed an ambitious Master Plan (PDA) proposing nature lots, nourishing lots, gathering lots, by-the-shore lots, and sponge lots [Source 1]. However, as of early 2024, this plan has not been fully implemented, largely because the Province has not released updated flood maps needed to confirm permissible land uses, and adequate funding and administrative guidance from the province remain absent [Source 1]. The case illustrates a recurring governance challenge: the entity with the financial resources to fund buyouts (the provincial government) has limited involvement in the post-buyout phase, while the entity responsible for managing the land (the municipality) lacks the resources and guidance to act [Source 1].

Case study: Pointe-Gatineau Home Buyout Program (Pointe-Gatineau, Quebec, Canada)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Primarily **Reactive**, with nascent **Proactive** elements in subsequent policy development.

**Narrative:** The managed retreat process in Pointe Gatineau was fundamentally reactive, triggered by two successive flood disasters in 2017 and 2019. Source 3 states explicitly: "retreat in Pointe Gatineau was reactive in nature and used as a response to the two 100-year floods." Source 1 further characterises the buyout program as the result of "the ad-hoc development of a buyout policy" following the 2017 and 2019 events. The Quebec buyout programme was introduced hastily in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 floods, piggybacking on the existing disaster financial assistance framework, and was then expanded after 2019 [Sources 1, 2, 3]. Multiple sources characterise the programme as "ad hoc" and confirm it was not part of a pre-existing proactive flood risk management strategy [Sources 1, 3].

However, there are nascent proactive elements in the subsequent policy trajectory. The introduction of the ZIS in 2019, the PPTFI (2020), lifetime limits on disaster assistance, and the province's planned development of new flood maps all represent forward-looking regulatory development [Source 1]. The post-buyout Master Plan (PDA) reflects proactive community visioning, even if implementation has stalled [Sources 1, 2]. Source 1 also notes that the province plans to release new flood maps potentially classifying up to 55,000 additional homes in the floodplain — a prospective regulatory shift, though not yet implemented managed retreat [Source 1].

**Coding:** Primarily **Reactive**; nascent **Proactive** elements in post-2019 policy development.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date:** Flood events in April–May 2017 and April–May 2019; buyout programme introduced following the 2017 floods and revised after 2019; ongoing post-buyout land use planning 2019–present.

- **Households affected — floods:** Approximately 1,800 homes were affected by flooding across the wider City of Gatineau in spring 2017 [Source 2]. In 2019, 923 properties were damaged in Pointe Gatineau [Source 3]. Disaster claims for the City of Gatineau: 643 homeowners, 232 tenants, and 181 businesses in 2017; 508 homeowners, 94 tenants, and 110 businesses in 2019; 139 homeowners, 17 tenants, and 23 businesses in 2023 [Source 1, Table 1].

- **Buyouts (Gatineau):** 126 homeowner buyouts and 56 business buyouts after the 2017 floods; 45 homeowner buyouts and 27 business buyouts after the 2019 floods; 0 buyouts after the 2023 floods [Source 1, Table 1]. Three years into the process, 185 properties had been demolished, of which 148 had been officially transferred to the City of Gatineau, with remaining plots in transfer [Source 3].

- **Tenants:** The reviewed sources document zero buyouts for tenants in all cycles [Source 1, Table 1]. Tenants were eligible for disaster financial assistance but not for buyouts based on program tables [Sources 1, 3].

- **Population affected:** More than 250 municipalities and more than 10,000 people were evacuated province-wide in the 2019 floods [Source 3]. Pointe Gatineau district has approximately 60,000 residents [Source 4].

- **Total funding:** Insurance losses from the 2017 and 2019 floods: approximately $58 million and $280 million respectively; more than $390 million in non-insured losses was covered by the provincial treasury [Source 1]. Compensation caps at time of the 2019 program: up to $200,000 (residence) + $50,000 (land); note that Source 1 also states compensation was "capped at $250,000 for the residence and the land" in the 2019 cycle — both figures appear in Source 1 and may reflect different program stages or components; increased to $325,000 + $60,000 in July 2022 [Source 1]. The PPTFI (2020) allocated $479 million province-wide [Source 1]. The City of Gatineau allocated $1.4 million for post-buyout revitalisation [Sources 2, 3]. Total buyout expenditure specifically for Pointe Gatineau is not disaggregated in the reviewed sources.

**Uncertainty:** Exact total programme costs for Pointe Gatineau buyouts and total individual compensation disbursed are not disaggregated in the reviewed sources. Population directly displaced by buyouts (as opposed to temporarily evacuated) is not precisely reported.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Single Hazard.**

**Narrative:** All reviewed sources focus exclusively on riverine/pluvial flooding as the hazard driving the managed retreat decision. The 2017 and 2019 flood events were caused by a combination of heavy rainfall and rapid snowmelt in the Ottawa River watershed, producing record water levels [Sources 2, 3]. No other hazards (earthquake, wildfire, coastal erosion, etc.) are mentioned as relevant to this case. The buyout programme and associated regulatory tools (ZIS, TRMFZBC) are uniformly framed as responses to fluvial flooding risk.

**Coding:** **Single Hazard.**

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard**, with climate change cited as an amplifying context.

**Narrative:** The flooding is a natural hazard driven by precipitation and snowmelt in the Ottawa River watershed. Multiple sources connect increasing frequency and severity of flood events to climate change [Sources 1, 3, 4, 5], and Source 1 notes the provincial buyout programme was developed in response to "a changing climate." However, per the codebook, the climate change classification was noted as discarded for the main analysis. The underlying hazard origin is natural.

**Coding:** **Natural Hazard.**

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding.**

**Narrative:** The managed retreat process in Pointe Gatineau was driven entirely by riverine flooding from the Ottawa and Gatineau Rivers, caused by river overflow combined with heavy precipitation and snowmelt. Sources consistently describe the hazard as "riverine flooding" or "spring flooding" from the Ottawa River system [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Flood zone designations (1:20-year and 1:100-year floodplains) and the regulatory framework (ZIS, PLRLF, TRMFZBC) are all framed in terms of riverine flood risk.

**Coding:** **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding.**

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes, A few streets, Neighbourhood, Entire community, Sub-watershed, Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Individual Homes** and **Neighbourhood.**

**Narrative:** Buyouts were processed at the individual parcel level — each homeowner submitted their own application, received an individual damage assessment, and was offered a buyout based on their individual property [Sources 2, 3]. However, the buyouts were geographically concentrated in the Pointe Gatineau district and produced a recognisable neighbourhood-scale pattern described as a "swiss-cheese" or "checkerboard" landscape [Sources 1, 2, 3]. The post-buyout planning process (Master Plan/PDA) was designed explicitly at the neighbourhood scale, covering the Pointe Gatineau and Lac-Beauchamp districts [Source 1]. The programme also operated province-wide (affecting 783 municipalities under the ZIS), but the Pointe Gatineau concentration represents the neighbourhood-scale case studied here.

**Coding:** **Individual Homes** (program structure); **Neighbourhood** (geographic concentration of outcomes and post-buyout planning).

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals, Groups/Neighbourhoods, Communities, Critical infrastructure, Hazard protection structures, Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Individuals** (primary); **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (descriptive, by virtue of concentration); some **Commercial** properties also received buyouts.

**Narrative:** The primary retreated population was individual homeowners in Pointe Gatineau who accepted buyout offers and vacated their properties [Sources 2, 3]. Businesses also received buyouts: 56 in Gatineau after 2017 and 27 after 2019 [Source 1, Table 1]. The geographic concentration of buyouts in Pointe Gatineau gives the retreat a neighbourhood-level character, but no coordinated community-wide relocation plan was implemented — households moved individually to destinations of their own choosing [Sources 2, 3]. The reviewed sources document no buyouts for tenants in any cycle [Source 1, Table 1]. The PPTFI allocated $75 million province-wide for municipalities to relocate critical infrastructure in high-risk areas, but this is a provincial-level programme rather than a direct feature of the Pointe Gatineau buyout case [Source 1].

**Coding:** **Individuals** (primary); neighbourhood-scale pattern is descriptive context. **Communities** is not coded, as no coordinated community relocation occurred [Source 3]. Commercial properties were a secondary retreated category.

---

### Other notes (General Information)

The case is notable as one of the few Canadian examples of a provincially funded property buyout programme with explicit managed retreat intent. The comparison case — Constance Bay, Ontario — received no buyout programme despite experiencing nearly identical flood events on the same river, illustrating the critical importance of provincial policy in enabling or foreclosing managed retreat [Sources 2, 3]. Source 4 explicitly notes that the Pointe Gatineau cases were "reactive in nature, relatively small in size and did not involve assisted relocation as part of the managed retreat process."

---

Case study: Pointe-Gatineau Home Buyout Program (Pointe-Gatineau, Quebec, Canada)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat, Community buyout/retreat, Leasebacks/easements/buffers, Other acquisition tools, Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (primary).

**Narrative:** The programme was structured as individual property buyouts — each homeowner applied separately, received an individual damage assessment, and was offered an individual compensation package [Sources 2, 3]. There was no coordinated community-wide resettlement plan or collective relocation process. Source 4 explicitly notes the cases "did not involve assisted relocation as part of the managed retreat process." The scale of buyouts in Pointe Gatineau and the accompanying regulatory restrictions (ZIS) produced de facto neighbourhood-scale effects, and the post-buyout planning process (PDA) was designed at the community level [Source 1]. However, the codebook definition of **Community buyout/retreat** specifies "collective relocation of a neighborhood or settlement through coordinated planning and community engagement" — since no coordinated collective relocation occurred, this code is not applied. The neighbourhood-scale effects are noted as descriptive context only.

Source 1 recommends "leaseback/rentback schemes" as a subject for future research, but no such mechanisms were part of the actual programme.

**Coding:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (primary).

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Multiple legal elements were engaged.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** The Protection Policy for Lakeshores, Riverbanks, Littoral Zones and Floodplains (PLRLF) governed construction in flood zones prior to 2022 [Sources 1, 3]. The ZIS (2019) imposed a moratorium on construction/reconstruction in the 0–20-year floodplain and in areas documented as flooded in 2017 or 2019 [Sources 1, 3]. The PLRLF was replaced in March 2022 by the TRMFZBC, which lifted the ZIS and empowered municipalities to authorise development in flood zones, though in practice it increased procedural burdens [Source 1]. Ontario's Planning Act and Conservation Authorities Act are mentioned in comparative context [Source 3].

- **Legal authority over retreat:** Provincial authority over disaster financial assistance and flood risk management policy is clear; the Ministry of Public Security (MPS) administered the buyout program. However, the decentralised governance structure in Quebec means municipalities bear significant responsibility for implementation, zoning, and land use planning, without always having the technical or financial capacity to do so [Source 1].

- **Home acquisition / Land acquisition:** The buyout programme constituted a formal home and land acquisition process [Sources 1, 3].

- **Title(s) transfer:** The programme stipulated that acquired properties must be demolished and land ownership ceded to the municipality for a nominal sum of $1 [Sources 1, 3].

- **Land rezoning:** Rezoning of retreated lands from residential to recreation/greenspace was planned as part of post-buyout redevelopment; as of the most recent source, this remained partially incomplete [Sources 1, 2].

- **Retreat land development:** Significant legal and regulatory uncertainty surrounds permissible uses of vacant lots, partly because updated provincial flood maps had not been publicly released as of early 2024, leaving municipalities uncertain about permissible development activities. Source 1 quotes a municipal official: "I'm a bit frustrated, because I've got a lot of property in my district, which is underused or not used because of the floods. And the data we're using is old data… we had to submit it to the province first for analysis. And they have not given us the okay to post it yet."

- **Compliance and enforcement:** Concerns were raised about illegal fill being added to occupied properties to raise lot elevations, and informal uses of vacant lots (squatting, garbage dumping). Calls for increased enforcement were noted [Source 1].

- **Litigation:** No explicit litigation is described in the reviewed sources, though significant contestation of the provincial flood maps by municipalities and developers led the province to retract 30 municipalities from the initial flood zone designations [Source 1].

**Coding:** **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Legal authority over retreat**, **Home acquisition**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Land rezoning**, **Retreat land development**, **Compliance and enforcement.** Litigation is not explicitly documented; map contestation fell short of formal legal action based on reviewed sources.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Multiple funders** — **Provincial** (dominant), **Local/Municipal** (supplementary).

**Narrative:** The buyout program was designed, funded, and administered by the Government of Quebec (Ministry of Public Security), making it primarily a **Provincial** funding source [Sources 1, 2, 3]. The City of Gatineau contributed through property tax deferrals, waiving fees, expediting demolition permits, and allocating $1.4 million from city council and councillor discretionary budgets for post-buyout revitalisation [Sources 2, 3]. The PPTFI (2020) allocated $479 million province-wide, including $270 million for municipalities for resilient development and $75 million for critical infrastructure relocation [Source 1].

Federal funding was not directly involved in the Pointe Gatineau buyouts. The reviewed sources note that federal DFAA funding required total provincial damage to exceed $46.2 million; in the Constance Bay comparison case, this threshold was not met [Sources 2, 3]. No evidence of insurance, NGO, or individual funding as primary sources for the buyout program.

**Coding:** **Multiple funders** — **Provincial** (dominant), **Local/Municipal** (supplementary).

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Limited explicit consideration; some discussion of redevelopment of retreat lands as a partial response.

**Narrative:** Municipal officials explicitly acknowledged the fiscal impact. As Source 1 quotes one municipal official: "our tax base has been cut by probably 30%… if we can find a way to offload properties in risky areas whilst trying to increase the tax-base, that'll help." The post-buyout Master Plan (PDA) was partly motivated by the goal of stimulating "local economic growth" through green infrastructure and recreational spaces [Source 1]. One informant mentioned the possibility of transferring small vacant lots to adjacent homeowners (with restrictions), which would offload maintenance costs and generate some property tax revenue [Source 1].

The reviewed sources note that retreat can lead to densification of other areas and sometimes result in homeowners moving from one risk zone to another, but no systematic receiving-area tax base planning was implemented [Sources 1, 2]. No dedicated new-industry, new-housing-for-BO-recipients, or livelihoods-support strategies were documented.

**Coding:** **Redevelopment of retreat lands** (planned but largely unimplemented). The explicit quotation from Source 1 documents awareness of the tax base problem but limited formal strategy to address it. Other tax base categories are not supported by evidence in the reviewed sources.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Administratively capped payments (**Other**), with limited **Free supports and services**.

**Narrative:** Compensation under the 2019 program was capped: Source 3 specifies up to $200,000 for the residence and $50,000 for the land; Source 1 separately refers to compensation "capped at $250,000 for the residence and the land" in the 2019 cycle — both figures appear in the sources and may reflect different stages or components of the 2019 programme. This was increased to $325,000 (residence) and $60,000 (land) in July 2022 [Source 1]. These caps were set administratively and were not indexed to pre-flood market values. Multiple sources note the caps were considered insufficient by some homeowners, particularly those with higher-value or extensively renovated properties [Sources 2, 3]. The average sale price in Pointe Gatineau in July 2019 ranged from $225,000–$300,000 [Source 3], suggesting many properties fell within the compensation range, but some did not.

The compensation structure does not meet the codebook definition of **Market value** (current market price under normal conditions) because the caps are administrative rather than appraisal-based, and may fall below market value for higher-valued properties. It also does not meet **Post-disaster value** (which would typically be lower). The structure is best coded as **Other** (capped administrative payment).

For properties in the ZIS (0–20-year floodplain), participation in the buyout or departure from the zone was effectively required, as rebuilding was prohibited [Sources 1, 3]. The lifetime limit on future disaster assistance ($100,000 maximum for those who refused buyouts) created strong additional pressure [Sources 1, 2, 3].

In terms of free supports: the municipality expedited demolition permits, waived some fees, and deferred property taxes [Sources 2, 3]. Broader supports (moving assistance, relocation advisory services, psychosocial support, help finding new housing) were largely absent [Sources 2, 3].

Eligibility criteria required properties to have sustained flood damage exceeding 50% of replacement cost or $100,000 in cumulative damages [Sources 1, 3]. Many homeowners who wanted to participate were excluded because their damages did not reach the threshold [Sources 2, 3].

**Coding:** **Other** (capped administrative payment — primary); **Free supports and services** (demolition, permit waivers, tax deferrals — limited municipal assistance). **Market value** is not coded given the administratively capped structure. The lifetime disaster assistance cap functioned as a punitive disincentive for non-participation rather than a positive additional incentive — this nuance is noted but does not warrant coding as **Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups** as a primary element.

---

Case study: Pointe-Gatineau Home Buyout Program (Pointe-Gatineau, Quebec, Canada)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

---

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Pre-retreat planning** (limited); **Immediate risks (1–5 years)**; **Anticipated future risks (10–100)**; **Post-retreat follow-up**.

**Narrative:** The programme was primarily reactive and did not involve substantial pre-retreat planning; the initial 2017 and 2019 buyout cycles were developed hastily in the immediate post-disaster period [Sources 2, 3]. The ZIS addressed immediate reconstruction risk in the 0–20-year floodplain. The lifetime limit on disaster assistance addressed the immediate near-term risk of repeat flooding [Sources 1, 3].

The post-buyout Master Plan (PDA) reflects a longer planning horizon, addressing medium-to-long-term land uses and flood risk reduction [Source 1]. The province's planned release of new flood maps — potentially classifying up to 55,000 additional homes in four categories of flood risk — points to consideration of a 10–100-year anticipated risk horizon [Source 1]. The province also committed to a new regulatory framework (OPI) governing modifications to flood protection structures [Source 1].

Post-retreat follow-up is evidenced by the PDA process, ongoing land use planning, and monitoring of vacant lots [Sources 1, 2].

**Coding:** **Pre-retreat planning** (limited, largely absent from initial buyout cycles but present in PDA); **Immediate risks (1–5 years)** (ZIS, buyout programme); **Anticipated future risks (10–100)** (planned flood maps, new regulatory framework); **Post-retreat follow-up** (PDA, ongoing land use planning).

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Multiple elements, with a predominantly top-down and reactive initial programme, and more participatory post-buyout planning.

**Narrative:**

- **Top-down:** The buyout programme was designed and mandated by the provincial government with limited community input during initial design [Sources 2, 3]. Source 3 explicitly states: "The managed retreat process evident in Pointe Gatineau can be described as a formal, top-down, ad hoc process."
- **Participatory/collaborative:** The post-buyout Master Plan (PDA) was designed with "an inclusive, iterative and participatory approach" using multiple consultation tools (postal flyers, newspapers, social media, online surveys, Zoom meetings, community information panels) [Source 1]. This applies to the PDA phase, not the initial buyout programme.
- **Coordination with other sectors and jurisdictions:** Significant intergovernmental tension and fragmentation between provincial and municipal levels was documented; nonetheless, the PPTFI sought coordination across ministries and levels [Source 1]. Ontario's policies were separate [Sources 2, 3].
- **Multi-stage retreat:** The programme operated in two stages (2017 and 2019 flood cycles), with post-buyout planning as a third phase [Sources 1, 2, 3].
- **Degree of transparency:** Buyout programme — limited transparency; critics noted lack of transparency about eligibility criteria, timelines, and compensation calculations [Sources 2, 3]. PDA process — stronger community engagement [Source 1].
- **Adaptive management:** The programme evolved between 2017 and 2022 (compensation caps raised, ZIS boundaries revised, TRMFZBC replacing PLRLF) — suggesting iterative policy development [Source 1].
- **Bureaucracy reduction:** Multiple sources criticise excessive bureaucracy; some simplifications were introduced (online application portal, expedited demolition permits) [Sources 1, 2, 3].

Case study: Hambantota Post-Tsunami Relocation (Hambantota, Sri Lanka)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

### Case Name and Location

Post-Tsunami Community Resettlement in Sri Lanka, with primary case material drawn from the Siribopura Resettlement Housing Program in Hambantota District, and supplementary coverage of resettlement sites in Ampara, Galle (Akmeemana), and Matara Districts. Sri Lanka, South Asia (Global South).

### Hazard(s)

The primary hazard driving relocation was the Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26 December 2004, a catastrophic coastal event. The tsunami affected nearly 65% of Sri Lanka's coastline (about 1,000 km), killed over 30,000 people, and displaced more than 500,000 people [1, 2]. Destruction of housing was the largest single category of physical damage [2].

### Type of Retreat

The retreat took the form of a mandatory, government-directed community resettlement away from a declared coastal buffer zone (initially 100–200 m, later revised to 55–100 m). Displaced households within the buffer zone were relocated to donor-built permanent housing in new inland settlement sites under a "donor-driven" model. An alternative "Owner-Driven Reconstruction" (ODR) program allowed households outside the buffer zone to rebuild in place with financial assistance.

### Scale

Initial estimates suggested approximately 50,000 families would need relocation; following policy revision after the November 2005 election, the no-building zone was reduced from 100–200 m to 55–100 m, lowering the estimated relocation requirement to approximately 30,000 households [1]. This translated to 29,830 housing units in relocated sites across affected districts [1]. By the middle of 2005, THRU had finalised plans to build 485 housing projects in 11 districts [2]. In Hambantota District, the Siribopura site accommodated 1,083 tsunami-affected households, along with others displaced for different reasons [3, 6]. Across the country, approximately 4,643 units were required in Hambantota's relocation sites (against a housing requirement of only 1,057 per initial TAFREN estimates), while Ampara required approximately 3,721 units [1].

### Key Actors

- **Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL)**: Set policy, declared buffer zones, established institutional mechanisms, and coordinated land acquisition and beneficiary selection through Divisional Secretariats.
- **Task Force for Rebuilding the Nation (TAFREN)** and **Tsunami Housing Reconstruction Unit (THRU)**: Primary initial coordinating bodies, both dissolved in November 2005 [2].
- **Reconstruction and Development Agency (RADA)**: Successor coordination body, created in November 2005 [1, 2].
- **Urban Development Authority (UDA)**: Responsible for layout preparation, guidelines, and coordination of permanent housing sites.
- **National Housing Development Authority (NHDA)**: Issued housing and planning guidelines.
- **International and domestic donor agencies and NGOs**: Constructed housing under the donor-driven model (Suchi Foundation, Singapore Red Cross, Sajith Foundation, Suboda Foundation, Care International, and others) [6].
- **Ports Authority of Sri Lanka**: Managed compensation for harbour development-related displacement in Hambantota, separate from the tsunami resettlement program [6].
- **University of Moratuwa**: Conducted the 2006 Rapid Environmental Assessment (REA) of 409 housing sites [2].
- **Affected communities**: Had limited and largely nominal involvement in planning; in practice, their preferences were often not reflected in final site allocations [1, 2, 5].

### Timeline

- **26 December 2004**: Tsunami strikes; government declares buffer zones (100–200 m).
- **Early 2005**: TAFREN and THRU established; donor-driven reconstruction begins; buffer zone at 100–200 m.
- **2005–2006**: Owner-driven reconstruction proceeds more rapidly and cost-effectively than donor-driven construction.
- **November 2005**: TAFREN and THRU dissolved; RADA created as successor coordination agency [1, 2].
- **After November 2005 election**: No-building zone revised from 100–200 m to 55–100 m, reducing estimated households requiring relocation to approximately 30,000 [1].
- **2005–2008**: Donor-built housing units progressively completed and handed over (Hambantota ahead of schedule; Ampara severely delayed).
- **2006**: University of Moratuwa REA of 409 sites conducted, though construction was already underway at most sites by that time [2].
- **2007/2008**: Harbour development-induced resettlement in Hambantota; Ports Authority compensation program implemented for 454 households [6].
- **2008–2009**: World Habitat Research Center (WHRC) study of relocation outcomes conducted in Ampara and Hambantota [1].
- **2011**: Primary surveys in Siribopura and Hambantota for land market and success/failure analyses [3, 6].
- **2016**: Household surveys conducted for long-term satisfaction study covering 12 sites in Galle, Matara, and Hambantota [2].
- **Status**: Post-retreat; follow-up studies confirm persistent dissatisfaction and unresolved land tenure issues more than a decade after the event.

### Key Outcomes

Outcomes were mixed and varied significantly by district and site. Hambantota benefited from disproportionate donor interest and political attention, as it was the native district of Sri Lanka's president at the time of the tsunami [1]. This resulted in far more housing being built than was required by tsunami-affected households; many units were distributed to non-tsunami-affected households through political patronage [1]. Ampara's reconstruction was severely delayed and constrained by ethnic conflict and LTTE activity [1, 4].

Physical housing quality varied substantially by district and site: Hambantota houses were generally assessed as satisfactory, while Ampara included several sites with poor construction and inadequate infrastructure [1]. Across all three southern districts studied by Manatunge et al. [2], construction defects, inappropriate designs, poor ventilation, and inadequate infrastructure were common.

Land tenure remained unresolved for the majority of resettlers for years after occupancy. In the Hambantota Siribopura sites, as of 2011, only 38 of the 1,083 tsunami-affected resettled households had received formal title deeds (free grants), while the majority possessed only informal letters from donor agencies [3]. This created informal land markets, barriers to credit, and ongoing tenure insecurity.

Livelihood disruption was severe, particularly for fishing communities relocated far from the coast. Women's livelihoods were disproportionately disrupted [1]. Community participation in planning was limited to nominal or token processes at best, and was identified across multiple sources as a primary cause of dissatisfaction [2, 5]. Long-term satisfaction surveys more than a decade after the tsunami confirmed widespread dissatisfaction across most sites [2].

### Narrative Summary

On 26 December 2004, the Indian Ocean Tsunami devastated Sri Lanka's coastline, killing over 30,000 people and displacing more than 500,000. The government's immediate response was to declare coastal buffer zones (initially 100–200 m from the sea) where no reconstruction would be permitted, requiring the relocation of approximately 50,000 households. This policy was announced in a context of "profound emotion" [1], without pre-existing legal or institutional frameworks for disaster-induced resettlement, and under enormous pressure from international donors and political actors to move quickly. There were no pre-existing policy frameworks or institutional arrangements readily available for post-tsunami resettlement [2]. Following a change in government in November 2005, the buffer zone was reduced to 55–100 m, reducing the relocation requirement to approximately 30,000 households. The scale of international aid flowing into the country was unprecedented, but so were the coordination failures.

For those within the buffer zone, the government and a large array of international and domestic NGOs constructed new housing in inland resettlement sites—a "donor-driven" model in which houses were planned and built by external agencies and then allocated to beneficiaries. Affected communities had limited and largely nominal involvement in planning; in practice, their preferences were often not reflected in final site allocations [1, 5]. People from different villages were placed in the same new settlements, breaking social networks. Sites were frequently located in unsuitable terrain—waterlogged, hilly, or remote—far from original livelihoods, especially fishing harbours and markets [1, 2]. Physical construction quality was often problematic, with cracked walls, collapsed roofs, inadequate ventilation and sanitation, and absent common spaces in many sites [2]. Most resettlers did not receive formal legal title to their land for years, leaving them unable to access formal credit and vulnerable to informal land market exploitation [3, 6].

Outcomes varied sharply by district. Hambantota received more housing than it needed, with political interference channelling units to non-tsunami-affected households. Ampara, affected by both the tsunami and civil conflict, saw severe reconstruction delays, with housing inequitably distributed across ethnic lines. For resettlers across the studied districts, incomes generally declined, expenditures rose, and women's livelihoods were particularly disrupted [1]. Studies conducted more than a decade later confirm that many resettlers remain dissatisfied, houses have been abandoned or sold informally, and the social and economic rehabilitation promised at the outset has largely not been achieved [2, 3, 6]. The case stands as a cautionary example of reactive, top-down, politically influenced disaster resettlement conducted without adequate community participation, planning, or attention to livelihood sustainability.
